# **Introduction**

I have been saying for years that class-and-level games do not work for superheroes.

Not "don't work for me." Not "I prefer something else." Flat-out do not work. Superheroes have always felt too broad, too weird, too personal, and too explosive to fit comfortably into rigid progression structures. A guy with a magic hammer, a woman who controls gravity, a billionaire inventor, a cosmic telepath, and a masked martial artist — all sharing the same advancement philosophy? I never bought it.

So naturally, I decided to challenge myself.

HEROIC 5e exists because I wanted to find out if I was wrong.

For years I have heard people say that 5e is "basically fantasy superheroes anyway," and honestly, I understand why. Modern fantasy heroes are larger than life. They leap across rooftops, survive impossible punishment, throw fire, battle gods, and reshape the world around them. The DNA overlap is obvious. But there is a difference between something that feels superheroic and actually building a superhero game from the ground up. Those are two very different things.

That became the experiment.

Could a class-and-level structure actually capture what it feels like to play comic-book heroes? Could it handle street vigilantes, armored inventors, cosmic champions, speedsters, psychics, martial artists, monsters, and paragons — without collapsing under its own weight? Could it still feel fast, cinematic, and distinctly superheroic rather than fantasy with the serial numbers filed off?

I think the answer is yes. At least, I think I proved myself wrong.

The final judgment belongs to you — the players sitting around the table. You are the ones who will test this thing in motion. You will discover whether the system sings when the dice hit and the city starts burning.

What I can tell you is that this game comes from a lifetime love of superheroes. Not the genre in the abstract, but specifically the eras that shaped me. Bronze Age comics. Big action. Strange science. Cosmic madness sitting right beside street-level grit. Heroes who could save the universe one month and get punched in the mouth in an alley the next. I have spent years discussing superhero RPGs on panels, podcasts, livestreams, and my YouTube channel. I have written and designed other superhero games before this one, including projects inspired by classics like the old Marvel FASERIP system. Superhero roleplaying has been part of my creative life for a long time, and I care deeply about what makes these games work — and what makes them fail.

HEROIC 5e is my response to all of that.

This is me stepping into the ring with my own opinions and seeing whether I could build the kind of superhero game I always claimed could not exist.

## **What This Game Is**

HEROIC 5e is not a simulation of comic books. It is a roleplaying game about superheroes. That distinction matters more than it may initially seem.

Comic books are carefully constructed illusions. They are built through the collaboration of writers, artists, editors, colorists, and continuity departments, backed by decades of evolving narrative shorthand. A comic can pause time for a dramatic splash page. A hero survives impossible punishment because the story demands it. A villain escapes because the next arc requires it. Entire scenes exist because the writer already knew the ending before the first panel was drawn.

A roleplaying game does not work that way.

In a roleplaying game, the story is alive while it is happening. Players are not readers turning pages — they are participants making choices in real time, often without certainty, perfect information, or narrative safety nets. The GM is not an editorial department overseeing continuity from above. They are reacting, adapting, improvising, and building the world alongside the players moment by moment. Dice create uncertainty. Consequences emerge naturally. Victories are earned rather than scripted.

Superhero roleplaying requires a different design philosophy than trying to faithfully reproduce comics. Attempting to perfectly emulate the source material often leads to systems that either collapse under their own contradictions or become so narratively rigid that player agency starts to disappear. And superhero comics are *deeply* inconsistent by nature — strength levels fluctuate, powers expand or contract depending on the writer, characters survive impossible odds one month and get hurt by ordinary threats the next. These inconsistencies work in serialized fiction because audiences accept the language of comics instinctively. Games need structure. Games need trust between mechanics and outcomes. Games need players to understand what their choices mean.

So HEROIC 5e approaches the genre from a different angle.

Rather than asking *how do we perfectly simulate comic books*, the game asks *how do we create exciting, dramatic, fast-moving superhero action at the table*. That question shapes every part of the design.

The mechanics lean into superhero tropes because those tropes are the language of the genre. Heroes throw cars. Villains monologue. Teams combine their powers in desperate moments. Secret identities matter. Mobility matters. Momentum matters. Spectacle matters. HEROIC 5e embraces all of that — but those elements are translated into mechanics built for playability, clarity, and player empowerment rather than strict comic-book accuracy.

A superhero comic can spend three pages on a single punch. A roleplaying game cannot survive if every attack takes fifteen minutes to resolve. A comic can decide retroactively that a hero had the exact gadget needed all along. A game needs rules that players can interact with fairly. A comic can bend physics because the audience only observes — a game must account for the fact that players will test boundaries, improvise solutions, and attempt things the designers never anticipated.

That is where the real magic of superhero roleplaying lives.

Not in reproducing panels exactly as they appear on the page, but in creating the *feeling* of being superheroes together. The impossible rescue. The desperate last stand. The rooftop confrontation during a thunderstorm. The split-second teamwork that saves a city. The collateral damage nobody wanted. The sacrifice. The triumph that nobody saw coming.

Those moments do not emerge from scripted narrative control. They emerge from play.

HEROIC 5e is built to support that kind of play. Dynamic action, meaningful teamwork, dramatic escalation, cinematic heroism — and a system real people can actually run at a real table.

Because superheroes are not interesting simply because they exist in comics. They are interesting because they struggle, fail, grow, inspire, and endure.

That is exactly the kind of story tabletop roleplaying games are uniquely suited to tell.

## **How This Book Is Organized**

HEROIC 5e opens with a **Glossary** — every mechanical term defined before you encounter it in the rules. You should never have to stop mid-read because a word hasn't been explained yet.

* **Chapter 1: The Basics** covers the eight Ability Scores, how dice and degrees of success work, and Campaign Rank — the table's decision about the scale of the campaign before a single character is built.  
    
* **Chapter 2: Character Creation** walks through the full hero-building process from concept to completed sheet, including a fully worked example.  
    
* **Chapters 3 through 13** cover each character layer in depth: Origins, Sides, Callings, Classes, Talents, Skills, Merits and Flaws, Powers, and Equipment & Gear.  
    
* **Chapter 14: Playing the Game** covers the Core Reference, Edge, Response, and Advancement — the systems that govern how heroes grow, how the world reacts to them, and how size functions mechanically in play.  
    
* **Chapter 15: Combat** covers the full combat system, including Grid and VTT rules for groups using battle maps or virtual tabletops.  
    
* **Chapter 16** gives the GM the tools to build encounters, villains, and campaigns that feel like superhero fiction.  
    
* **Chapter 17** provides the Opponents chapter — five scalable tiers of opposition built for fast use at the table.  
    
* **Chapter 18** provides thirty Ready to Play Templates — complete Level 1 heroes across all three Campaign Ranks, ready to hand to a player and start playing immediately.  
    
* **Chapter 19** closes out with Random Adventure Generation for when you sit down with nothing prepared and need a session worth running.

If you are a player, start with Chapter 1 and work through Character Creation. If you are a GM running your first session tonight, read the Introduction, skim Character Creation, then go straight to Chapter 15: Combat. Everything you need for a first fight is there.

## **A Note on the Playtest**

This is a playtest document. It is complete enough to run and designed to be played — but it is also a draft, and your table's experience at the table is the point. Where something does not work, we want to know. Where something *does* work — where the dice hit and something surprising and cinematic happens — we want to know that too.

Play it. Break it. Tell us what you find.

Above all else…

BE HEROIC\!

# **Glossary**

---

**A**

**Ability Score** — One of eight numerical values that define a hero's fundamental capabilities: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Fighting, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma, and Perception.

**Ability Score Improvement (ASI Pick)** — An advancement option that allows a hero to improve Ability Scores or modify Merits and Flaws. *See also: ASI Pick.*

**Action** — The primary activity a character performs on their Turn.

**Action Scene** — A scene type in which time is measured in Turns and the full action economy applies.

**Active Defense** — The defensive roll a hero makes when targeted by an attack. Four types exist: Parry/Block, Dodge, Willpower, and Social.

**Advantage** — A positive roll modifier representing favorable circumstances.

**Advancement Table** — The level-by-level chart showing what a hero gains at each level from 1 to 10\.

**Apex Power** — The capstone power within a Power Set's Core Track, available only to World Class heroes.

**ASI Pick** — *See: Ability Score Improvement.*

**At-Will Power** — A Power available every Turn without limit.

**Attack Roll** — A roll made to determine whether an offensive action connects.  
**Attack Value** — The static number representing an NPC or enemy's attack capability.

---

**B**

**Banished** — A condition in which a creature has been removed from the current plane, dimension, or reality and cannot act until it returns.

**Beacon** — A character Class defined by Charisma as its primary Attribute and Wisdom as its secondary.

**Blinded** — A condition in which a creature cannot see.

**Blindsight** — A form of perception that detects the position and shape of creatures and objects without relying on sight.

**Bloodied** — A rules state indicating a character is at or below half their maximum HP.

**Bonus Action** — A secondary activity available on a character's Turn.

**Bonus HP** — Additional Hit Points a GM adds to an NPC to extend its role in an encounter beyond what its tier alone would provide.

**Boss** — A special designation for the most dramatically important enemy in an encounter.

**Branch Power** — A specific ability within a Power Set.

**Breather** — A brief recovery pause between action sequences.

**Bruiser** — A character Class defined by Strength as its primary Attribute and Constitution as its secondary.

**Burning** — A condition representing ongoing fire damage.

**Burnout** — A cumulative penalty representing a hero pushing beyond their limits.

---

**Burnout Check** — The roll a hero makes when pushing a Power beyond its safe limits, determining whether the strain takes hold.

**C**

**Calling** — A hero's defining motivational drive, expressed through three Edge Triggers: Minor, Major, and Defining.

**Campaign Rank Multiplier** — The number by which a hero's Constitution score and Hit Die are multiplied when Starting Hit Points are calculated, determined by Campaign Rank.

**Campaign Rank** — A table-wide setting defining the scale of play. Three ranks exist: Street Level, Mid-Level, and World Class. Campaign Rank is not a character stat.

**Campaign-Scale** — A qualifier indicating a Power or effect that operates beyond the scope of a single scene or encounter.

**CHA** — Abbreviation for Charisma. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Charisma score, not the score itself.

**Charisma** — An Ability Score measuring force of personality, leadership, and social magnetism.

**Charmed** — A condition in which a creature's attitude or behavior has been altered by an outside influence rather than its own judgment.

**Class** — One of eight archetypes defining how a hero instinctively acts under pressure.

**Class Capstone** — The final Class Feature, gained at Level 10\.

**Class Effect Value** — The difficulty number enemies must beat to resist a hero's Class feature effects.

**Close Range** — The nearest range band, covering the same Zone as the attacker.

**Collateral Damage** — The incidental destruction resulting from superhero combat, tracked narratively.

**Complexity** — The rating that sets how many successes a HEROIC Challenge requires.

**CON** — Abbreviation for Constitution. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Constitution score, not the score itself.

**Condition** — A temporary game state applying specific penalties or restrictions to a character.

**Condition Cap** — A Boss rule limiting the number of different Conditions that can affect a Boss simultaneously.

**Constitution** — An Ability Score measuring endurance, toughness, and stamina.

**Core Formula** — The foundational resolution mechanic used throughout the game.

**Core Reference** — The single page in Chapter 14 on which every core formula in the game is printed. Where any other passage disagrees with it, the Core Reference is correct.

**Core Track** — The structured step-by-step progression within a Power Set.

**Cover** — Physical obstruction that improves a defender's Active Defense.

**Critical Hit** — The result of a natural 20 on an attack roll.

---

**D**

**Daily Power** — A Power available once per day, refreshing only on Downtime.

**Damage Source** — The origin category of an instance of damage, distinct from its Damage Type. Mundane, Technological, Powered, Mystical, Cosmic, and Environmental are the six.

**Dash** — An Action option that increases movement.

**Dazed** — A condition representing disrupted focus.

**Deafened** — A condition representing inability to hear.  
**Defense Value** — The static number representing a target's passive resilience when they cannot roll. For NPCs and enemies, this replaces the rolled Active Defense.

**Degrees of Success** — A system for measuring how well a roll succeeds, based on margin. Three tiers exist: Success, Strong Success, and HEROIC Success.

**DEX** — Abbreviation for Dexterity. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Dexterity score, not the score itself.

**Dexterity** — An Ability Score measuring agility, coordination, accuracy, and fine motor control.

**Darkvision** — The ability to see in total darkness as though in dim light.

**Difficulty Class (DC)** — The target number a Skill check must meet or beat to succeed.

**Difficult Zone** — A Zone containing terrain that impedes movement.

**Disadvantage** — A negative roll modifier representing unfavorable circumstances.

**Disengage** — An Action option that allows a character to move away from an enemy without provoking an Opportunity Attack.

**Dodge** — One of the four Active Defense types, used against ranged and area attacks.

**Downtime** — The recovery period between major story beats.

**Downtime Scene** — A scene type covering recovery, training, and preparation between major story beats.

---

**E**

**Edge** — HEROIC 5e's heroic currency representing dramatic momentum, effort, and determination.

**Edge Trigger** — A specific moment during play when a Calling fires and the player earns Edge.

**Effect Value** — The static difficulty number a target must overcome to resist a hero's Power or Class feature.

**Encounter** — A structured engagement with a defined resolution condition.

**Encounter Power** — A Power available once per encounter.

**Enhancement** — A small improvement to a Power, Utility, or Core Track step the hero already possesses.

**Enhancement Power Set** — A Power Set that directly enhances a hero's core capability.

**Evade** — An Action option devoted entirely to avoiding incoming attacks.

**Expertise** — A level of Skill mastery above standard training.

**Extreme Range** — The farthest range band.

---

**F**

**Failure Threshold** — The number of failures that ends a HEROIC Challenge unsuccessfully.

**Falling** — Uncontrolled descent through the air, and the damage it causes on landing.

**FIG** — Abbreviation for Fighting. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Fighting score, not the score itself.

**Fighting** — An Ability Score measuring close-combat skill, martial instinct, and accuracy in melee.

**Flat Damage Reduction** — A fixed amount subtracted from incoming damage before HP loss is applied.

**Flaw** — A character element representing a story-facing complication, obligation, or limitation.

**Frightened** — A condition representing fear of a specific source.

**Frozen** — A condition representing a character encased or immobilized by ice or a similar effect.

---

**G**

**Gear** — The physical equipment a hero carries.

**Gear Dependent** — A Limitation and Flaw indicating a hero's Powers require a removable physical object.

**Gliding** — A Utility Power allowing controlled descent through the air using wings, a cape, or similar surfaces.

**Goon** — The middle Minion tier.

**Governing Ability** — The Ability Score that drives a Power Set's attack rolls and Effect Values.

**Grappled** — A condition representing being physically seized and held.

**Grit Save** — A roll made at the start of each Turn while a hero is at 0 HP.

**Guardian** — A character Class defined by Constitution as its primary Attribute and Strength as its secondary.

---

**H**

**Help** — An Action option used to assist an ally or to set up a Team Combo.

**HEROIC Challenge** — An optional extended-action subsystem in which a group accumulates successes against a Failure Threshold to resolve a complex undertaking.

**HEROIC Effect** — A scene-defining consequence available on a HEROIC Success.

**HEROIC Success** — A degree of success achieved by beating the target number by 10 or more.

**Hidden** — A condition in which a creature's position is unknown to those it is concealed from.

**Hide** — An Action option used to become Hidden.

**Hit** — The unit by which Minions absorb damage.

**Hit Die** — The die type representing a hero's resilience and recovery potential, determined by Class.

**Hit Points (HP)** — A numerical measure of a hero's remaining capacity to sustain punishment.

---

**I**

**Immobilized** — A condition representing complete prevention of movement.

**Immunity** — A property that prevents incoming damage of a specific type entirely.

**Incapacitated** — A condition in which a creature can take no Actions, Bonus Actions, or Reactions.

**Initiative** — The roll that determines Turn order at the start of combat.

**Injured** — A condition representing a specific physical impairment.

**INT** — Abbreviation for Intelligence. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Intelligence score, not the score itself.

**Intelligence** — An Ability Score measuring reasoning, technical understanding, logic, and memory.

**Investigation and Social Scene** — A scene type covering situations where the stakes are information, reputation, or relationship.

---

**K**

**Killing Blow** — A deliberate lethal attack made against a Defeated character. Always a choice, never an accident.

**Kitbashing** — Improvised invention under pressure using available materials mid-scene.

---

**L**

**Lethal** — A tag marking a weapon, Power, or NPC attack as carrying genuine death risk.

**Lethal Save** — The save a hero makes at 0 HP in place of a Grit Save when downed by a Lethal source.

**Level** — A measure of how experienced and developed a hero is, running from 1 to 10\.

**Lieutenant** — The highest Minion tier.

**Limitation** — A chosen drawback applied to a Power Set that grants an additional Power Pick.

**Long Range** — A range band covering the far end of a typical battlefield.

---

**M**

**Medium Range** — A range band covering mid-battlefield distances.

**Merit** — A character element representing a story-facing advantage, resource, or beneficial circumstance.

**Mid-Level** — The middle Campaign Rank.

**Minion** — A category of enemy tracked by hits rather than HP. Three tiers exist: Thugs, Goons, and Lieutenants.

**Modifier** — The number derived from an Ability Score and added to rolls.

**Momentum Effect** — A short cinematic consequence created by exceptional success.

**Mortal Wound** — A lasting consequence suffered by a hero who survives a Killing Blow.

**Multiclassing** — Taking levels in a second Class within the ten-level structure.

---

**N**

**Natural 1** — A result of 1 on the d20 before modifiers.

**Natural 20** — A result of 20 on the d20 before modifiers.

**Notice** — The Skill governing awareness, spotting danger, and vigilance. Governed by Perception (PER).

**NPC** — A non-player character controlled by the GM.

---

**O**

**Opportunity Attack** — A Reaction triggered when a creature moves in a way that exposes them to a nearby combatant.

**Origin** — The foundational layer of a hero answering where their exceptional nature comes from.

**Origin Talent** — A Talent granted automatically by a hero's Origin at character creation.

**Overkill** — A single hit that deals damage equal to or exceeding twice the target's maximum HP.

**Overloaded** — A condition representing temporary disruption of technological systems, armor, or Powers.

---

**P**

**Paralyzed** — A condition representing complete physical incapacitation.

**Parry/Block** — One of the four Active Defense types, used against melee attacks and physical strikes.

**Passive Power** — A Power that is always active, requiring no action or declaration.

**PER** — Abbreviation for Perception. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Perception score, not the score itself.

**Perception** — An Ability Score measuring awareness, sensory sharpness, and vigilance.

**Pinned** — A condition representing being simultaneously held and brought to the ground.

**Poisoned** — A condition representing the effect of a toxin or venom.

**Power** — What a hero can do that no ordinary human can.

**Power Die** — The die used to roll damage or healing for Powers, with size determined by Campaign Rank.

**Power Disrupted** — A condition representing temporary loss of access to a specific Power Set or Power type.

**Power Effect Value** — The difficulty number enemies must beat to resist a hero's Power specifically.

**Power Pick** — The currency used to purchase Powers, gained at character creation and through advancement.

**Power Set** — A family of related abilities organized around a theme or capability.

**Power Stunt** — An improvised use of one of the hero's existing Power Sets.

**Power Stunt: Emulation** — A high-risk Power Stunt allowing a hero to reach for an unpurchased ability within an owned Power Set.

**Power Tier** — The measure of an NPC's raw capability, which determines its Tier Bonus, Power Die, and Hit Point multiplier. Five exist: Day Player, Low Power, Medium Power, High Power, and Cosmic Power.

**Prone** — A condition representing a character on the ground.

**Prowess (PRO)** — The flat bonus representing overall heroic competence, added to attacks, defenses, trained skills, and Class features. Scales with level.

---

**R**

**Reaction** — An action taken in response to a trigger, outside of a character's normal Turn.

**Recovery** — The Action taken during a Breather to restore HP.

**Recovery Modifier** — The class-specific bonus added to Hit Die rolls made during Recovery or Second Wind.

**Resist Defeat** — An Edge expenditure that keeps a hero standing when they would otherwise be Defeated.

**Resistance** — A property that reduces incoming damage of a specific type.

**Resolve** — A Boss rule allowing it to shrug off a condition or effect once per encounter.

**Respec** — Short for *re-specialization*. A voluntary character rebuild allowing a hero to change mechanical choices outside of Origin, Class, and Ability Scores.

**Response** — A scene-level measure of how an NPC, crowd, or faction currently regards a hero or team.

**Restrained** — A condition in which a creature is physically bound or held in place.

**Round** — A complete cycle of all characters' Turns in initiative order.

---

**S**

**Save** — A roll made when a hero resists something dangerous that bypasses Active Defense.

**Save Expertise** — A level of save training above trained, representing mastery of a particular kind of resistance.

**Save Training** — A class benefit representing innate resistance to certain types of threats.

**Save Value** — An NPC's static resistance to an effect.

**Search** — An Action option devoted to actively looking for something.

**Second Wind** — A once-per-encounter ability allowing a hero to recover under pressure.

**Secondary Attack** — Any attack made beyond the first on a Turn, whether granted by a feature, a Reaction, or an ally.

**Sentinel** — A character Class defined by Perception as its primary Attribute and Dexterity as its secondary.

**Settle** — A Momentum Effect that clears a minor condition from an ally.

**Shaken** — A condition representing momentary loss of nerve or composure.

**Short Range** — A range band covering adjacent Zones.

**Side** — A character's declared narrative position: Heroic, Unaligned, or Villainous.

**Size Bonus Die** — An additional damage die granted to creatures of Large size or greater.

**Skill** — A broad area of learned competency separate from Ability Scores and Powers.

**Skill Check** — A roll covering trained and natural competency outside of attacks and saves.

**Slowed** — A condition representing impaired movement.

**Social Active Defense** — One of the four Active Defense types, used against manipulation, intimidation, and social pressure.

**Specialty** — Focused expertise within a broader Skill.

**Speed** — The distance a character can cover with their movement on their Turn. Every character has the same base Speed unless a Power, Talent, or Class feature changes it.

**Speed Action** — An additional Action granted by certain movement-based Powers, usable only for movement or for the specific purposes the Power names.

**STR** — Abbreviation for Strength. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Strength score, not the score itself.

**Strength** — An Ability Score measuring raw physical power, lifting capacity, and brute force.

**Street Level** — The lowest Campaign Rank.

**Strategist** — A character Class defined by Intelligence as its primary Attribute and Perception as its secondary.

**Striker** — A character Class defined by Fighting as its primary Attribute and Dexterity as its secondary.

**Strong Success** — A degree of success achieved by beating the target number by 5 or more.

**Stunned** — A condition representing severe physical or mental shock.

**Surprise** — A state at the start of combat when a creature is caught unaware.

**Swinging** — A Utility Power allowing movement between anchor points on webbing, lines, or cables.

**Sustained Power** — A Power that remains active as long as the hero maintains it.

---

**T**

**Talent** — HEROIC 5e's equivalent of Feats — trained heroic edges and signature techniques that differentiate heroes of the same class and powers.

**Team Combo** — A coordinated action between two or more heroes, fueled by Edge.

**Temporary HP** — A buffer of Hit Points that absorbs damage before permanent HP is affected.

**Thug** — The lowest Minion tier.

**Tier** — The relative power level of a Branch Power or Core Track step.

**Tier Bonus** — The flat competence bonus applied to an NPC's attack, defense, save, and effect numbers, determined by its Power Tier. The NPC counterpart to a hero's Prowess.

**Turn** — A character's segment of action within an initiative Round.

---

**U**

**Unaligned** — A Side representing characters who operate according to their own internal logic rather than conventional heroic or villainous expectations.

**Unconscious** — A condition representing complete loss of awareness and physical control.

**Use an Object** — An Action option covering interaction with equipment, terrain, and scene elements.

**Utility Power** — A noncombat Branch Power providing movement, sensory, or support capabilities.

---

**V**

**Vanguard** — A character Class defined by Dexterity as its primary Attribute and Perception as its secondary.

**Vertical Range** — Distance measured upward or downward, using the same range bands as horizontal distance.

**Vigilance** — A hero's passive awareness threshold, always active and requiring no action.

**Vulnerability** — A property that increases incoming damage of a specific type.

---

**W**

**Warden** — A character Class defined by Wisdom as its primary Attribute and Constitution as its secondary.

**WIS** — Abbreviation for Wisdom. When abbreviated, refers to the modifier derived from the Wisdom score, not the score itself.

**Willpower** — One of the four Active Defense types, used against psychic attacks, magic, and supernatural assault.

**Wisdom** — An Ability Score measuring judgment, intuition, discipline, and emotional balance. Intentionally distinct from Perception.

**World Class** — The highest Campaign Rank.

---

**Z**

**Zone** — A defined area of the battlefield used to measure movement and range.

Eight Ability Scores. How dice work. Degrees of Success. Campaign Rank. Everything you need before you build a hero.

This Chapter Covers

* The Eight Ability Scores  
* Why Fighting & Perception  
* Score & Modifier Reference
