## **The Eight Ability Scores**

Every hero in HEROIC 5e is defined, at the most fundamental level, by eight numbers.

Not their powers. Not their costume. Not their origin story. Those things matter enormously, but before any of them enter the picture, there are eight Ability Scores that describe the person underneath. Their raw capability, their conditioning, their instincts, their presence. The baseline of what they are before the extraordinary begins.

Ability Scores are not powers. A hero with Super Strength can lift a tank because of a power, but their Strength score still reflects bodily leverage, physical conditioning, and muscular force. A genius inventor's Intelligence score reflects how they think, not what they have built. A razor-sharp detective's Perception score reflects their awareness, not their wisdom or their gadgets. The score is always the person. Everything built on top of it is the hero.

Design Note

#### **Why Eight?**

Most d20 games use six Ability Scores. HEROIC 5e uses eight, and two of those additions — **Fighting** and **Perception** — are deliberate genre-specific decisions that carry weight throughout every part of the game.

**Fighting** exists because raw strength and combat skill are not the same thing. A powerhouse who can throw a car is not automatically accurate in a fight. A gymnast with exceptional agility is not automatically a skilled striker. Standard fantasy systems tie combat accuracy to Strength or Dexterity, which breaks down almost immediately in superhero fiction. Fighting solves this — measuring martial instinct, technique, accuracy in close quarters, and tactical timing separately from physical power or agility. Fighting governs melee. Ranged accuracy belongs to Dexterity.

**Perception** exists because awareness and wisdom are genuinely different capabilities, and superhero fiction makes that difference visible constantly. A hyper-aware detective who spots a sniper's laser dot from across a rooftop does not need to be a person of deep spiritual wisdom. A wise mentor with calm judgment can still fail to notice a threat in their blind spot. Bundling those under Wisdom — as most d20 systems do — forces a tradeoff that doesn't exist in the source material. Perception also carries mechanical weight throughout: every Active Defense roll uses PER as one of its two score modifiers, because noticing a threat is always part of surviving it.

### Reading Score Notation

Convention — Used Throughout This Book

When you see a full Ability Score name — **Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Fighting, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma, Perception** — it refers to the score itself. The raw number written in the box on your sheet.

When you see the abbreviation — **STR, DEX, CON, FIG, INT, WIS, CHA, PER** — it refers to the modifier derived from that score. The number you actually add to rolls.

This distinction matters because some rules call for the score directly and others call for the modifier, and they produce very different results. Starting HP \= (full Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × Campaign Rank \+ Prowess — that rule wants the score, so it spells the name out. Attack rolls, defense rolls, and Effect Values all use abbreviations because they call for the modifier.

When the rule wants the score, it spells the full name out. When it wants the modifier, it abbreviates. No exceptions.

### The Eight Ability Scores

STR

Strength

Force. Not precision, not expertise, not reflex.

Strength measures raw physical power: muscular force, lifting capacity, leverage, grappling ability, and brute impact. Heroes with high Strength overpower opponents physically, force open sealed doors, carry enormous weight, and deliver devastating blows.

Strength governs lifting and carrying, grappling and restraining, breaking objects, feats of raw athletic power, and brute melee force. It does not govern accuracy. Being powerful does not mean knowing how to land an attack. That is Fighting's job.

DEX

Dexterity

Movement refined into instinct.

Dexterity measures agility, coordination, balance, accuracy, and fine motor control: the quality of movement rather than the power behind it.

Dexterity governs acrobatic movement, dodging hazards, stealth, parkour, delicate handwork, land ranged attacks, and evasive maneuvers. It does not represent close-combat skill. A gymnast can be extraordinarily agile without knowing how to hold their own in a brawl. A veteran melee fighter may not be particularly graceful outside of one.

CON

Constitution

Staying power.

Constitution measures endurance, toughness, resilience, stamina, and the ability to keep going when the body wants to stop. In superhero stories, durability takes many forms. Some heroes are biologically enhanced. Others run on iron discipline and the refusal to stay down. Constitution is what all of them share.

Constitution affects Hit Points, resistance to poison and disease, survival in extreme environments, stamina under prolonged strain, and recovery from injury. It is not necessarily about size. A lean endurance runner may have exceptional Constitution while a massive bodybuilder burns out quickly under sustained pressure.

FIG

Fighting

Not about how hard you hit. About whether you know how to fight.

Fighting measures close-combat skill, martial instinct, tactical aggression, and accuracy in melee. It represents martial arts training, combat experience, hand-to-hand precision, melee weapon proficiency, battlefield reflexes, and the ability to read and exploit an opponent in motion. Fighting applies to melee attacks only; ranged accuracy is governed by Dexterity.

A hero with high Fighting understands spacing, momentum, pressure, counters, and timing, regardless of how physically powerful they are. The disciplined martial artist, the street vigilante, the trained soldier, the savage brawler, the expert swordsman: all of them express their competence through Fighting, though what that looks like at the table differs enormously depending on their powers, class, and concept.

INT

Intelligence

The mind applied through logic.

Intelligence measures reasoning, education, technical understanding, logic, memory, and analytical ability. In superhero fiction, Intelligence is frequently a superpower in its own right. Inventors create impossible technology. Detectives unravel impossible mysteries. Scientists push past the edges of human understanding and keep pushing.

Intelligence governs scientific knowledge, investigation and deduction, engineering, hacking, medicine, research, tactical analysis, and puzzle-solving. It is not the same thing as awareness or emotional insight. A brilliant scientist may still walk past an obvious social cue or fail to notice a threat standing directly in front of them.

WIS

Wisdom

Inner balance. Not sharpness — depth.

Wisdom measures judgment, intuition, discipline, emotional balance, and inner understanding. This is the score of the calm center: the hero who maintains control under pressure, who understands consequences and people and themselves, who serves as the psychological anchor of a team.

Wisdom governs intuition, emotional control, meditation, spiritual insight, moral reasoning, empathy, and psychological resilience. HEROIC 5e intentionally separates Wisdom from awareness. A person can be highly perceptive without being emotionally wise, and vice versa. These are different capabilities and they deserve different mechanical weight.

CHA

Charisma

Presence turned outward.

Charisma measures force of personality, leadership, confidence, social magnetism, and the ability to project yourself outward into the world. This is not simply attractiveness. Some heroes inspire through compassion. Others command through presence. Some dominate through intimidation. Charisma is what all of them share: the capacity to make other people feel something and act on it.

In superhero fiction, Charisma matters enormously because heroes are symbols as much as individuals. Public trust, morale, negotiation, inspiration, and intimidation can change the course of a conflict as decisively as any power. Villains often have exceptional Charisma too — cult leaders, tyrants, celebrity masterminds, and manipulative geniuses all weaponize personality in different ways.

PER

Perception

Awareness sharpened into action.

Perception measures awareness, sensory sharpness, vigilance, and the ability to notice what the world is doing before it acts against you. Superheroes operate in a world of high-speed combat, hidden threats, and danger from any direction. A sniper's laser sight, a cloaked infiltrator, a faint shift in crowd behavior: these things determine whether people live or die, and the heroes who catch them early do so because of Perception, not because they are spiritually wise.

Perception governs spotting hidden threats, detecting ambushes, tracking movement, reading body language, maintaining situational awareness, and interpreting sensory input quickly. It also appears in three of the four Active Defense formulas, because noticing a threat is always part of surviving it. → Active Defense, p. X

### The Score Scale

| Score | What It Means |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 to 3 | Severely impaired |
| 4 to 5 | Poor, well below average |
| 6 to 7 | Below average |
| 8 to 9 | Slightly below average |
| 10 to 11 | Human average |
| 12 to 13 | Trained or talented, noticeably above average |
| 14 to 15 | Exceptional, clearly superior to most people |
| 16 to 17 | Elite, world-class capability |
| 18 to 19 | Legendary, once-in-a-generation |
| 20 | Peak human — the absolute ceiling of unaugmented capability |
| 21 and above | Superhuman. Only possible through Powers, Origin, or extraordinary circumstance. |

The standard human scale runs to 20\. A score of 20 represents the absolute ceiling of what an unaugmented human being can achieve. Scores above 20 reflect something beyond that. They are not achievable through training alone and must come from Powers, Origin, or exceptional circumstance.

### Score to Modifier

| Score | Modifier |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 | −5 |
| 2 to 3 | −4 |
| 4 to 5 | −3 |
| 6 to 7 | −2 |
| 8 to 9 | −1 |
| 10 to 11 | \+0 |
| 12 to 13 | \+1 |
| 14 to 15 | \+2 |
| 16 to 17 | \+3 |
| 18 to 19 | \+4 |
| 20 to 21 | \+5 |
| 22 to 23 | \+6 |
| 24 to 25 | \+7 |
| 26 and above | Scale continues (-10 then /2 round down) |

### **Prowess**

Almost every roll a hero makes is going to include a number called Prowess. It is worth knowing what that number is before the dice start hitting the table.

**Prowess (PRO)** is the flat bonus representing a hero's overall heroic competence. It is not tied to any single Ability Score — it is what character Level buys on its own. As a hero gains Levels, Prowess rises and lifts attack rolls, Active Defenses, trained Skill checks, Power Effect Values, and most Class features all at once.

| Level | Prowess |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1–3 | \+2 |
| 4–6 | \+3 |
| 7–9 | \+4 |
| 10 | \+5 |

Prowess shows up constantly from this point forward, so the rest of this book simply uses the term without re-explaining it. → Chapter 14: Playing the Game covers exactly when Prowess increases and what else comes with each Level.

## **Dice, Rolls & Degrees of Success**

HEROIC 5e is built on the d20. Most of what happens at the table flows through one core action: roll a twenty-sided die, add the relevant numbers, and find out what happens. The game does not ask you to track many different dice systems or learn a new resolution engine for each type of scene. The same basic structure handles combat, skill use, Saves, and social conflict. Once you understand how rolls work, you understand the whole game.

### **When to Roll**

Not everything requires a die roll. Roll when the outcome is genuinely uncertain *and* both success and failure produce something interesting. If a hero with Super Strength tries to lift a car, there is no roll. They lift it. If that same hero tries to throw the car precisely through a third-floor window to knock out a specific target while avoiding the civilians below, that is uncertain and consequential. Roll.

The GM decides when a roll is warranted. If success is automatic given the hero's abilities, skip the roll. If failure would simply mean nothing happens and the hero tries again with no consequence, skip the roll. Dice are for moments that matter.

Terminology — Three Key Terms

#### Effect Value · Defense Value · Attack Value

**Effect Value** — The static number a Power or Class Feature generates when it forces a save. Formula: 10 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess. This number sits on its owner's side and does not change once set. When an NPC or hazard applies an effect to a hero, the player rolls 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against that Effect Value. When a hero applies an effect to an NPC, the player instead rolls against the NPC's static Save Value. Either way, the player rolls and the static number is the target to beat.

**Save Value** — The static number representing an NPC or enemy's resistance to an effect. When a hero applies an effect to an NPC, the player rolls 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against this number. It is the NPC-side counterpart to the Effect Value a hero generates. Formula: 10 \+ governing modifier \+ Tier Bonus.

**Defense Value** — The static number representing a target's passive resilience when they cannot roll. For NPCs and enemies, this replaces the rolled Active Defense. Formula: 10 \+ two relevant modifiers \+ Tier Bonus — Parry/Block, Dodge, and Willpower each add PER alongside their primary modifier; Social uses CHA \+ INT.

**Attack Value** — The static number representing an NPC or enemy's attack capability. When an NPC attacks a hero, the GM provides this number and the hero rolls Active Defense against it.

The dice always belong to the players. NPCs provide static numbers. Heroes roll against them.

### The Core Formula

Every d20 roll in HEROIC 5e follows the same basic structure.

Roll \= 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess

The relevant modifier is always an Ability Score modifier (STR, DEX, CON, FIG, INT, WIS, CHA, or PER). Prowess is the flat bonus that represents overall heroic competence and scales with level. Both are added to the d20 result to produce the final total, which is then compared to a target number.

Failure in HEROIC 5e does not mean nothing happens. It means the situation shifts in an unfavorable direction. The story keeps moving.

**Core Design Principle**

#### The Dice Always Belong to the Players

Player Characters always roll. NPCs and enemies never roll in any exchange that involves a PC.

* PC attacks → rolls against the enemy's static Defense Value.  
* PC defends → rolls Active Defense against the enemy's static Attack Value.  
* PC resists an effect → rolls against the enemy's static Effect Value.  
* PC applies an effect → rolls against the enemy's static Save Value.

The enemy never picks up a die. The GM reads a static number from the NPC stat block. The PC rolls against it. This applies universally. NPC vs. NPC interactions may use rolls at GM discretion. Everything that involves a PC is resolved by that PC's roll.

### **The Three Roll Types**

#### **Attack Rolls**

An attack roll determines whether a hero’s offensive action connects. The hero rolls their attack total against the target’s static Defense Value.

**Attack Roll** \= 1d20 \+ delivery modifier \+ Governing Ability modifier \+ Prowess

Two ability modifiers apply to every attack. The first is determined by the **delivery method** of the attack:

* **Melee attacks** use FIG, always.  
* **Ranged attacks** use DEX, always.  
* **Mental attacks** use INT, always.  
* **Social attacks** use CHA, always.

#### **Power Attacks**

When you make an attack using a **Power** (including any attack granted by a Power Set), you add **both** of the following modifiers:

* The modifier for the **delivery method** (FIG, DEX, INT, or CHA), **and**  
* The **Governing Ability modifier** of the Power Set being used.

Basic attacks that do not use a Power use only the delivery method modifier.

**Example:** A Telepath whose Power Set is governed by **WIS** makes a mental attack.

* Delivery method \= Mental → uses **INT**.  
* Governing Ability \= WIS.

They roll: **1d20 \+ INT \+ WIS \+ Prowess**.

The target defends with their **Willpower** Active Defense: **1d20 \+ WIS \+ PER \+ Prowess** (or the static Defense Value).

**Important: Attack Roll vs. Effect Value — Two Separate Questions**

The attack roll answers: *does the effect land?*

The Effect Value answers: *does the secondary consequence stick?*

These can (and often do) use different Attributes.

**Continuing the Example:** If the Telepath’s attack lands and applies a condition (such as Dazed), the target then makes a save against the Telepath’s **Effect Value** (10 \+ WIS \+ Prowess). The attack roll used INT \+ WIS, but the Effect Value uses only the Power Set’s Governing Ability (WIS).

#### **Active Defense**

When a hero is attacked, they roll to defend. The GM provides the attacker's static Attack Value. The hero rolls their Active Defense and compares the result to that number. If the hero's roll meets or beats the Attack Value, the attack fails.

Active Defense \= 1d20 \+ two modifiers \+ Prowess

There are four Active Defense types, each reflecting a different way of surviving a threat.

| Defense | Formula | Used Against |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Parry / Block | 1d20 \+ FIG \+ PER \+ PRO | Close combat, martial strikes, grabs |
| Dodge | 1d20 \+ DEX \+ PER \+ PRO | Projectiles, energy blasts, thrown objects |
| Willpower | 1d20 \+ WIS \+ PER \+ PRO | Mind control, psychic attacks, fear, illusions |
| Social | 1d20 \+ CHA \+ INT \+ PRO | Manipulation, intimidation, deception, taunts |

The hero pre-calculates the bonus for each defense type and records it on their sheet. Perception appears in three of the four defenses because noticing a threat is always part of surviving it. Social replaces PER with INT because recognizing a rhetorical trap requires clear thinking, not sharp senses.

#### Saves

Saves represent a character reacting to something dangerous that bypasses active defense entirely: an explosion, a collapsing structure, a psychic pulse blanketing an area, a poison taking hold.

Save Roll \= 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess

Effect Values follow a consistent formula: 10 \+ acting character's relevant modifier \+ Prowess. The relevant Ability Score for a save is determined by the nature of the threat — explosive force calls for CON or STR, psychic attacks call for WIS, toxic effects call for CON.

**Untrained saves:** A character who has not been trained in a particular save still rolls, but does not add their Prowess. Prowess on saves reflects practiced resistance, not raw instinct.

#### Skill Checks

Skill checks cover everything that is not an attack or a save: investigation, persuasion, acrobatics, stealth, technology use, driving, climbing, and any other trained or natural competency.

Skill Check \= 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess (if trained)

A trained character adds their full Prowess. An untrained character rolls without it. A character with Expertise in a Skill adds double their Prowess. → Chapter 8: Skills

### Advantage and Disadvantage

Some situations give a character Advantage or Disadvantage on a roll — the game's core dial for representing favorable or unfavorable conditions without adding a pile of situational modifiers.

* **Advantage:** Roll 2d20 and take the higher result.  
* **Disadvantage:** Roll 2d20 and take the lower result.

Two Rules — Both Matter

**Multiple sources do not stack.** If three different abilities all grant Advantage on the same roll, you still roll 2d20 and take the higher. The maximum is always two dice, regardless of how many Advantage sources apply.

**Advantage and Disadvantage cancel each other.** If a roll has both from any sources, the two cancel out and the roll is made normally with a single d20. It does not matter how many sources of each type exist. One source of each is enough for the cancellation. Three Advantage sources and one Disadvantage source still produces a normal roll.

### Degrees of Success

A roll does not simply succeed or fail. It succeeds by a margin, and that margin matters. The gap between an attack total and a defense total — or between a skill check and its DC — determines whether the success is ordinary or exceptional.

| Result | Requirement | What Happens |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Failure | Roll falls short of the target | The action fails. The situation shifts against you. |
| Success | Roll meets or beats the target | The action succeeds normally. |
| Strong Success | Beat the target by 5 or more | The action succeeds and may create 1 Momentum Effect. |
| HEROIC Success | Beat the target by 10 or more | The action succeeds and may create 2 Momentum Effects, or 1 HEROIC Effect. |

A natural 20 on an attack roll is still a critical hit when the rules specifically call for one. A HEROIC Success is different — it is based entirely on the margin between rolls, not the number shown on the die. A character can achieve a HEROIC Success on a roll of 8 if the target number is low enough. A character can roll a natural 20 and still only achieve a standard Success if the defender also rolls well. These two things do not interact.

### Momentum Effects

A Momentum Effect is a short cinematic consequence that exceptional success creates. It is not a separate subsystem. It is an additional outcome layered on top of a roll that already succeeded.

When a character achieves a Strong Success, they may choose one Momentum Effect appropriate to the action. On a HEROIC Success, they may choose two Momentum Effects or one HEROIC Effect.

| Effect | What It Does | Save? |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Push | Target is moved one Zone (grid: 10 ft) | Yes |
| Knockdown | Target falls Prone | Yes |
| Off-Balance | Target loses Reactions until end of its next turn | Yes |
| Pressure | Target has Disadvantage on its next roll | Yes |
| Opening | The next attack against the target gains Advantage | Yes |
| Delay | Target cannot Dash, and its movement is halved until end of its next Turn | Yes |
| Disarm | Target drops one held object | Yes |
| Suppress | Target cannot gain Advantage until end of its next turn | Yes |
| Expose | Target loses the Hidden condition and any Cover it is using | Yes |
| Rattle | Target becomes Shaken until end of its next turn | Yes |
| Shift | Acting character repositions within their Zone (grid: 10 ft) without provoking Reactions | No |
| Rally | One ally gains temporary HP equal to Prowess | No |
| Contain | Reduce collateral damage from the action | No |
| Settle | End Shaken or Slowed on one ally | No |

When a Momentum Effect allows a save, the player rolls to apply it: 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against the target's static Save Value. The relevant Ability Score is whichever fits the action best — STR for a Bruiser smashing someone aside, CHA for a Beacon humiliating an enemy, INT for a Strategist exploiting a tactical weakness.

Momentum Effects do not stack with themselves. Applying Push twice does not move the target 10 feet. Reapplying a Momentum Effect refreshes its duration if it has one. The GM can decline a Momentum Effect that does not fit the fiction.

### HEROIC Effects

HEROIC Effects are the bigger version. They represent genuine splash-page moments: the kind of consequence that makes everyone at the table stop and react. They are available on a HEROIC Success as an alternative to two Momentum Effects, and also through certain class features, powers, and team actions. The structure is the same as Momentum Effects: the player rolls 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against the target's static Save Value. The difference between the player's roll and the target's static Save Value determines how dramatic the outcome is. → Chapter 14: Playing the Game

A Complete Exchange

#### From Start to Finish

Crashpoint throws a chunk of concrete at a mercenary lieutenant across the battlefield.

**GM:** The lieutenant's static Dodge Value is 15 — derived from 10 \+ DEX +1 \+ PER +2 \+ Tier Bonus +2.

**Crashpoint:** Throwing an object is a ranged delivery, so she rolls 1d20 \+ DEX (delivery) \+ STR (the Governing Ability of her Power Set) \+ Prowess. She rolls a 14, adds DEX +1, STR +5 and Prowess +2, for a total of 22\.

**Result:** 22 beats 15\. The margin is 7 — 5 or more — so this is a Strong Success. Crashpoint deals damage and chooses one Momentum Effect.

**Crashpoint:** Chooses Knockdown. Rolls to apply it: 1d20 \+ STR \+ Prowess. She rolls a 9, adds STR +5 and Prowess +2, for a total of 16\.

**GM:** The lieutenant's static STR Save Value is 12\. 16 beats 12\. The effect lands. The lieutenant hits the ground.

Two rolls, both Crashpoint's. A clear result. The fiction is richer than it was before.

## Campaign Rank

Before you build a single hero, the whole table makes one decision together: **what kind of superhero story are you telling?**

Not which heroes. Not which city. Not which villains. Those questions come later and belong to the players and the GM working together over time. This question is more fundamental: what is the scale of the world these heroes inhabit, and what does that mean for how dangerous, powerful, and consequential everything is?

That decision is called Campaign Rank.

### What Campaign Rank Is

Campaign Rank is not a character stat. It does not change as heroes level up. It does not measure how experienced the team is or how many enemies they have defeated. It is the lens through which every number in the game is read, set once at the beginning of the campaign and held there for the life of that story.

Three Campaign Ranks exist: **Street Level** , **Mid-Level** , and **World Class**. These are not difficulty settings. They are scale settings. The dangers at Street Level feel personal and immediate. The dangers at World Class feel mythic and civilization-shaking. Both can be brutal. Both can be moving. The difference is the register of the fiction you are all agreeing to inhabit.

### The Three Campaign Ranks

Street Level

Personal. Immediate. Neighbourhood-focused.

Vigilantes, martial artists, detectives, gadgeteers, and anyone who operates in alleys and rooftops rather than in front of cameras and orbital platforms. The threats are drug operations, crime syndicates, corrupt officials, and enhanced criminals. The stakes feel immediate because they involve people and places the heroes can touch. Works well for grounded, morally complex stories with tight geographic focus.

Mid-Level

Classic. City-shaking. Wide canvas.

Classic costumed heroism, city-shaking action, and threats with national or international reach. These are the heroes most people picture when they think of the genre. Powerhouses, energy manipulators, flyers, psychics, and established super-teams operating with public recognition and government attention. The most versatile Campaign Rank and a strong default choice for a first HEROIC 5e campaign.

World Class

Mythic. Civilization-shaking. Iconic.

Icons, cosmic champions, and heroes whose actions reshape history. The threats operate at global or reality-adjacent scale. A World Class villain is not planning to rob a bank — they are threatening entire nations, dimensional barriers, or the continuation of life as it exists. World Class campaigns reward players who want their heroes to feel iconic from session one and are prepared for stories where the consequences of failure are enormous.

### What Campaign Rank Governs

Campaign Rank determines four specific things for every hero in the campaign.

#### Ability Score Array

Heroes assign one of these arrays to their eight Ability Scores at character creation. There are no restrictions on which score goes where — put the highest numbers where they matter most to the hero concept.

| Campaign Rank | Ability Score Array |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 8 |
| Mid-Level | 18, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8 |
| World Class | 20, 18, 16, 15, 14, 12, 10, 8 |

#### Power Dice

All Power rolls use a Power Die whose size is determined by Campaign Rank. This applies to every Power, regardless of Tier. Tier determines what a power does — its effects, scope, and narrative scale. Campaign Rank determines how hard it hits.

| Campaign Rank | Power Die |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | d8 |
| Mid-Level | d10 |
| World Class | d12 |

#### Starting Power Picks & Maximum Power Sets

Heroes at higher Campaign Ranks begin with more Power Picks and access to more Power Sets, reflecting that World Class heroes are already established figures with broader capability at Level 1\. Every hero should, but does not have to, begin with at least one Core Track purchase, at least two At-Will Powers, and at least one Encounter Power — that is the baseline for feeling like a hero from the first session. → Chapter 10: Powers

| Campaign Rank | HP Multiplier | Max Power Sets | Max Power Tier | Starting Power Picks | Max Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | ×1 | 3 | Tier 1 | 8 | 2 |
| Mid-Level | ×2 | 5 | Tier 2 | 10 | 4 |
| World Class | ×3 | 7 | Tier 3 | 12 | 6 |

Note on Tier Access During Play

At Level 5, Street Level characters may begin taking Tier 2 Powers, showing their growth. Mid-Level characters may begin selecting Tier 3 Powers at Level 5\. In both cases, their Power Dice remain at their Campaign Rank — a Street Level hero with Tier 2 Powers still rolls d8s. Tier determines what you can do. Campaign Rank determines how hard it hits.

#### Starting Edge

Edge is HEROIC 5e's heroic currency. → Chapter 14: Playing the Game   The direction of this table is deliberate: Street Level heroes start with more because their campaigns are scrappier, more desperate, and more reliant on the characters pushing beyond their limits to survive. World Class heroes start with less because when they spend Edge it should feel like a significant moment rather than a routine resource.

| Campaign Rank | Starting Edge Per Session |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 3 |
| Mid-Level | 2 |
| World Class | 1 |

Edge accumulates up to a cap of Level \+ Prowess. It resets to the Campaign Rank starting value at the beginning of each session.

### Level Is Not Campaign Rank

Important Distinction

#### Two Different Axes

**Level** measures how experienced and developed a hero is. It determines Prowess, class features, advancement options, and how many Power Picks a hero has accumulated through play. A Level 10 hero has been through a great deal and has the mechanical depth to show for it.

**Campaign Rank** measures the scale of the world the hero inhabits. It is set at the campaign's beginning and does not change as heroes level up.

A Level 1 World Class hero is powerful and already iconic in the world's eyes — they are simply early in their personal arc. A Level 10 Street Level hero has seen everything their scale of story can throw at them and survived all of it. They are not less heroic for operating at street level. They are exceptional within it.

*Level answers: how seasoned is this hero? Campaign Rank answers: what scale of superhero fiction is this table playing?*

### Choosing Your Campaign Rank

This is a group conversation, not a GM mandate. Campaign Rank shapes the tone and texture of every session the group will play together, and everyone at the table should feel good about the direction before character creation begins.

Some questions that help land on the right choice:

* **Do you want threats that feel close and personal, or massive and civilization-level?** Street Level leans toward the former. World Class toward the latter. Mid-Level can carry both.  
* **Do you want heroes who feel like people operating at the edge of human possibility, or heroes who are already visibly extraordinary?** Street Level grounds the fantasy. World Class leans into the iconic.  
* **Have most players played HEROIC 5e before?** Mid-Level is a comfortable starting point for a first campaign — wide enough to support most hero concepts while remaining grounded enough for consequences to feel real.  
* **Is there a strong shared vision of the kind of story the table wants to tell?** If the group knows they want a cosmic ensemble, start at World Class. If they want a gritty urban investigation story with vigilantes and moral grey areas, Street Level is the right fit.

There is no wrong answer. Pick the one that matches the story the table is excited to tell, and start building heroes.

# **Chapter Two · Character Creation**

Character  
Creation

Fifteen steps. One complete hero. Built with Crashpoint alongside as a real example every step of the way.

The Fifteen Steps

* Step 1: Create the Concept  
* Step 2: Assign Ability Scores  
* Step 3: Choose an Origin  
* Step 4: Choose a Class  
* Step 5: Choose a Side  
* Step 6: Choose a Calling  
* Step 7: Calculate Hit Points  
* Step 8: Skills & Specialties  
* Step 9: Merits & Flaws  
* Step 10: Powers & Limitations  
* Step 11: Choose a Talent  
* Step 12: Active Defenses & Saves  
* Step 13: Record Edge  
* Step 14: Choose Gear  
* Step 15: Finalize Identity

A HEROIC 5e hero is built in layers.

Not one decision, not a single defining choice, but a sequence of them, each adding something distinct to the character until a complete person stands at the end of the process. Someone with a history, a method, a set of extraordinary capabilities, a reputation, relationships, and complications. Someone who is recognizably themselves from session one.

The layers move in a specific direction. They start with who this person is, move through how they operate, and finish with what they can do and what their life looks like around the edges of the heroic work. That sequence is not arbitrary. Origin answers where the exceptional nature comes from. Class answers how the hero instinctively operates under pressure. Powers answer what they can do that nobody else can. Everything else fills in the texture of a real life being lived in extraordinary circumstances.

Before any of those decisions are made, the table has already completed Chapter 1 and knows the Campaign Rank. That number sets the scale for everything that follows.

## The Steps at a Glance

Character creation moves through fifteen steps. Each is explained in full below, with Crashpoint built alongside as a real example.

Design Note

#### Complete at Level 1

A HEROIC 5e character should feel complete at Level 1\. Not finished. Not at the peak of what they will become. But recognizable. A person with a clear identity, a functioning power concept, a role on the team, a story hook, and something that complicates their life.

Growth in this game is not about waiting to become a hero. It is about becoming a sharper, deeper, more iconic version of the hero you already are.



Step 01

Create the Concept

Start with a sentence.

Not a stat block. Not a power list. One sentence that tells everyone at the table what kind of comic-book character is being built before mechanics enter the picture.

The concept does not need to be perfect. It needs to be directional. It answers the question: *what is this hero?* From that answer, every subsequent decision becomes easier because there is something to build toward.

The concept guides the choices ahead. It is not a constraint. If a decision later in the process suggests something more interesting than the original sentence, follow it.

| Concept | Direction |
| :---- | :---- |
| A mutant speedster who protects her neighborhood | Enhanced Vanguard |
| A billionaire detective with armor, drones, and contingency plans | Trained Strategist |
| A cursed monster trying to become a hero | Monster Guardian |
| A star-born champion who channels solar fire | Cosmic Beacon |
| A martial artist who sees every attack before it lands | Trained Sentinel |
| A synthetic person trying to prove they have a soul | Artificial Warden |
| A legacy heroine carrying her mother's shield | Legacy Guardian |

Crashpoint — Step 1

The player wants to build a young woman who survived an experimental gravity accident and now hits like a collapsing building. The concept is immediate and specific: a physics student turned living impact event, still figuring out the difference between controlled force and catastrophic damage. That tension between power and consequence is going to shape every decision that follows.

Step 02

Assign Ability Scores

Take the Ability Score array for the campaign's Campaign Rank and assign the eight values to the eight Ability Scores in any order. There are no restrictions on placement. Put the highest numbers where they matter most to the concept.

| Campaign Rank | Array |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 8 |
| Mid-Level | 18, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8 |
| World Class | 20, 18, 16, 15, 14, 12, 10, 8 |

The eight Ability Scores are Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Fighting, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma, and Perception. Their roles are covered in Chapter 1\. Assign them now and calculate the modifier for each using the score-to-modifier table from Chapter 1\. The scores go in the boxes. The modifiers are what actually get added to rolls.

Important

Origins in the next step can increase some scores. Assign first, then apply Origin bonuses on top. If a bonus pushes a score above 20, record the new total — scores above 20 are superhuman and only achievable through Origin, Powers, or extraordinary circumstance.

Crashpoint — Step 2

The campaign is Mid-Level. The array is 18, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8\. The player assigns them based on the concept of a physical powerhouse with scientific training and a rough social presence.

| Ability Score | Score | Modifier |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Strength | 18 | STR \+4 |
| Dexterity | 12 | DEX \+1 |
| Constitution | 16 | CON \+3 |
| Fighting | 15 | FIG \+2 |
| Intelligence | 13 | INT \+1 |
| Perception | 14 | PER \+2 |
| Wisdom | 10 | WIS \+0 |
| Charisma | 8 | CHA −1 |

Strength goes highest because the concept is built around impact. Constitution follows because this hero is going to take hits. Perception comes next because she needs to track fast-moving objects and react to danger. Intelligence reflects a scientific background. Charisma sits low because she is blunt, not charming — and that is a character choice as much as a mechanical one.

Step 03

Choose an Origin

Origin answers one question: *where does your exceptional nature come from?*

It is not a power list. It is a history. An Origin provides Ability Score bonuses, Skill training, a built-in Merit, a built-in Flaw, and an Origin Talent that reflects something specific about how this kind of exceptional person moves through the world. Ten Origins are available, each covering a different category of superhero background.

Origins are covered in full in Chapter 3. Read them before making this choice. The brief summaries below are enough to point the concept in the right direction, but the full entries carry the mechanical detail.

| Origin | The Short Version |
| :---- | :---- |
| Trained | Human excellence through discipline, preparation, and refusal to accept limits |
| Enhanced | Changed at the biological or superhuman level by accident, experiment, or awakening |
| Alien | Not of this world, carrying the biology, culture, or burden of somewhere else |
| Artificial | Built, not born: android, synthetic, AI, living machine |
| Mystic | Touched by the supernatural through magic, spirits, curses, or ancient power |
| Cosmic | Empowered by forces operating at universal or dimensional scale |
| Monster | Visibly outside ordinary society and still choosing to be a hero |
| Legacy | Carrying a name, mantle, or symbol that belongs to history |
| Gearbound | Heroic capability that lives in what you carry, wear, or wield |
| Transcendent | Becoming something beyond ordinary categories entirely |

Apply the Origin's Ability Score bonuses to the scores assigned in Step 2\.

Crashpoint — Step 3

The player chooses **Enhanced**. The gravity accident that created her was not an experiment she consented to — it was a lab incident during a university research placement. Something went wrong with a prototype gravity regulator and she walked out of it changed.

Enhanced grants \+2 Strength and \+1 Constitution, plus Origin Skill training, the Merit *Altered Physiology 1* , the Flaw *Marked by Change 1* , and the Origin Talent *Adaptive Biology*. Her scores update: Strength rises from 18 to 20, giving STR \+5. Constitution rises from 16 to 17, giving CON \+3.

Step 04

Choose a Class

Class answers a different question from Origin. While Origin explains *where* the exceptional nature comes from, Class answers *what this hero instinctively does* when the pressure hits.

Eight Classes exist, each tied to a primary Ability Score and each representing a distinct method of engaging with conflict — whether that conflict is physical, tactical, social, or psychological.

| Class | Primary Score | The Method |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Bruiser | Strength | Force applied until something stops resisting |
| Vanguard | Dexterity | Never where the enemy expects |
| Guardian | Constitution | Between danger and the people who cannot protect themselves |
| Striker | Fighting | Combat as a precise and deliberate art |
| Strategist | Intelligence | The one who already knew how this was going to go |
| Warden | Wisdom | The still point in the chaos |
| Beacon | Charisma | Changing how people feel, and therefore what they do |
| Sentinel | Perception | The threat that has not happened yet |

Design Note

#### Class Is Instinct, Not Capability

Class does not determine what powers a hero can access. A Bruiser with telepathy attacks minds like a battering ram. A Beacon with super strength turns presence into a morale event. The power defines capability. The Class defines the instinct behind it.

Each Class provides a Hit Die, Save training in two Ability Scores, and a set of Class Features beginning at Level 1\. The full Class entries are in Chapter 6.

Each Class also establishes a Class Effect Value, used for features and powers that force an enemy to make a save:

Effect Value \= 10 \+ primary Ability Score modifier \+ Prowess

Crashpoint — Step 4

The player chooses **Bruiser**. A Bruiser solves problems through overwhelming force and physical pressure, which fits a gravity-powered impact character exactly. She is not a martial artist with technique and timing — she is someone who hits things until they stop being a problem, and whose biggest challenge is making sure the right things get hit.

Bruiser grants a d10 Hit Die and Save training in Strength and Constitution. Her Level 1 Class Features are *Heavy Hitter* and *Heavy Impact*. Her Class Effect Value: 10 \+ STR \+ Prowess \= 10 \+ 5 \+ 2 \= 17\.

Step 05

Choose a Side

Every hero in HEROIC 5e has a Side. A Side is a simple declaration of narrative position: the broad direction a character's actions tend to move in, and what that means for how the world reads them.

Side shapes two things. It determines which Callings are available to the character, and it sets the emotional register of the hero's public presence — the lens through which their reputation is understood by the people who know it.

Three Sides exist: **Heroic** , **Unaligned** , and **Villainous**. Heroic and Unaligned are the natural home of player characters. Villainous is defined for GM use with NPCs and antagonists; it is not a supported player character choice in the core game.

* **Heroic** characters protect, save, defend, inspire, and act for others. They choose from Callings marked Heroic in the catalog in Chapter 5\.  
* **Unaligned** characters operate according to their own logic — personal code, professional ethics, self-interest, or a private moral framework that does not map cleanly onto heroic idealism. They are not villains. They have access to the full Callings catalog.

This decision should take about thirty seconds. Think about the character concept. Think about why this person does what they do and who they do it for. If the answer is *"for other people, because that is the right thing to do,"* the character is Heroic. If the answer is *"for their own reasons, according to their own code, and the fact that it sometimes helps people is secondary,"* they are Unaligned.

The full rules for Side — including how it colors reputation Merits and shapes NPC reactions — are in Chapter 4\. → Chapter 4: Sides

Crashpoint — Step 5

Her instinct is to protect people, even when it costs her. The work is not about her. She is **Heroic**.

Step 06

Choose a Calling

A Calling is the emotional and moral engine underneath everything else. Not a backstory. Not a power set. The thing that gets a hero back up after the last fight nearly ended them. The answer to one question that everything else in the game orbits around: *why does this person keep doing this, when doing it costs them so much?*

That answer is also where Edge comes from.

Every Calling contains three Edge Triggers. One Minor, one Major, one Defining. Each trigger describes a specific moment during play when the Calling fires and the player earns Edge.

| Trigger | Edge Earned | What It Requires |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Minor | 1 Edge | Acting on the Calling in a way that costs something small or creates real narrative weight |
| Major | 2 Edge | A genuine fork in the road. The character chose the harder path because of who they are |
| Defining | 3 Edge | Real cost. Something is lost, damaged, or changed because the Calling demanded it |

Important

Triggers do not fire for empty roleplay. Saying the right words does not earn Edge. Doing the thing, at the moment it means something, does.

Choose one Calling from the catalog in Chapter 5\. → Chapter 5: Callings  Side availability is listed with each Calling. Heroic characters choose from Callings marked Heroic. Unaligned characters have access to the full list.

If nothing in the catalog exactly fits the concept, talk to the GM — any Calling can be renamed or reframed to better reflect a specific character without changing its mechanical structure. A character whose concept does not fit any existing Calling can work with the GM to build a new one using the Creating Custom Callings section at the end of Chapter 5 as a framework.

Crashpoint — Step 6

She chooses **Protector**. The triggers all land for her: placing herself physically between a threat and someone who cannot protect themselves, holding a position alone so others can escape, and taking real damage or loss specifically because she refused to abandon the people she was protecting. She acts because people get hurt when nobody steps in, and she knows what it feels like to be the person the system failed.

Step 07

Calculate Hit Points

At Level 1, every hero takes the maximum value of their Hit Die rather than rolling. This is the one place in the game where the die result is predetermined: everyone starts with the best possible outcome.

Starting HP is determined by Campaign Rank:

Starting HP \= (Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × Campaign Rank \+ Prowess

| Campaign Rank | Starting HP Formula |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | (Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × 1 \+ Prowess |
| Mid-Level | (Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × 2 \+ Prowess |
| World Class | (Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × 3 \+ Prowess |

Note — Score, Not Modifier

This step uses the full **Constitution score** , not CON. Heroes should feel durable from session one — and at higher ranks, they should feel proportionally harder to put down.

Prowess Sits Outside the Multiplier

Prowess is added after the Campaign Rank multiplier, never inside it. It represents hard-won resilience rather than raw physiology, and it is worth the same amount to a street vigilante as to a world-class titan.

After Level 1, each level grants HP equal to the Hit Die median \+ CON \+ your current Prowess. Because Prowess rises as you advance, the HP gained per level rises with it.

Multiclassed characters: Level 1 always uses the standard Starting HP formula with the Primary Class's Hit Die. Every subsequent level uses the Hit Die specific to the class whose level is being gained. The die does not flatten to a single type across all levels. → Chapter 6: Multiclassing

Crashpoint — Step 7

Bruiser Hit Die is d10; maximum is 10\. Constitution score is 17\. Prowess at Level 1 is \+2. The campaign is Mid-Level: HP \= (17 \+ 10) × 2 \+ 2 \= 56 HP. At Street Level the same character would begin with (17 \+ 10) × 1 \+ 2 \= 29 HP.

Step 08

Choose Skills and Specialties

Skills represent broad areas of competency: things the hero knows how to do, earned through training, experience, or background. They are not powers and they are not Class features.

Each Origin provides a set of Skills automatically. Beyond those, heroes choose **4 additional Skills** from the full list. A hero trained in a Skill adds their Prowess to rolls using that Skill. An untrained hero rolls without it.

If a hero would gain training in a Skill they already have from their Origin, they may instead choose one Specialty tied to that Skill. Specialties are focused expertise within a Skill. When a Specialty applies directly to the situation, the hero gains Advantage on that check.

The full Skill list and how Skills work are in Chapter 8\. → Chapter 8: Skills

Crashpoint — Step 8

Her Origin Skills from Enhanced cover her changed physiology and survival instincts. She adds: **Athletics** , covering physical feats and her ability to use her own mass effectively. **Intimidation** , because people who have watched her punch through a concrete wall tend to listen. **Science** , reflecting her university background. **Survival** , because the accident left her with new instincts about dangerous environments.

She takes one Specialty: *Science: Gravity Physics* , which applies whenever she is working with gravitational theory, analyzing gravity-based powers, or assessing structural impact. Advantage on those checks.

Step 09

Choose Merits and Flaws

Merits and Flaws are story-facing traits with mechanical weight. They represent the texture of a hero's life: who trusts them, who hunts them, what they owe, what they carry, what advantages their circumstances provide, and what complications their situation creates.

Merits and Flaws are rated 1 through 3\. A Rating 1 Merit is a modest advantage. A Rating 3 Merit is significant and campaign-shaping. The same scale applies to Flaws: a Rating 1 Flaw creates occasional complications, while a Rating 3 Flaw is a persistent and serious burden.

Heroes begin with a Merit and Flaw budget based on the starting framework the GM establishes for the campaign. A trait's Rating is its cost in slots. The Standard Start framework is:

3 slots of Merits  +  3 slots of Flaws

Origin Merits & Flaws Don't Count Against Budget

Merits and Flaws earned through Origin do not count against this budget. Flaws earn Edge when they meaningfully complicate a scene — this is a reward structure, not a punishment mechanic. Heroes with interesting complications have more fuel for dramatic moments.

The full Merits and Flaws catalog is in Chapter 9\. → Chapter 9: Merits & Flaws

Crashpoint — Step 9

Her Origin already granted *Marked by Change 1* as a built-in Flaw, representing the visible physical changes from the accident and the public reaction they produce. That does not count against her budget.

From her 3-slot Merit budget she chooses: **Local Support 1** (1 slot) — a neighborhood that knows her, looks out for her, and occasionally passes information. **Mentor 1** (1 slot) — a scientist who knew something about the gravity research and feels responsible for what happened. **Prepared Cache 1** (1 slot) — a workshop space and a stash of tools and spare kit she can reach when she needs it.

From her 3-slot Flaw budget she chooses: **Enemy 2** (2 slots) — someone with a direct connection to the accident who is not finished with her. **Vulnerable Reputation 1** (1 slot) — gravity manipulation at her scale causes damage, and people who have seen it are not always sure she is on their side.

Step 10

Choose Powers and Limitations

This is the step that makes the hero superhuman.

Powers are organized into Power Sets, each representing a family of related abilities. A hero selects powers by spending Power Picks, drawn from the budget established by Campaign Rank and expanded with each level gained through play.

The number of Starting Power Picks, the maximum number of Power Sets a hero can draw from, the highest Power Tier available at character creation, and the maximum number of Limitations a hero can take are all determined by Campaign Rank.

| Campaign Rank | HP Multiplier | Max Power Sets | Max Power Tier | Starting Power Picks | Max Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | ×1 | 3 | Tier 1 | 8 | 2 |
| Mid-Level | ×2 | 5 | Tier 2 | 10 | 4 |
| World Class | ×3 | 7 | Tier 3 | 12 | 6 |

Minimum Baseline

Every hero should, but does not have to, begin with at least one Core Track purchase, at least two At-Will Powers, and at least one Encounter Power. That is the baseline for feeling like a hero from the first session. Remaining Starting Power Picks are spent as the player chooses within the limits above.

### Power Pick Costs

| Purchase | Cost |
| :---- | :---- |
| Core Track 1 | 1 Pick |
| Core Track 2 | 2 Picks |
| Core Track 3 | 3 Picks |
| Core Track 4 | 3 Picks, Tier 3 Apex |
| Tier 1 Power | 1 Pick |
| Tier 2 Power | 2 Picks |
| Tier 3 Power | 3 Picks |
| Utility Power | 1 Pick |
| 2 Enhancements | 1 Pick |

### Limitations

Limitations are meaningful restrictions attached to specific Powers or Power Sets. Each Limitation grants 1 additional Power Pick in exchange for a real constraint on how a power functions. They are not general life complications — those belong in Merits and Flaws. A Limitation must directly affect the use of a specific Power or Power Set. The number of Limitations a hero can take is capped by Campaign Rank, as shown in the table above.

The full Powers chapter is Chapter 10\. Power Sets are in Chapter 11\. → Chapter 10: Powers

Crashpoint — Step 10

She is Mid-Level, so she has 10 Starting Power Picks, a maximum of 5 Power Sets, a maximum Power Tier of Tier 2, and can take up to 4 Limitations. She chooses **Gravity Control** as her Power Set and spends:

* Gravity Control Core Track 1 — 1 Pick  
* Gravity Strike At-Will — 1 Pick  
* Crushing Field At-Will — 1 Pick  
* Gravity Pulse Encounter (Tier 2\) — 2 Picks  
* Density Anchor Utility — 1 Pick  
* 2 Enhancements — 1 Pick

That is 7 Picks spent, leaving 3 remaining. She takes the Limitation *Uncontrolled* : her gravity powers cause collateral damage under stress, pulling objects and people unpredictably when she is pushed past her limits. This reflects the accident that created her and the fact that she does not yet have complete control. The Limitation grants 1 additional Pick, bringing her to 4 remaining. She spends all four on Enhancement pairs — eight Enhancements in total, refining the reach, precision, and control of the powers she already has.

Step 11

Choose a Talent

Every hero begins play with one Talent, chosen from the catalog in Chapter 7\. → Chapter 7: Talents

This is separate from the Talents gained through advancement at Levels 3 and 9\. Those come later and are in addition to this starting pick. Think of the starting Talent as the signature edge the hero already had before the campaign began: a trained technique, an operational habit, or a hard-won instinct that is already part of who they are when the story opens.

Talents are narrow and deliberate. They are not powers. They do not grant flight, telepathy, or energy blasts. They represent the kind of thing a person learns through repetition, pressure, and experience: a combat trick, a way of moving, a social skill honed under fire, a mental discipline. Browse Chapter 7 and choose one that fits the concept and feels like something this specific person would have already earned.

Crashpoint — Step 11

She takes **Tough**. Her maximum HP increases by 2 per character level, and once per encounter when she drops below half HP she gains temporary HP equal to her Prowess. It fits a character who is essentially a living impact event: she does not dodge, she endures, and the ability to keep standing when things go wrong is as much a part of her identity as the gravity powers. It also reflects the physical changes from the accident — a body that is simply harder to stop than it used to be.

Step 12

Calculate Active Defenses and Saves

In HEROIC 5e, the hero always rolls to defend. When something attacks a hero, the GM provides a static Attack Value derived from the attacker's stats. The hero rolls their Active Defense and compares the result to that number. The GM never rolls to hit a hero. The dice stay in the player's hands.

Calculate the bonus for each of the four Active Defense types and record it on the sheet before play begins. When attacked, the hero adds that bonus to a 1d20 roll and compares the total to the attacker's static Attack Value. The higher number wins. Ties go to the hero.

| Defense Type | Formula |
| :---- | :---- |
| Parry / Block | 1d20 \+ FIG \+ PER \+ Prowess |
| Dodge | 1d20 \+ DEX \+ PER \+ Prowess |
| Willpower | 1d20 \+ WIS \+ PER \+ Prowess |
| Social | 1d20 \+ CHA \+ INT \+ Prowess |

Pre-calculating the bonus for each defense type means there is no arithmetic needed mid-session. When an attack comes in, the player picks up the d20, adds one pre-written number, and rolls.

Saves Work the Same Way

When an effect forces a save on the hero, the GM provides the static Effect Value. The hero rolls their Save and compares the result to that number. A hero trained in a save adds their Prowess to the roll. An untrained hero does not. Class determines which two saves are trained.

Crashpoint — Step 12

Prowess at Level 1 is \+2.

* **Parry/Block:** 1d20 \+ FIG \+ PER \+ PRO \= \+2 \+ 2 \+ 2 \= **\+6**  
* **Dodge:** 1d20 \+ DEX \+ PER \+ PRO \= \+1 \+ 2 \+ 2 \= **\+5**  
* **Willpower:** 1d20 \+ WIS \+ PER \+ PRO \= \+0 \+ 2 \+ 2 \= **\+4**  
* **Social:** 1d20 \+ CHA \+ INT \+ PRO \= −1 \+ 1 \+ 2 \= **\+2**

Her Bruiser training covers Strength and Constitution saves. On those she adds her Prowess when rolling. On all others she does not.

Step 13

Record Edge

Edge is HEROIC 5e's heroic currency. It is earned through Callings, Flaws, and meaningful play. It is spent to push past limits, reroll, reduce collateral damage, and create the moments people talk about after the session ends.

Starting Edge is determined by Campaign Rank. The Edge cap is Level \+ Prowess.

| Campaign Rank | Starting Edge Per Session |
| :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 3 |
| Mid-Level | 2 |
| World Class | 1 |

Callings are covered in Chapter 5\. → Chapter 5: Callings  The Calling chosen in Step 6 is the primary ongoing engine for earning Edge during play.

Crashpoint — Step 13

The campaign is Mid-Level. She begins each session with **2 Edge**. Her cap at Level 1 is Level \+ Prowess \= 1 \+ 2 \= 3\. Her Calling is Protector: she acts because people get hurt when nobody steps in, and she knows what it feels like to be the person the system failed. Edge triggers when she puts herself at genuine risk specifically to keep someone else safe.

Step 14

Choose Gear

Gear in HEROIC 5e is not a spreadsheet. Heroes do not track ammunition, inventory weight, or the exact contents of their pockets. Ordinary equipment appropriate to the concept is assumed present without requiring purchase or tracking.

A hero with no wealth-related Merit or Flaw is assumed to have a stable, ordinary income — enough to cover rent, basic living expenses, and standard professional equipment appropriate to their concept. They can acquire standard gear without a Resource check. Significant purchases — specialized technology, vehicles, safe houses, restricted equipment — require a relevant Merit or GM approval.

What matters is **signature gear** : equipment that is part of the hero's identity, that can be lost or damaged in ways that carry narrative weight, and that may have mechanical significance through Merits like Gear Access or through Powers if the hero is Gearbound. Gear is covered in full in Chapter 13\. → Chapter 13: Equipment & Gear

Crashpoint — Step 14

She does not rely on gear for her powers. The gravity manipulation is internal. What she carries is practical: reinforced clothing that survives her own force expressions, a basic forensic kit from her science background, and communication gear. Her *Prepared Cache 1* Merit gives her access to a workshop where she continues improving the suit between missions.

Step 15

Finalize Identity

The sheet has numbers. Now make the hero real.

These questions do not need long answers. A sentence each is enough. But they should be answered before the first session, because superhero games run on identity, reputation, relationships, and consequence. The numbers describe a character. The answers to these questions describe a person.

| Question | Crashpoint |
| :---- | :---- |
| What is your hero name? | Crashpoint |
| What is your civilian name? | Yara Osei |
| Is your identity public or secret? | Not public, but not carefully hidden either |
| What does the costume look like? | Reinforced dark grey suit, no mask, impact-absorption plating at the shoulders and forearms |
| What symbol do people associate with you? | A compressed circle, like something collapsing inward |
| Who trusts you? | The neighborhood that has seen her work, her Mentor |
| Who fears or hates you? | Her Enemy, people who witnessed the collateral damage up close |
| What does the public think of you? | Dangerous, possibly unstable, maybe trying |
| What line will you not cross? | She does not let civilians absorb the cost of her mistakes |
| What makes her heroic? | She knows exactly what uncontrolled force does to people, and she shows up anyway |

Design Note

#### Why These Questions

Every question in Step 15 points outward. Who trusts you. Who fears you. What the public thinks. The line you will not cross. None of them asks where the hero grew up, what their parents were like, or what happened in the years before the powers arrived.

That is deliberate. Superhero fiction runs on reputation and relationship far more than on biography. A reader who has never seen an origin story still knows what a city thinks of its protector, who answers when that protector calls, and what that protector will not do. Those are the things that generate stories. The childhood rarely comes up, and when it does it works better discovered in play than written down in advance.

The answers are also load-bearing rather than decorative. Who trusts the hero tells the GM where to find allies and what it costs to lose them. Who fears them supplies antagonists who are not villains. What the public thinks sets the difficulty of every scene that happens in daylight. And the line the hero will not cross is the most reliable Edge generator on the sheet, because a Calling only fires when holding to it costs something.

A player who answers these ten questions has not written a backstory. They have written the hero's position in a world, which is the part the table will actually use.


Worked Example — Complete Character

Crashpoint at a Glance

| Element | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Campaign Rank | Mid-Level |
| Origin | Enhanced |
| Class | Bruiser |
| Side | Heroic |
| Calling | Protector |
| Talent | Tough |
| Level | 1 |
| Prowess | \+2 |

Now It Is Your Turn

Fifteen steps, and there is a hero at the end of them. Before the first session, read back over the sheet and check that the person on it is the person you meant to build.

If something does not fit, change it now. Nothing is fixed until play begins, and a choice made at Step 4 often looks different once Step 10 has shown you what the hero can actually do. Working backward through the steps is normal — most players do it at least once.

If the doubt only arrives later, three sessions deep, that is what a Respec is for. At Levels 3, 6, and 9 a hero may rebuild: Powers, Limitations, Skills, Specialties, Talents, Merits, Flaws, and even their Calling, provided something in the fiction justifies the change. → Chapter 14: Playing the Game

Three things a Respec will not touch: Origin, Class, and Ability Scores. Those are identity rather than loadout, and they are the decisions worth sitting with before you leave this chapter. Everything else can be revised later by a hero who has learned something about themselves.


# **Chapter Three · Origins**

Ten Origins. One question each answers: where does your exceptional nature come from?

**The Ten Origins**

* Alien  
* Artificial  
* Cosmic  
* Enhanced  
* Gearbound  
* Legacy  
* Monster  
* Mystic  
* Trained  
* Transcendent

Origin is the foundation of every hero in HEROIC 5e.

Not their powers. Not their class. Not their costume or their city or their enemies. Before any of that, there is one question that everything else builds on top of:

*Where does your exceptional nature come from?*

That is what an Origin answers. It is not a power list and it is not a personality template. It is a history, a foundation, a set of facts about what this person is and where they came from. Two heroes with identical powers and the same class can feel completely different at the table if one is a trained human who earned every edge through discipline and the other is a biological accident who woke up one morning fundamentally changed. Origin is what creates that difference.

## What Origin Is Not

**Origin does not determine powers.** An Alien hero does not automatically fly. A Mystic hero does not automatically cast spells. A Cosmic hero is not automatically more powerful than everyone else in the room. Powers are chosen separately. Origin describes the source of the exceptional nature, not the nature itself.

**Origin does not replace Class.** A Trained martial artist and an Enhanced martial artist can both be Strikers. Their Class is the same. Their Origin explains why they move through the world differently.

**Origin does not lock a concept into a narrow archetype.** Enhanced covers mutants, accident survivors, supersoldiers, experimental subjects, and anyone else whose biology was pushed beyond human limits. Monster covers everything from a gentle swamp creature to a cursed vampire to a stitched-together science experiment. The Origins are intentionally broad because superhero fiction is broad.

## What Every Origin Provides

Every Origin gives the hero five things, in the same format, every time. No exceptions, no special cases outside this structure.

* **Ability Score Bonuses.** Two bonuses applied on top of the array from character creation. Usually \+2 to one score and \+1 to another, with options for where to place them. The two bonuses cannot go into the same score.  
* **Skill Training.** Automatic training in Skills relevant to this background. If the Origin grants a Skill the hero already has from another source, take one Specialty within that Skill instead.  
* **Built-In Merit.** One Merit reflecting the advantages of this Origin. Does not count against the character creation Merit budget.  
* **Built-In Flaw.** One Flaw reflecting the complications of this Origin. Does not count against the character creation Flaw budget.  
* **Origin Talent.** A Talent unique to this Origin, granted automatically. This is separate from and in addition to the starting Talent chosen during character creation. Every hero begins play with both their Origin Talent and their chosen starting Talent.

#### Important

Origin-granted Merits and Flaws are not optional. They are part of what this character is. The GM may permit a substitution in rare cases where the standard Merit or Flaw fundamentally contradicts a specific concept, but that is a conversation to have before character creation begins, not a unilateral player decision.

## Choosing the Right Origin

Choose the Origin that best describes the foundation of the character, not every detail of it.

A hero can be complicated without needing to invent a new Origin or try to straddle two. A mutant raised by aliens is probably Enhanced or Alien depending on which part of that history matters most to how they actually play. A power-armored alien princess might be Alien if her biology and culture are central, or Gearbound if the armor is the point. A cursed knight carrying an enchanted weapon could be Mystic, Gearbound, Legacy, or Monster depending on where the concept's center of gravity sits.

The right question is not *"which Origin covers every nuance of this character."* It is *"which Origin should the rules recognize first?"*

That answer is the Origin.

## The Ten Origins

### Alien

*Not of this world — carrying the biology, culture, or burden of somewhere else.*

Alien heroes are not of this world.

They may come from another planet, a lost interstellar civilization, a hidden empire, a living nebula, a parallel dimension, or a refugee fleet crossing lightyears to reach safety. Some look almost human. Others are visibly, profoundly strange. Some were raised on Earth and know no other home. Others arrive carrying the customs, biology, technology, politics, and weight of cultures that predate human civilization by millennia.

Alien does not automatically mean physically superior. Some alien species are stronger and tougher than humans. Others are fragile but psychically powerful, or brilliant but socially incomprehensible, or aquatic, insectile, silicon-based, or built on biological assumptions that have no human equivalent. The Origin describes non-human nature. The Powers describe what that nature can actually do.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Constitution | Strength, Wisdom, or Perception |
| Intelligence | Perception, Wisdom, or Charisma |
| Perception | Intelligence, Wisdom, or Dexterity |
| Charisma | Wisdom, Constitution, or Intelligence |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Culture, Insight, Notice, Science, Survival, Technology.**

**Built-In Merit: Strange Biology 1**

Choose one alien biological trait reflecting your species' specific adaptations.

| Trait | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Environmental Adaptation | Gain Advantage on saves against one chosen environment: cold, heat, low oxygen, pressure, radiation, or low gravity. |
| Unusual Diet | You can safely consume substances toxic to humans and go significantly longer without food, water, or sleep without mechanical penalty. |
| Natural Camouflage | Gain Advantage on Stealth checks in environments matching your homeworld's terrain type. |

**Built-In Flaw: Alien Outsider 1**

You do not read as human to social systems, medical systems, or people relying on ordinary cultural assumptions. Bureaucracies may not recognize you. Medical care built for human biology may not help you or may actively harm you. Cultural miscommunication is a constant low-level risk.

When your alien nature creates genuine difficulty rather than merely cosmetic background, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Not From Here**

Once per encounter, when you fail an Insight, Science, Notice, or Survival check, you may draw on an alien perspective that no human has access to. Reroll the check and use the second result. This represents biological senses, off-world knowledge, or a completely different framework for understanding the situation that the people around you simply cannot replicate.

### Artificial

*Built, not born — android, synthetic, AI, living machine.*

Artificial heroes were built, not born.

They are androids, synthetic people, AIs housed in physical shells, uplifted programs, living machines, robotic entities, or digital minds running in engineered bodies. Some are obviously mechanical. Others pass as human so convincingly that they have lived human lives for years without detection. Some were built as weapons and are trying to become something else. Some were built as tools and are fighting to be recognized as people.

Artificial is the correct Origin when the hero's fundamental nature is constructed rather than biological. It covers the full range from a chrome-plated war machine to a synthetic human who cries at films and cannot explain why.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Intelligence | Constitution, Perception, or Strength |
| Constitution | Intelligence, Strength, or Perception |
| Strength | Intelligence, Constitution, or Fighting |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Investigation, Science, Stealth, Technology, Vehicles.**

**Built-In Merit: Synthetic Construction 1**

Choose one mechanical advantage reflecting your design and construction.

| Trait | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Integrated Systems | Once per encounter, gain Advantage on a Technology or Science check by directly interfacing with a compatible system. |
| Modular Repair | During a Breather, you may restore additional HP equal to your Prowess through self-maintenance rather than rest. |
| Environmental Hardening | Gain Advantage on saves against environmental hazards: extreme temperature, pressure, vacuum, radiation, or electrical surge. |

**Built-In Flaw: Constructed Nature 1**

Your artificial origin creates complications that biological heroes do not face. Standard medical treatment may be useless or harmful. People may question your legal status, your rights, or whether you count as a person at all. Authorities may seek to claim ownership, deactivate, reprogram, or disassemble you.

When your constructed nature creates real mechanical or social pressure rather than abstract background detail, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Synthetic Edge**

Once per encounter, before making an attack roll, skill check, or Save, you may run a rapid internal calculation. Gain Advantage on that roll. This represents your ability to access tactical data, internal sensors, or processing capability that biological heroes simply cannot match in that moment.

### Cosmic

*Empowered by forces operating at universal or dimensional scale.*

Cosmic heroes are empowered by forces operating at universal or dimensional scale.

Their power may come from stellar radiation, dimensional storms, living stars, universal entities, quantum transformation, celestial artifacts, abstract concepts given form, or the deep machinery of reality itself. Some were chosen. Others were accidents. Some are vessels for power too vast to fully understand and are still learning what that means. Some have been carrying it so long they have forgotten what it felt like not to.

#### Cosmic vs. Alien: Two Different Things

Cosmic is distinct from Alien. An Alien is a non-human being. A Cosmic hero is empowered by forces that operate beyond biology entirely. A human astronaut transformed by stellar energy is Cosmic. An alien soldier from a technologically advanced civilization is Alien. An alien chosen by a universal force might fit either concept, but the player should pick whichever Origin is more central to how the hero actually plays.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Charisma | Constitution, Wisdom, or Perception |
| Constitution | Charisma, Strength, or Wisdom |
| Wisdom | Charisma, Perception, or Intelligence |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill from the following list, plus one Specialty tied to the Cosmic concept: **Science, Occult, Notice, Survival, Influence.**

*Specialty examples:* Astronomy, Dimensional Theory, Cosmic Entities, Energy Signatures, Space Survival, Universal Forces.

**Built-In Merit: Cosmic Signature 1**

You are attuned to cosmic, dimensional, stellar, or universal energy. Gain Advantage on checks to detect, identify, resist, or interpret cosmic phenomena when they are directly present in the scene.

**Built-In Flaw: Too Bright to Hide 1**

Your power leaves a trace that certain things can follow. Cosmic entities, advanced sensors, mystics, alien technology, dimensional beings, or energy-sensitive enemies may detect your presence when you use major Powers or enter unstable cosmic environments. Attempts to track your cosmic signature gain Advantage when the tracker has appropriate means.

When this creates active danger rather than background atmosphere, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Stellar Endurance**

Choose one of the following features when you take this Origin.

| Feature | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Vacuum-Touched | You can hold your breath for 10 × Prowess minutes and gain Advantage on saves against vacuum, pressure, and radiation hazards. |
| Energy-Born | Choose one damage type: Fire, Electrical, Radiant, or Cold. Once per encounter, reduce incoming damage of that type by your Prowess \+ CON. |
| Universal Perspective | Once per encounter, gain Advantage on a Wisdom, Science, Occult, or Notice check involving cosmic scale, alien phenomena, or dimensional danger. |

### Enhanced

*Changed — by accident, experiment, or awakening. The change is real, internal, and the hero's own.*

Enhanced heroes have been changed.

Something happened. A lab accident, a radiation event, a military enhancement program, a genetic awakening, an experimental procedure that went wrong or went exactly right. They came out the other side different in ways that are permanent, biological, and impossible to reverse. Their body or mind now operates outside the boundaries of ordinary human biology, whether visibly or not.

Enhanced is deliberately broad. Mutants, supersoldiers, accident survivors, experimental subjects, next-stage humans, and anyone else whose fundamental biology has been pushed beyond human limits belongs here. The common thread is not how the change happened. It is that the change is real, internal, and the hero's own rather than something they carry or channel.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Strength | Constitution, Dexterity, or Perception |
| Constitution | Strength, Dexterity, or Wisdom |
| Dexterity | Strength, Constitution, or Perception |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Athletics, Intimidation, Science, Stealth, Survival.**

**Built-In Merit: Altered Physiology 1**

Choose one biological advantage reflecting your specific transformation.

| Trait | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Heightened Reflexes | Gain Advantage on Initiative rolls once per encounter. |
| Enhanced Recovery | Once per Breather, when you spend Hit Dice, reroll one die and use the better result. |
| Unusual Senses | Gain Advantage on Notice checks tied to one chosen sense: sight, hearing, smell, touch, or an exotic sense appropriate to the concept. |

**Built-In Flaw: Marked by Change 1**
