Your alteration leaves traces. These may be visible mutations, unusual medical readings, unstable energy signatures, genetic markers, scars, strange eyes, or public classification as a metahuman. Attempts to identify you as Enhanced through medical, scientific, or technological means gain Advantage when the investigator has appropriate tools or access.

When this creates meaningful social or narrative pressure in a scene, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Adaptive Biology**

Choose one Power Set you possess. Once per encounter, when you use an At-Will Power from that Power Set, choose one of the following effects.

| Option | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Controlled Surge | Add your Prowess to one damage, healing, protection, or forced movement roll from that use. |
| Instinctive Control | Ignore Disadvantage from stress, pain, or unstable conditions on that Power use. |
| Biological Push | Gain temporary HP equal to your Prowess after using the Power. |

This does not grant a new Power. It is an expression of your body's ongoing adaptation to its own capabilities.

### Gearbound

*Heroic capability that lives in what you carry, wear, or wield.*

Gearbound heroes' exceptional capability lives in what they carry, wear, or wield.

The armored inventor in a suit that took a decade to build. The warrior whose sacred weapon chooses its bearer. The gadgeteer whose utility belt is ten years of field experience compressed into two dozen pieces of equipment. The relic-bearer carrying a cursed ring that has passed through fifty hands across three centuries. What they share is that the source of their extraordinary capability is external. They are the hero because of something they have, not something they are.

#### Gearbound vs. Trained: The Key Distinction

Gearbound is distinct from Trained, who may use gear but whose foundation is personal excellence. It is distinct from Artificial, who is built from their construction. A Gearbound hero uses something that was built, and the relationship between the hero and the gear is the heart of the concept.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Intelligence | Dexterity, Perception, or Fighting |
| Dexterity | Intelligence, Perception, or Fighting |
| Fighting | Intelligence, Dexterity, or Perception |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Acrobatics, Investigation, Science, Technology, Vehicles.**

**Built-In Merit: Gear Access 1**

You have reliable access to the tools, maintenance parts, storage, charging infrastructure, workshop space, or supply channels needed to support your heroic equipment. This Merit does not grant additional Power effects, but it means the logistical foundation of your heroic work is established and does not need to be negotiated session by session.

**Built-In Flaw: Gear Dependent 1**

Some or all of your heroic capabilities depend on equipment that can be damaged, stolen, disabled, jammed, hacked, lost, or separated from you. When your gear creates a specific vulnerability that an opponent exploits or a situation removes, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

Note that Powers specifically tied to gear may also take the Gear Dependent Limitation separately for the Power Pick bonus, but this Origin Flaw applies to the hero's overall situation rather than granting additional Picks on its own.

**Origin Talent: Field Systems**

Once per encounter, when your gear, armor, weapon, vehicle, relic, or device would fail, jam, be disabled, run out of charge, or suffer a complication, you may make a Technology, Science, or Vehicles check as appropriate to the situation. On a success, choose one of the following.

| Option | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Keep It Running | The gear continues functioning until the end of the encounter. |
| Emergency Bypass | Ignore Disadvantage caused by gear damage or interference for one turn. |
| Reroute Power | Regain use of one spent Encounter Power tied to the gear, but gain 1 Burnout. |
| Controlled Failure | The gear fails, but you prevent collateral damage, injury to allies, or loss of critical data. |

### Legacy

*Carrying a name, mantle, or symbol that belongs to history.*

Legacy heroes carry something that belongs to history.

A family name that means something in the superhero community. A mantle passed down from a retiring champion. A sidekick role that outlasted the hero they served. An ancient bloodline with expectations attached. A sacred office held by someone in every generation for five hundred years. A famous costume that half the city recognizes before they know who is inside it.

A Legacy hero is never starting from nothing. They arrive with recognition, resources, enemies they did not make, allies they did not earn, and the weight of comparison to whoever came before. Whether that weight is an anchor or a foundation depends entirely on what the hero chooses to do with it.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Charisma | Intelligence, Wisdom, or Fighting |
| Fighting | Charisma, Dexterity, or Perception |
| Wisdom | Charisma, Intelligence, or Perception |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Athletics, Influence, Insight, Investigation, Streetwise.**

**Built-In Merit: The Name 1**

Your Legacy carries weight that opens doors and commands attention. Choose one of the following.

| Trait | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Inherited Network | You begin with Connected 1, representing the allies, informants, and institutional relationships inherited from the Legacy. |
| Famous Symbol | You begin with Public Trust 1 among people who recognize the Legacy's symbol or name. |
| Mentor's Gift | You begin with Mentor 1, representing someone with deep knowledge of the Legacy who remains available to you. |

**Built-In Flaw: The Expectation 1**

Carrying a Legacy means being measured against it constantly. People who respected the original may resent you, test you, or refuse to take you seriously until you prove yourself on their terms. People who opposed the original may target you specifically because of what the Legacy represents.

When the expectations or history attached to the Legacy create active pressure in a scene rather than background texture, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Inherited Instinct**

Once per encounter, when you make a save or skill check related to the Legacy's area of expertise — such as combat for a martial Legacy, investigation for a detective Legacy, or leadership for a symbol-bearing Legacy — you may add your Prowess to the result after seeing the roll. If the roll already succeeds, you may instead treat it as a Strong Success.

### Monster

*Visibly outside ordinary society — and still choosing to be a hero.*

Monster heroes are visibly or spiritually marked as something outside ordinary society.

They may be bestial, undead, grotesque, reptilian, fungal, aquatic, insectile, stitched together, vampiric, cursed into a form they did not choose, or simply impossible to look at without flinching. Some are gentle souls in terrifying bodies, heroes whose biggest challenge is making the world understand that the frightening thing in front of them is not the threat. Some are predators who decided to become protectors. Some have fully embraced what they are and use the fear it generates as a weapon against worse things.

Monster is the correct Origin when the character's unnatural body or presence is central to how they interact with the world — not as a cosmetic detail, but as something that actively shapes every social encounter, every public appearance, and every scene where someone new sees them for the first time.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Strength | Constitution, Perception, or Wisdom |
| Constitution | Strength, Wisdom, or Charisma |
| Perception | Strength, Constitution, or Dexterity |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill from the following list, plus one Specialty tied to the monstrous nature: **Athletics, Intimidation, Notice, Stealth, Survival.**

*Specialty examples:* Scent Tracking, Night Hunting, Urban Lurking, Fearsome Presence, Predatory Instincts, Unnatural Anatomy.

**Built-In Merit: Inhuman Body 1**

Choose one monstrous physical trait reflecting your specific form.

| Trait | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Natural Weapons | Your unarmed strikes deal slashing, piercing, or bludgeoning damage as appropriate to your form. |
| Night Creature | Gain Low-Light Vision, or Advantage on Notice checks made in darkness or near-darkness. |
| Terrifying Form | Gain Advantage on Intimidation checks when your appearance is a relevant factor in the scene. |
| Strange Anatomy | Gain Advantage on saves against poison, disease, or effects that target mundane human biology. |

**Built-In Flaw: Feared 1**

You are visibly not human, and most people react accordingly. Ordinary social spaces, legal systems, public institutions, and civilian interactions carry friction that other heroes do not experience. Some people will be hostile on sight. Others will report you to authorities. Crowds may panic.

When your appearance actively complicates a scene rather than serving as background detail, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Closing Instinct**

Once per encounter, when you move toward a target and close distance aggressively, you may make that movement without provoking Reactions. If you reach the target and attack on the same turn, gain Advantage on that attack roll. This represents the combination of physical capability and primal threat presence that makes Monster heroes dangerous in ways that go well beyond raw statistics.

### Mystic

*Touched by the supernatural — magic, spirits, curses, or forces that predate physics.*

Mystic heroes are touched by the supernatural.

Their power may come from magic, spirits, curses, divine favor, an ancient bloodline, occult study, a sacred office, a haunted relic, a bargain with something that should not exist, or forces that predate the laws of physics as currently understood. Some Mystic heroes cast spells. Others wield enchanted weapons, channel sacred fire, bind ghosts, commune with the dead, or carry a curse so old nobody remembers who placed it.

#### Origin vs. Powers

The Origin explains why the supernatural is involved. The Powers explain what that means at the table. A Mystic hero who channels divine fire still takes their fire damage from the Fire Control Power Set. The Origin is the story. The Power Set is the mechanic.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Wisdom | Charisma, Intelligence, or Perception |
| Charisma | Wisdom, Intelligence, or Constitution |
| Intelligence | Wisdom, Charisma, or Perception |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill: **Insight, Occult, Notice, Influence, Investigation.**

**Built-In Merit: Mystic Attunement 1**

You can sense the presence of obvious supernatural forces, active magic, curses, spirits, divine influence, or occult disturbances within close narrative range. This does not reveal exact details without an Occult check. You gain Advantage on Occult checks to identify a mystical source you can directly observe.

**Built-In Flaw: Supernatural Burden 1**

Your connection to the unseen world attracts attention from things that live there. Spirits, demons, cults, occult enemies, divine messengers, cursed relics, or supernatural obligations may seek you out. You may also be vulnerable to wards, holy sites, profane sites, ritual bindings, or mystical laws appropriate to your specific connection.

When this creates meaningful complications in a scene rather than atmosphere, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Ward the Soul**

Once per encounter, when you or an ally within 30 feet makes a save against fear, charm, possession, curse, psychic intrusion, or mystical manipulation, you may add your Prowess to the roll. You must be conscious and able to express your mystical practice in some form — whether through speech, gesture, prayer, focus, or concentrated will.

### Trained

*Human excellence through discipline, preparation, and refusal to accept limits.*

Trained heroes are exceptional because they made themselves exceptional.

Not through transformation. Not through accident or cosmic intervention or supernatural gift. Through effort. Sustained, deliberate, often punishing effort applied over years to become something that ordinary people are not. A Trained hero might be a masked detective, elite spy, martial artist, soldier, acrobat, Olympic-level athlete, precision archer, escape artist, or tactical genius whose only advantage over a powered opponent is that they are better prepared, better disciplined, and harder to surprise.

#### Design Note: Trained Doesn't Mean Unpowered

Trained does not mean unpowered. A Trained hero may still have Powers through gadgets, martial arts technique pushed to its absolute limit, or conditioning that borders on the superhuman. What defines them is that their foundation is human excellence rather than transformation or external force. They earned it.

This is also the Origin for heroes who need to stand in a room full of gods and make the gods nervous.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Fighting | Dexterity, Intelligence, Perception, or Wisdom |
| Dexterity | Fighting, Intelligence, Perception, or Charisma |
| Intelligence | Fighting, Dexterity, Perception, or Wisdom |

**Skill Training — Two Picks**

Choose **two** Skills from the following list. Trained heroes receive two Skill picks because preparation and breadth of capability are core to the concept.

**Acrobatics, Athletics, Investigation, Notice, Stealth, Streetwise, Technology, Vehicles.**

**Built-In Merit: Prepared Foundation 1**

You begin with one of the following Merits at Rating 1, chosen when you take this Origin. It does not count against your starting Merit allowance.

**Base of Operations, Connected, Gear Access, Legal Authority, Local Support, Mentor, Prepared Cache,** or **Safehouse Network.**

**Built-In Flaw: Only Human 1**

Your body remains fundamentally mortal unless your Powers specifically say otherwise. Effects that target mundane biology, exhaustion, injury, aging, hunger, thirst, or ordinary physical limits may affect you where they would not affect an Enhanced or Cosmic hero.

When this vulnerability creates meaningful pressure at a critical moment, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Trained to Survive**

Once per encounter, when you fail a skill check using a Skill you are trained in, you may reroll the check. You must use the second result. This is not luck. It is the reflex of someone who has rehearsed failure enough times to know how to recover from it.

### Transcendent

*Becoming something beyond ordinary categories — metaphysical change, identity drift, existence in motion.*

Transcendent heroes are becoming something beyond ordinary categories.

They may be ascending toward godhood, merging with a cosmic principle, transforming into living thought, becoming a dimensional constant, carrying a divine spark that is slowly consuming whoever held it first, evolving past biology, or existing partly outside normal reality in ways that have no clean vocabulary. Their nature is often unstable, symbolic, terrifying, beautiful, or poorly understood by the people around them — and sometimes by themselves.

#### Important: Transcendent Requires GM Buy-In

Transcendent is the rarest Origin and the most campaign-shaping. It should only be taken with the GM's active support for the implications it creates. This Origin is not simply about being powerful. A physically strong hero is not Transcendent. A hero with cosmic energy blasts is not Transcendent. This Origin is about *metaphysical change*, identity drift, and a relationship with existence that is moving in a direction mortal frameworks cannot fully contain.

**Ability Score Bonuses**

Choose one primary bonus and one secondary bonus. The two bonuses cannot apply to the same score.

| Primary (+2) | Secondary (+1) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Wisdom | Charisma, Constitution, or Perception |
| Charisma | Wisdom, Constitution, or Intelligence |
| Constitution | Wisdom, Charisma, or Strength |

**Skill Training**

Choose one Skill from the following list, plus one Specialty tied to the transformation: **Insight, Occult, Notice, Science, Influence.**

*Specialty examples:* Divine Spark, Reality Fractures, Dimensional Existence, Apotheosis, Fate, Abstract Entities, Metaphysical Identity.

**Built-In Merit: Beyond Mortal 1**

Choose one benefit reflecting the nature of your transformation.

| Benefit | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Ageless | You do not age normally and gain Advantage on saves against mundane aging effects. |
| Strange Perception | Gain Advantage on Notice or Insight checks involving supernatural, cosmic, psychic, or dimensional anomalies. |
| Death-Touched | Gain Advantage on Grit Saves or saves against instant-death effects. |
| Conceptual Presence | Gain Advantage on Influence or Intimidation checks when your otherworldly nature is obvious and directly relevant to the situation. |

**Built-In Flaw: Losing Humanity 1**

Your transformation separates you from ordinary life in ways that accumulate rather than stabilize. You may struggle with emotion, memory, morality, bodily needs, relationships, the scale of your perspective, or your sense of your own identity. People may worship, fear, exploit, study, or reject you.

When your changing nature creates alienation, temptation, collateral risk, emotional distance, or metaphysical danger rather than serving as abstract background, the GM may invoke this Flaw and award you 1 Edge.

**Origin Talent: Beyond the Moment**

Once per encounter, when you fail a save against fear, charm, psychic manipulation, emotional control, death, transformation, or reality alteration, you may add your Prowess to the result after seeing the roll. If this turns the failure into a success, you also gain temporary HP equal to your WIS or CHA modifier \+ Prowess.

This represents not resilience in the ordinary sense but something stranger: a nature that is difficult to fully affect because it is not entirely contained within the moment being targeted.

## A Note on Overlap

#### Choose the One That Matters Most

The ten Origins are broad by design. They are meant to establish the foundation of a hero, not account for every event, influence, transformation, or contradiction in their history. Most superhero concepts could reasonably fit more than one Origin when examined closely. That overlap is intentional.

Do not try to split the difference between two Origins simply to capture every nuance of a complicated character. Instead, decide which part of the concept the rules should recognize first. Choose the Origin that represents the hero's deepest foundation — the central truth upon which everything else was built.

A hero raised on another world, altered by an experiment, and carrying an ancient weapon might qualify as Alien, Enhanced, or Gearbound. Any of those answers could be valid. The right choice depends on which element defines the character most strongly and most often shapes how they experience the world.

Let Powers describe what the hero can do. Let Class describe how they act under pressure. Let Merits, Flaws, and character history carry the secondary influences, complications, and details that make the concept unique.

When in doubt, ask one question: *What is the most important truth about where this hero comes from?*

That is the Origin.

# **Chapter Four · Sides**

Sides

Not alignment. Not a moral cage. A simple declaration of narrative position — and what it means for how the world reads you.

This Chapter Covers

* What Side Is (and Isn't)  
* Side and Reputation  
* Heroic  
* Unaligned  
* Villainous  
* Side and Callings  
* Choosing a Side

Every character in HEROIC 5e has a Side.

Not a moral judgment. Not an alignment grid. Not a philosophical category that needs debating before anyone picks up a die. A Side is a simple declaration of narrative position: the broad direction a character's actions tend to move in, and what that means for how the world reads them.

Side shapes two things. It determines which Callings are available to the character. And it sets the emotional register of the hero's public presence — the lens through which their reputation is understood by the people who know it.

Three Sides exist: Heroic, Unaligned, and Villainous. The first two are the natural home of player characters. The third is defined here because the GM needs it fully defined for NPCs, recurring antagonists, and the villains who drive the story. Its place in the game is addressed directly at the end of this chapter.

| Side | The Short Version | Availability |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Heroic | Protect, save, defend, inspire, act for others. In this for the people who cannot protect themselves. | Player Character |
| Unaligned | Own logic. Personal code. Not a villain — not trying to be a hero in the conventional sense either. | Player Character |
| Villainous | Dominate, control, impose. Defined here for GM use with NPCs and antagonists. | GM Use — NPCs Only |

## Side Is Not Alignment

Side does not tell a character what to do in any given situation. It does not lock them into specific choices, restrict their options in play, or punish them for acting in unexpected ways. A Heroic character can do ruthless things. An Unaligned character can make enormous sacrifices for people they barely know. Side is where a character *generally sits* in the moral landscape of the story, not a cage built around their decisions.

It is also not permanent. Side can shift through play if the character's actions consistently push in a new direction. A hero who spends a campaign operating outside institutions, trusting no one, and answering only to their own code may find that Unaligned better describes who they have become. An Unaligned character who keeps choosing to put strangers first, without expectation of reward, may drift toward Heroic.

Side Shift

Side shifts do not happen because of a single decision. They reflect sustained patterns of behavior that the GM and the table recognize together. No mechanical trigger — the table notices, names it, and updates the sheet when the shift has clearly happened.

## Side and Reputation

Reputation in HEROIC 5e is handled through Merits. Fame, Public Trust, Infamy, Street Reputation, Connected, and similar Merits represent how well known a character is and what that recognition means when it matters. A hero with Public Trust 1 is known in their neighborhood and people react accordingly. A hero with Fame 3 changes rooms when they walk into them.

What Side does is color the interpretation of that reputation. Two characters with the same Fame rating produce different reactions from the same crowd if one is Heroic and the other is operating outside the law or building an empire through fear. The Merit establishes that the reputation exists. The Side tells the GM what kind of reputation it is.

In Play

#### Side and Social Response

This matters most in social scenes, where the GM uses the five Response states — covered in Chapter 14 alongside the full social scene rules — to track how NPCs and crowds are reacting in the moment. Starting Response for any given NPC or group is determined by the fiction first: what does this person know about this character, and how do they feel about it? Side and reputation Merits inform that judgment. They do not replace it.

## The Three Sides

### Heroic

Heroic characters protect, save, defend, inspire, and act for others.

This does not mean they are perfect. Heroic characters make mistakes, carry doubts, struggle with the personal cost of the work, and sometimes fail the people they were trying to protect. What defines them is the direction of intention. They are in this for the people who cannot protect themselves. When they show up, the goal is that things go better for someone other than themselves.

How the world reads a Heroic character depends on their reputation Merits and their history in the fiction. A Heroic hero with Public Trust 2 gets a different starting Response from civilians than a Heroic hero who is brand new and unknown. What the Side guarantees is the direction: recognition of a Heroic character, when it exists, tends to produce trust, relief, and the particular emotional weight of someone arriving who is on your side.

When they show up, the goal is that things go better for someone other than themselves.

Heroic characters choose from the Heroic Callings catalog in Chapter 5\. → Chapter 5: Callings  These Callings are built around protection, sacrifice, duty, compassion, justice, and the specific pressure that comes from genuinely caring about the outcome.

### Unaligned

Unaligned characters operate according to their own logic.

That logic might be personal loyalty, professional code, survival, curiosity, self-interest, profit, a private moral framework that does not map cleanly onto heroic idealism, or some combination of all of the above. Unaligned characters are not villains. They are also not trying to be heroes in the conventional sense. They do what makes sense to them, for reasons that are genuinely their own.

This Side covers an enormous range of archetypes:

* The mercenary with a strict personal code who will not hurt civilians no matter what the contract says  
* The information broker who trades in secrets and trusts nobody but occasionally does the right thing for reasons they would deny  
* The former villain building something new who is not ready to call themselves a hero yet  
* The street operator who protects their neighborhood fiercely but has no interest in the wider heroic community and its politics  
* The cosmic wanderer who helps when it suits them and disappears when it does not

How the world reads an Unaligned character is entirely contextual, determined by what their specific reputation Merits represent and who is doing the reading. A street-level operator known for protecting their neighborhood lands differently with criminals than with police. A famous mercenary with Infamy 2 reads differently to their clients than to the heroes who have crossed paths with them. Side establishes that the reputation does not carry a clear moral promise in either direction. Everything else is up to the fiction.

Unaligned characters have access to a broader range of Callings than Heroic characters, including Callings that reflect more self-interested, morally complicated, or personally driven motivations.

### Villainous

Villainous characters seek to dominate, destroy, control, exploit, or impose their will.

This Side exists in the player-facing rules for one reason: the GM needs it fully defined to run NPCs, recurring antagonists, and the villains who drive the story. The mechanics of how a Villainous reputation reads to the world, how it produces fear and obedience rather than trust and hope, how henchmen and civilians and institutions react to its presence, are real parts of the game that belong in this chapter so the full picture is present in one place.

For Player Characters

#### Villainous Is Not a Supported PC Choice

HEROIC 5e is a game about superheroes. The word *hero* is doing real work in that sentence. The system is designed around characters who are, at minimum, operating according to some framework that is not pure domination and harm.

Heroic and Unaligned together cover the full range of morally complicated, legally questionable, personally flawed, sometimes ruthless heroic archetypes the genre contains. There is enormous room within those two Sides for dark, complex, and morally ambiguous characters.

Running a Villainous player character is a conversation for a specific table with specific players and a GM who wants to run that kind of campaign deliberately. It is not something the core game supports or provides Calling frameworks for. The GM section covers Villainous characters fully as NPCs, including how their reputation reads to different groups and how to make them feel like real threats rather than obstacles.

## Side and Callings

Callings are the emotional engine beneath the mask, covered in full in Chapter 5\. → Chapter 5: Callings  Side determines which Callings a character can take.

Heroic characters choose from Heroic Callings. Unaligned characters have access to the full catalog, including Callings that reflect more personal, self-interested, or morally complex motivations. Some Callings can sit on either Side depending on how the character expresses them. A character driven by justice might be Heroic if they work within or alongside institutions, and Unaligned if they have concluded those institutions are broken beyond repair and they are operating outside them entirely.

The Callings chapter lays this out clearly for each entry so there is no ambiguity at character creation.

## When a Side Changes

A Side shift is not a decision made between sessions. It is a conclusion the table arrives at after watching a character behave a particular way for long enough that the old label stopped fitting. By the time the sheet changes, everyone should already have noticed.

The difference is easiest to see as a contrast.

**Not a Side shift.** Panther-Man's player opens a session by announcing that he is Unaligned now. Nothing in the previous four sessions pointed that way. He has been protecting his neighbourhood, working alongside the police when it helped, and putting himself between civilians and harm for the entire campaign. The player wants access to the wider Callings catalog and has worked backward from there. That is a sheet edit wearing a story as a costume. The right answer from the GM is not *no* — it is *not yet, show me*.

**A Side shift.** Over a dozen sessions, Panther-Man watches the same three blocks get worse. He hands a trafficker to the police and sees him back on the corner within a week. He testifies, and the case collapses on a technicality nobody will explain to him. A councilman he had trusted turns out to be taking money from the people hollowing out his neighbourhood. So he stops calling things in. He starts handling them himself, and then he starts handling them harder. When a detective tells him to stand down, he does not. Nobody announces anything. But somewhere around session fifteen, *in this for the people who cannot protect themselves* is no longer the most accurate sentence about how he operates, because he has stopped believing anyone else is coming.

He is still trying to heal his home. That has never changed. What changed is that his logic became his own, and that is precisely what Unaligned means.

The second Panther-Man is not a worse person than the first. Unaligned is not a step down from Heroic, and a drift in either direction carries no judgment. A mercenary who keeps choosing strangers over contracts moves toward Heroic by exactly the same process, on exactly the same kind of accumulated evidence.

**What a Side shift costs: nothing.** There is no roll to make, no penalty to absorb, no resource to spend, and no bonus to collect. The Side entry on the sheet changes and the Callings available to the character change with it. If the hero's underlying motivation has moved as well, that is a Calling change and belongs to a Respec. The Side shift itself is free, because it is not a mechanical event at all. It is character development that the rules agree to notice.

Name it out loud when it happens. A Side shift nobody acknowledges is just a player and a GM holding two different pictures of the same character.


## Choosing a Side

This decision should take about thirty seconds.

Think about the character concept. Think about why this person does what they do and who they do it for.

* If the answer is *"for other people, because that is the right thing to do"* — the character is **Heroic**.  
* If the answer is *"for their own reasons, according to their own code, and the fact that it sometimes helps people is secondary"* — they are **Unaligned**.

If neither of those fits and the player is reaching for something darker, that is a conversation to have with the GM about what kind of campaign this actually is.

Bottom Line

Most heroes in HEROIC 5e are Heroic. Some are Unaligned. Both are valid. Both produce interesting stories. Both have full mechanical support throughout the game.

Pick the one that fits the character and move forward.

# **Chapter Five · Callings**

Callings

Twenty-four Callings. One question each answers: why does this person keep doing this, when doing it costs them so much?

Every hero has a reason.

Not a backstory. Not a power set. Not a class. A reason. The thing that gets them back up after the last fight nearly ended them. The thing that drives them forward when the rational choice would be to stop. The emotional and moral engine underneath everything else.

That is a Calling.

A Calling is not a personality template or a behavioral cage. It does not tell a character what to do in any given scene. What it does is answer a single question that everything else in the game orbits around: *why does this person keep doing this, when doing it costs them so much?*

The answer to that question is where Edge comes from.

## How Callings Work

Every Calling contains three Edge Triggers. One Minor, one Major, one Defining. Each trigger describes a specific moment during play when the Calling fires and the player earns Edge.

| Trigger | Edge Earned | What It Requires |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Minor | 1 Edge | Acting on the Calling in a way that costs something small or creates real narrative weight |
| Major | 2 Edge | A genuine fork in the road. The character chose the harder path because of who they are |
| Defining | 3 Edge | Real cost. Something is lost, damaged, or changed because the Calling demanded it |

Critical Rule

Triggers do not fire for empty roleplay. Saying the right words does not earn Edge. Doing the thing, at the moment it means something, does.

The player is responsible for tracking their own Calling and flagging when a trigger fires. The GM makes the final call, but the job of noticing belongs to the player. If you miss it, you miss the Edge. The GM is already running the world. Calling triggers are yours to watch for.

A trigger must affect the scene in some meaningful way. A consequence must exist, even a small one. If nothing changes and nothing is at stake, the trigger does not fire.

## Choosing a Calling

Choose one Calling at character creation. If nothing in the list exactly fits the concept, talk to the GM. Any Calling can be renamed or reframed to better reflect a specific character without changing its mechanical structure. A character whose concept does not fit any existing Calling can work with the GM to build a new one using the Creating Custom Callings section at the end of this chapter as a framework.

Side availability is listed with each Calling. Heroic characters choose from Callings marked Heroic. Unaligned characters have access to the full list. A Calling marked Heroic only is not available to Unaligned characters without GM discussion about whether the concept genuinely fits.

| Calling | Availability |
| :---- | :---- |
| Adventurer | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Advocate | Heroic only |
| Avenger | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Beast Within | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Boy Scout | Heroic only |
| Champion | Heroic only |
| Defender | Heroic only |
| Fame | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Hotshot | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Human Nature | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Idealist | Heroic only |
| Investigator | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Journeyman | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Lone Wolf | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Mentor | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Mercenary | Unaligned only |
| Outsider | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Protector | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Redeemer | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Role Model | Heroic only |
| Seeker | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Soldier | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Survivor | Heroic · Unaligned |
| Wiseacre | Heroic · Unaligned |

## The Twenty-Four Callings

### Adventurer

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero believes the world has lost something essential: the willingness to step into the unknown without a guarantee of survival and see what happens. They chase that feeling not out of recklessness but out of genuine conviction that the audacious life is the only one worth living. The plan is usually improvised. The results are usually extraordinary.

* **Minor** — The character chooses a direct, high-risk approach when a safer option was available, and something genuinely goes wrong as a result *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character throws themselves into a dangerous situation without backup or preparation, and their intervention meaningfully changes the outcome *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character's refusal to play it safe costs them something significant: an injury, a failed mission, a damaged relationship, or a lost resource that mattered *(3 Edge)*

### Advocate

*Heroic only*

Your hero has found something worth fighting for beyond themselves. A cause, a community, a principle, a movement. They will not knowingly act against it. They will make the case for it whenever they have the platform and sometimes when they do not. The cause is not abstract to them. It has faces.

* **Minor** — The character publicly argues for their cause in a situation where doing so creates friction with allies, authorities, or public perception *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character takes a significant personal risk, turns down a reward, or sacrifices a tactical advantage specifically to advance or protect the cause *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character discovers their cause has been compromised, betrayed from within, or used against its own people, and they must decide what comes next *(3 Edge)*

### Avenger

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Something was taken. Someone was hurt. The world moved on. Your hero did not. They are not consumed by blind rage, at least not most of the time. But every step they take moves toward a reckoning that the world has not yet delivered. The cost of carrying this is something they have chosen to pay rather than let the wrong stand unanswered.

* **Minor** — The character encounters someone or something directly connected to what was taken, and the encounter forces a choice between the mission at hand and the vendetta *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character has the opportunity to strike at what they have been hunting and chooses to protect someone else instead, delaying the reckoning *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character reaches a moment of potential resolution — whether confrontation, forgiveness, or the realization that the reckoning will not deliver what they imagined — and acts on it at genuine personal cost *(3 Edge)*

### Beast Within

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero has a dangerous side. Not metaphorically. Something in them — biological, psychological, supernatural, or otherwise — is a threat to the people around them if it slips its leash. They fight it. Sometimes they lose. The struggle is not a character flaw to be solved. It is the central reality of who they are.

* **Minor** — The character's inner nature creates an unforeseen consequence in a scene: a power that misfires, an instinct that complicates a situation, a response that frightens an ally *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character exercises genuine restraint when losing control would have been easier or even tactically advantageous, and that restraint costs them something *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character loses control in a meaningful way: the inner nature takes over, causes real harm, damages a relationship, or forces the character to face what they actually are *(3 Edge)*

### Boy Scout

*Heroic only*

Your hero believes in doing the right thing. Not the smart thing. Not the tactical thing. The right thing. They will let the villain escape to pull a stranger from a burning car. They will take responsibility when no one would know the difference. They hold themselves to a standard that other heroes find admirable and occasionally infuriating. They are what the word *hero* is supposed to mean.

* **Minor** — The character helps someone with no tactical value to the mission, at a cost to the mission itself *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character publicly takes responsibility for a failure or mistake that they could have concealed, and faces real consequences for the honesty *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character allows a villain or significant threat to escape, or accepts a major personal loss, because doing the right thing in this moment required it *(3 Edge)*

### Champion

*Heroic only*

Your hero cannot walk past a wrong. Not because they know the victim, not because it advances a cause, not because someone is watching. Because it is wrong and they were there. They do not require a personal stake. The existence of an injustice is sufficient reason to act. This is not righteousness. It is something simpler and harder to argue with.

* **Minor** — The character intervenes in a situation with no personal connection, no tactical benefit, and no promise of reward, and the intervention creates a real complication *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character challenges a person, institution, or authority they cannot easily afford to challenge, specifically because an injustice demands a response *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character pays a significant personal price — public standing, a relationship, physical harm, or something they needed — because refusing to act was not an option they could live with *(3 Edge)*

### Defender

*Heroic only*

Your hero has placed themselves between danger and everyone who cannot protect themselves. This is not something they decided once. It is something they decide again every time the situation demands it. They are the first one into harm's way and the last one to leave it. When an ally is about to be blindsided or a hostage is about to be executed, this is the hero who moves without being asked.

* **Minor** — The character places themselves physically between a threat and someone who cannot protect themselves, absorbing or redirecting the danger *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character holds a position against a superior threat alone so that others can escape, recover, or regroup *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character is defeated, critically injured, or loses something significant specifically because they refused to abandon the people they were protecting *(3 Edge)*

### Fame

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero wants to be known. Not as a symptom of insecurity but as a genuine drive: to matter, to be seen, to leave a mark on the world that cannot be ignored. The hunger for recognition shapes how they engage with every situation and every audience. They are not always wrong about their own importance. The problem is they cannot stop needing to prove it.

* **Minor** — The character uses their powers or heroic abilities openly in a public or semi-public situation without concealing their identity, creating a consequence they did not fully anticipate *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character forces their way into a situation they were deliberately excluded from, or publicly claims credit for an outcome in a way that creates friction with allies *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character faces a genuine public failure, humiliation, or loss of recognition, and the way they respond to it reveals something true and costly about who they are *(3 Edge)*

### Hotshot

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero wants to be the best and is constitutionally incapable of pretending otherwise. They are the first one into the fight and the last one to admit they are outclassed. They boast, they compete, they push harder than necessary to prove a point nobody asked them to prove. They are also usually the one still standing when it matters most, which is the part that is hardest to argue with.

* **Minor** — The character targets the most dangerous opponent in a scene specifically because they are the most dangerous, taking on a risk others would reasonably avoid *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character's arrogance or competitive drive directly creates a complication: a miscalculation, a damaged alliance, or a problem that would not exist if they had shown some restraint *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character delivers the decisive blow against a genuinely powerful enemy, or is taken out of the fight at a critical moment and must watch the victory happen without them *(3 Edge)*

### Human Nature

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero is not fully human, and they feel the distance. They study the people around them. They practice emotions they do not yet fully understand. They make genuine efforts to bridge a gap that may never fully close. The tragedy and the beauty of this Calling is that the effort itself — the reaching toward something they cannot quite grasp — is one of the most human things there is.

* **Minor** — The character attempts to engage with a human emotional experience, succeeds or fails in a way that is genuine and specific rather than performed, and the attempt creates a meaningful moment in the scene *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character prioritizes an emotional or human consideration over a tactical or logical one, choosing connection over efficiency at real cost *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character makes a sacrifice for their teammates or for someone they care about, acting from something that functions like love or loyalty even if they cannot fully name it *(3 Edge)*

### Idealist

*Heroic only*

Your hero believes the world can be better and acts as though it already is. Not naively. They have seen enough to know exactly how bad things get. They choose the standard anyway. They hold it even when it costs them, even when the world demonstrates once again that it does not deserve it. The point of an ideal is not that it is achievable. The point is that it is worth holding.

* **Minor** — The character upholds their ideal in a situation where doing so creates meaningful friction, pressure, or disadvantage *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character is tested against their ideal by someone with power or authority and refuses to compromise it, facing real consequences for the refusal *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character is genuinely shaken in their conviction — either convinced they are unworthy to hold it or required to defend someone else's right to hold theirs — and the resolution costs something real *(3 Edge)*

### Investigator

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero approaches the world like a detective approaches a crime scene: nothing is coincidence, everything means something, and the truth is always more interesting than the obvious explanation. They are never happier than when their wits are genuinely challenged. The problem is they sometimes pursue the mystery past the point where the mystery is safe to pursue.

* **Minor** — The character pursues a lead, follows a clue, or presses for information in a situation where doing so creates friction, danger, or a complication for the team *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character chooses to help people or solve a problem despite having an active investigation that demands their attention, and the choice costs them progress on both fronts *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character uncovers a truth that changes the nature of the situation significantly, or walks away from a case specifically to protect the people around them from what following it would cost *(3 Edge)*

### Journeyman

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero does not have a grand philosophy. They became a hero because it was the right thing to do, they stayed because the work was real, and they keep going because stopping would mean all of it was for nothing. They do not strive to be great. They refuse to be mediocre. That turns out to be enough.

* **Minor** — The character points out an uncomfortable truth about a situation or a person, in a way that creates real friction, because it needed to be said *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character draws on their own past experience to help an ally through a personal setback or professional failure, at genuine cost to their own time, resources, or emotional reserves *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character resolves something they have been carrying for a long time — whether a trauma, a past failure, or a complicated relationship — and moves forward from it in a way that changes them *(3 Edge)*

### Lone Wolf

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero works alone. Or they say they do. The reality is that they are constitutionally incapable of abandoning people who depend on them, no matter how loudly they announce their indifference. They push people away and then refuse to let those same people come to harm. The contradiction is the character. They have not resolved it. They may never resolve it.

* **Minor** — The character pushes back against someone else's plan, authority, or leadership in a way that creates genuine tension rather than just flavoring the scene *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character goes into a dangerous situation alone rather than accepting help, and the decision to go alone creates a specific consequence they would have avoided with backup *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character makes a meaningful commitment to a team or a person, taking a step they cannot easily walk back, at the cost of the independence they have been protecting *(3 Edge)*

### Mentor

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero measures their success by what they build in others. They are called to teach, to protect the growth of someone less experienced, to prepare people for dangers they cannot yet see. The joy of this Calling is watching someone become more than they were. The cost is that the people you care about most are also the most effective weapons anyone can use against you.

* **Minor** — The character takes time to teach, guide, or support someone in their development, at a cost to the immediate tactical situation or their own priorities *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character intervenes to protect or recover their protégé from a setback, failure, or danger, placing themselves at significant risk or disadvantage to do so *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character either prepares their protégé for a threat the character may not survive, or is forced to let them go, knowing the separation is the right thing and accepting the loss of it *(3 Edge)*

### Mercenary

*Unaligned only*

Your hero gets paid. That is the arrangement and they are honest about it in a world where most people are not honest about what they want. Money is the metric. Help, hurt — it does not matter in principle. In practice, they have a code about what they will and will not do for money, and that code is non-negotiable even when violating it would be profitable. The code is the only thing that makes this sustainable.

* **Minor** — The character is offered significantly more money or a better contract to do something their code prohibits, and they decline it and face a real consequence for the refusal *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character renegotiates, walks away from, or defies a contract because the situation has changed in a way that their code cannot accommodate, at significant financial or professional cost *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character abandons a paying arrangement entirely to do something their code requires, with no financial compensation and a meaningful loss of resources, standing, or opportunity *(3 Edge)*

### Outsider

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero is hated or feared for something they cannot change. A power, a nature, a past allegiance, a visible difference, a history the world has decided makes them suspect. They have learned to navigate a world that does not fully accept them, and that navigation has given them a perspective and a resilience that the people who fear them will never understand. They may want to be left alone. They cannot stop being what they are.

* **Minor** — The character is recognized or treated differently because of what they are, and this creates meaningful friction in a scene rather than serving as background detail *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character's outsider status is weaponized against them — used by an enemy, an institution, or someone they trusted — and they face the full weight of that targeted prejudice *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character reconciles a relationship that their outsider status had damaged or destroyed, moving to a new stage with real consequence, or accepts that the relationship cannot be salvaged and moves forward from that loss *(3 Edge)*

### Protector

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero is not protecting humanity in the abstract. They are protecting specific people: a neighborhood, a family, a community, a city block, a team. The distinction matters enormously. When the threat is to the people they have claimed, the response is personal in a way that duty alone could never produce. This is not obligation. This is love in the form of action.

* **Minor** — Someone within the character's protected circle is threatened or harmed, and the character responds in a way that prioritizes them over the larger mission *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character makes a significant sacrifice specifically for their protected circle: resources, standing, safety, or an opportunity that mattered *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character fails to protect someone they claimed as their own, and faces the full weight of that failure rather than deflecting it *(3 Edge)*

### Redeemer

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero is carrying something. A past action, a choice they cannot take back, a cost that was paid by someone who did not deserve to pay it. They are not certain redemption is achievable. They are trying anyway. Every person they save is part of a debt they are not sure they can ever fully repay, and the uncertainty is something they have learned to live with rather than resolve.

* **Minor** — The character is forced to confront their past directly — an old enemy, someone affected by what they did, or evidence of the harm they caused — and they do not run from it *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character extends mercy, forgiveness, or genuine help to someone who reminds them of who they used to be, at personal cost and without expectation of reward *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character either defeats a major threat without surrendering to their darker impulses when every circumstance would have justified it, or fails that test and must face what they have done *(3 Edge)*

### Role Model

*Heroic only*

Your hero carries a community's hope. Whether they chose this or not, they represent something larger than themselves: a people, a cause, a legacy, a proof of concept that the world needs to exist. They shoulder the weight of expectation, hide personal pain to maintain the symbol, and act not just for themselves but for every person watching who needs to see that someone like them can do this. The burden is real. They carry it anyway.

* **Minor** — The character absorbs public failure, unfair criticism, or personal pain in front of an audience and maintains the symbol rather than responding to the wound *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character faces a significant setback while trying to change the mind of a public figure, authority, or institution, and the attempt costs them standing, resources, or influence *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character steps back from leadership, prominence, or recognition specifically to protect the movement or community they represent, accepting the personal cost of the sacrifice for the greater good *(3 Edge)*

### Seeker

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero cannot leave a mystery alone. The need to understand, to find the truth, to pull back whatever is concealing what is actually happening, is not intellectual curiosity. It is closer to compulsion. They will follow a lead past the point of safety. They will ask the question even when the answer is going to make everything worse. The truth matters more to them than the comfort of not knowing it.

* **Minor** — The character pursues information, answers, or understanding in a situation where the pursuit creates danger, friction, or a meaningful complication *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character uncovers a truth that significantly changes the nature of the situation or the relationships in it, and the discovery comes with a real cost *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character follows a line of inquiry to its conclusion even when the conclusion is dangerous, personally devastating, or something they genuinely would have preferred not to know *(3 Edge)*

### Soldier

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero values the chain of command, the mission, and the professional standard of someone who has done this long enough to know what it costs when things fall apart. They may fight for money, for duty, or for validation they would never name aloud, but they fight with discipline and they do not abandon the people depending on them. The code they follow is internal and non-negotiable even when orders conflict with it.

* **Minor** — The character follows a superior's orders or defers to a chain of command in a situation where their personal judgment conflicts with the directive, and the compliance creates a consequence *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character defies orders or breaks from the chain of command specifically because following them would violate their personal code, and faces real consequences for the insubordination *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character stands with their people in direct defiance of their orders, or abandons a personal loyalty to complete the mission, and either choice costs them something they cannot recover easily *(3 Edge)*

### Survivor

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero is still here. That is not a small thing. Against the odds, against the evidence, against every circumstance that should have finished them, they are still here. They protect others partly because they know exactly what it costs when nobody does. They are not driven by a cause or an ideal. They are driven by the refusal to let what happened to them happen to someone else on their watch.

* **Minor** — The character endures a situation that directly echoes their past trauma or the circumstances that made them who they are, and keeps moving forward rather than stopping *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character uses their survival experience to pull someone else through a crisis, putting their own recovery or resources at significant risk to do it *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character faces the direct source or equivalent of what they survived — whether a person, a situation, or a consequence — and acts in the face of it at genuine personal cost *(3 Edge)*

### Wiseacre

*Heroic · Unaligned*

Your hero uses humor as a tool, a shield, and occasionally a weapon. They crack a joke in the middle of a fight, deflect every sincere conversation with a well-timed quip, and make everyone around them feel the absurdity of what they are all doing before the terror sets in. The humor is not a flaw. It is load-bearing. The question is what happens when the situation is too heavy for it.

* **Minor** — The character uses humor or levity in a genuinely dangerous or emotionally charged moment, and the choice to joke rather than engage sincerely creates a real consequence *(1 Edge)*  
* **Major** — The character's humor is stripped away by circumstance and they have to engage with a situation or a person directly, without the armor, at emotional cost *(2 Edge)*  
* **Defining** — The character either declares a situation genuinely serious and drops the performance entirely in a way that changes the scene, or says exactly the wrong thing and irrevocably damages a relationship they valued *(3 Edge)*

## Creating Custom Callings

The twenty-four Callings above are intentionally broad. They cover the full range of heroic and unaligned archetypes the genre regularly produces. But superhero fiction is enormous, and no list covers everything.

If a concept does not fit any existing Calling, the player and GM can build a custom one. The process is straightforward.

Custom Calling Framework

* **Start with the motivation.** What does this character want, and why do they keep risking themselves to pursue it? The answer should be specific enough to produce real moments at the table — not so specific that it only fires in one type of scene.  
* **Build three triggers.** Minor at 1 Edge, Major at 2 Edge, Defining at 3 Edge. Each trigger should describe a specific action or event, not a disposition. "Acts protectively" is not a trigger. "Steps between an attack and someone who cannot defend themselves, taking the hit" is a trigger.  
* **Check the bar.** The Minor trigger should be achievable in most sessions by a player who is paying attention and playing into the Calling. The Major trigger should fire occasionally. The Defining trigger should fire rarely and should always mean something when it does.  
* **Check the Side.** A custom Calling should be honest about which Sides it fits. Some Callings work across Heroic and Unaligned. Some belong to one Side only. The Calling's triggers should make it clear where it lives.  
* **Run it by the table.** A custom Calling should feel fair to everyone. If the triggers are too easy, they inflate Edge and flatten the drama. If they are too hard, the player never fires them and the Calling becomes decoration.

Design Note

#### Renaming and Reframing

The existing Callings are also open to renaming and reframing. An Avenger whose specific vendetta has been resolved might reframe the Calling as *Reckoning* , shifting the trigger language to reflect a character who now pursues justice for others rather than themselves. The structure stays. The story moves.

Three more, to show the range.

*Beast Within* assumes something biological or supernatural straining against a leash. An artificial hero running a combat subroutine they cannot suppress fits all three triggers untouched — the misfire, the costly restraint, the loss of control. Call it *The Override*.

*Human Nature* is written for a hero who is not human and feels the distance. That fits a synthetic person. It fits equally a god worshipped for nine centuries who has forgotten how to be spoken to rather than prayed at. Rename it *So Long Away*; no trigger changes.

*Mercenary* takes the heaviest hand, because all three of its triggers name money. But the shape underneath is a code that holds when the profitable answer argues against it, and that survives the currency being swapped.

What cannot change is the machinery: three triggers at 1, 2 and 3 Edge, each describing an action rather than a disposition. Rewrite the trigger text as far as the new framing needs, and leave the count and the Edge values alone. A concept that needs a fourth trigger is not a reframe — build it from scratch.


# **Chapter Six · Character Classes**

Character  
Classes

Eight classes. One question each answers: what does this hero instinctively do when the pressure hits?

This Chapter

* What Class Is  
    
* Class Summary Table  
    
* Beacon  
    
* Bruiser  
    
* Guardian  
    
* Sentinel  
    
* Strategist  
    
* Striker  
    
* Vanguard  
    
* Warden  
    
* Multiclassing  
    
* Beyond Level 10  
    
**A Class is not what your hero can do.** That belongs to Powers.
    
**A Class is not where your hero comes from.** That belongs to Origins.
    
**A Class is how your hero acts when the pressure hits.**

It is the question answered instinctively, without thinking, in the moment between the building starting to fall and the decision to act. A Bruiser does not calculate. They apply force until something stops resisting. A Vanguard does not dig in. They move. A Guardian does not retreat. They put themselves between the threat and whoever needs protecting. A Sentinel does not react to the fight. They read it before it starts.

Class is the operating system running beneath everything else. Beneath the powers, the training, the reputation, the story. It is what your hero is made of when there is no time to be anything else.

HEROIC 5e uses eight Classes, each tied to one of the eight Ability Scores. Every Ability Score describes a quality of a person. Each Class takes one of those qualities and asks: what kind of hero does this produce? Strength produces the Bruiser. Dexterity produces the Vanguard. Constitution produces the Guardian. Fighting produces the Striker. Intelligence produces the Strategist. Wisdom produces the Warden. Perception produces the Sentinel. Charisma produces the Beacon.

Design Note

#### Method, Not Source

Class does not mean a Bruiser must be physically strong above all else, or that a Beacon must be the most charming person in the room. A psionic Bruiser attacks minds like a battering ram. An armored Vanguard moves through the battlefield with mechanical precision. A monstrous Guardian absorbs punishment that would destroy anything else. What matters is the method, not the source of the power behind it.

Every Class must feel heroic at Level 1\. Not almost heroic. Not promising. *Heroic.* A Level 1 Bruiser already hits like trouble. A Level 1 Guardian already stands in front of things that should not be survived. A Level 1 Beacon already changes the emotional temperature of the room. Leveling makes a hero deeper, sharper, and more experienced. It does not make them wait half the campaign to become themselves.

Class features follow the same structure for every Class: two Core Features at Level 1, a Secondary Feature at Level 3, Major Features at Levels 5 and 7, and a Capstone at Level 10\. Six features total. The features are designed to be fast to resolve, clear in their effects, and meaningful from the first session.

## The Eight Classes

| Class | Primary | Hit Die | Save Training | Effect Value | Rec. Mod. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Beacon | Charisma | d8 | CHA, WIS | 10 \+ CHA \+ PRO | \+1 |
| Bruiser | Strength | d10 | STR, CON | 10 \+ STR \+ PRO | \+1 |
| Guardian | Constitution | d12 | CON, STR | 10 \+ CON \+ PRO | \+2 |
| Sentinel | Perception | d8 | PER, DEX | 10 \+ PER \+ PRO | \+1 |
| Strategist | Intelligence | d8 | INT, PER | 10 \+ INT \+ PRO | \+0 |
| Striker | Fighting | d8 | FIG, DEX | 10 \+ FIG \+ PRO | \+0 |
| Vanguard | Dexterity | d8 | DEX, PER | 10 \+ DEX \+ PRO | \+0 |
| Warden | Wisdom | d8 | WIS, CON | 10 \+ WIS \+ PRO | \+2 |

## Class Feature Progression

| Level | Feature Gained |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Two Core Class Features |
| 3 | Secondary Feature |
| 5 | Major Class Feature |
| 7 | Major Class Feature |
| 10 | Class Capstone |

### Beacon

| Primary | Hit Die | Saves | Effect Value | Rec. Mod. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Charisma | d8 | CHA, WIS | 10 \+ CHA \+ PRO | \+1 |

Beacons shape people. Leadership, inspiration, intimidation, morale, emotional influence, and force of personality define them. They are not a social class in the narrow sense. They are emotional gravity. They change how people behave simply by entering the room, and they change how people fight simply by being in the fight.

Some Beacons inspire hope. Others project fear. Some unite teams through words that land at exactly the right moment. Others dominate through sheer presence, humiliating enemies into mistakes and provoking villains into taking their eyes off what matters.

The Beacon is not moral. They are social force. Their method is influence over the emotional state of everyone around them, ally and enemy alike. When pressure hits, they make everyone else feel it differently.

**Commanding Presence** — Level 1 · Core Feature

While you are conscious and perceived by allies within Medium range, those allies have Advantage on saves against Shaken and Frightened. This is passive and requires no action to maintain.

Additionally, when you make an Influence or Intimidation check, you may add your WIS to the roll in addition to your CHA.

**Taunt** — Level 1 · Core Feature

Once per Turn, as a Bonus Action, choose one creature you can perceive and provoke them. Roll 1d20 \+ CHA \+ Prowess against that creature's static Social Defense Value. On a success, until the start of your next Turn that creature's Attack Value is reduced by 3 against any target other than you. The first attack the taunted creature makes against you this Turn grants you or one ally you can perceive Advantage on one attack roll or Active Defense roll before the start of your next Turn. On a Strong Success, the creature is also Shaken until the end of its next Turn. On a HEROIC Success, the creature is Frightened of you until the end of its next Turn instead of Shaken.

**Rally the Human Spirit** — Level 3 · Secondary Feature

Once per Turn, when one of the following triggers occurs, you may spend your Bonus Action to grant one ally within Medium range who can perceive you one benefit from the list below. Each ally may only receive this benefit once per Turn.

**Triggers:** you or an ally you can perceive defeats an enemy; you succeed on an Influence or Intimidation check; you successfully Taunt a creature; you use Second Wind or Steady On; or you spend Edge.

**Benefits:** temporary HP equal to your CHA plus your Prowess; Advantage on their next save before the end of their next Turn; 10 feet of additional movement on their next Turn; or end one instance of Shaken currently affecting them.

**Rally Cry** — Level 5 · Major Feature

Once per encounter, as your Action, every ally who can perceive you immediately gains temporary HP equal to your CHA plus your Prowess, ends one Condition of their choice currently affecting them, and may immediately move up to half their speed as a free action. This movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks.

**Break Them** — Level 7 · Major Feature

When you successfully Taunt a creature or apply Shaken or Frightened to any creature through any Beacon feature or Power, you may spend your Bonus Action to spread that emotional state. Roll 1d20 \+ CHA \+ Prowess against the static Social Defense Value of every enemy within Short range of the original target. Each enemy whose Social Defense Value your roll meets or beats becomes Shaken until the end of their next Turn.

**Living Legend** — Level 10 · Capstone

Once per encounter, when you hit with an attack or Power that deals damage, you may spend your Bonus Action to declare Living Legend. The effect depends on your Degrees of Success on that attack roll compared to the target's Defense Value:

* **Normal Success:** until the start of your next Turn every ally who can perceive you adds your CHA to their damage rolls on a hit.  
* **Strong Success:** the Normal Success effect applies, and roll 1d20 \+ CHA \+ Prowess once and compare it to the Willpower Defense Value of every enemy who can perceive you. Any enemy whose Defense Value your roll meets or beats is Shaken until the end of its next Turn.  
* **HEROIC Success:** both previous effects apply, and every ally who can perceive you immediately regains their Reaction if they have spent it this round.

### Bruiser

| Primary | Hit Die | Saves | Effect Value | Rec. Mod. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Strength | d10 | STR, CON | 10 \+ STR \+ PRO | \+1 |

Bruisers solve problems through force. Not just strength, though they have plenty of that. The Bruiser weaponizes impact itself. They turn every environment into a battlefield, every collision into a threat, and every engagement into a contest of momentum that they intend to win. A psionic Bruiser attacks minds like a battering ram. An energy Bruiser channels power through pure aggressive output. A gadgeteer Bruiser builds for maximum impact. What they share is method: force applied until something stops resisting.

The Bruiser is often first through the wall and last one standing when the smoke clears.

**Heavy Hitter** — Level 1 · Core Feature

When you hit with an attack or Power that deals damage, add your STR to the damage roll. This applies to all damage types and all attack forms, not melee only. It is in addition to any other modifier you already add to damage.

Because melee damage already adds STR as its damage modifier, this feature adds STR a second time on melee attacks — and adds STR to ranged, mental, and social attacks that would otherwise never benefit from it. A Bruiser throws a car as hard as they punch.

**Heavy Impact** — Level 1 · Core Feature

Once per encounter, when you hit with an attack or Power that deals damage, you may spend your Bonus Action to declare Heavy Impact. Roll 1d20 \+ STR \+ Prowess against the target's static STR Save Value. On a success, choose one: push the target 10 feet plus five feet per point of your STR modifier; knock the target Prone; or leave the target Dazed until the end of their next Turn. On a Strong Success, choose two. On a HEROIC Success, choose all three.

**Breakthrough** — Level 3 · Secondary Feature

Choose one damage type when you take this feature. Your attacks and Powers ignore Resistance to that damage type entirely. Against all other damage types, when you deal damage to a target that has Resistance or flat damage reduction, reduce that Resistance or reduction by your Prowess before it is applied.

**Devastating Force** — Level 5 · Major Feature

Once per encounter, when you hit with an attack or Power that deals damage, you may spend your Bonus Action to declare Devastating Force before rolling damage. Deal maximum damage on all dice rather than rolling. Then compare your attack roll against the static Defense Value of every creature within 10 feet of the primary target, using the same defense type as the original attack. Any creature whose Defense Value your roll meets or beats takes half the maximum damage dealt to the primary target.

**Unstoppable** — Level 7 · Major Feature

When you are reduced to half your maximum HP or below, for the rest of the encounter you gain temporary HP equal to your STR modifier at the start of each of your Turns, and you have Advantage on all saves. This activates automatically and requires no action.

**Irresistible Force** — Level 10 · Capstone

Your attacks and Powers treat Immunity to your Breakthrough damage type as Resistance instead. This Resistance is not subject to the reduction granted by Breakthrough.

Once per encounter, when you hit with an attack or Power that deals damage, you may spend your Bonus Action to trigger **Chain Strike**. Make up to a number of additional attacks equal to your Prowess, each against the same target or a target in the same Zone as the previous one, using the same attack type. These attacks are exempt from the secondary attacks rule and are not made at Disadvantage. Each hit deals 2 less damage than the previous strike, cumulatively — the first chain strike takes −2, the second −4, and so on. Chain strikes after the first use standard damage rolls and do not inherit modified damage totals from other features. The chain ends early if you miss, run out of targets, or the damage reaches zero. Each target may only be struck once per Chain Strike.

### Guardian

| Primary | Hit Die | Saves | Effect Value | Rec. Mod. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Constitution | d12 | CON, STR | 10 \+ CON \+ PRO | \+2 |

Guardians endure. They absorb punishment, place themselves between danger and the people who cannot protect themselves, and remain standing long after the situation has stopped making sense. Durability alone is not what defines them. Many heroes are durable. What defines a Guardian is the active choice to protect: to intercept, to absorb, to refuse to let the attack through.

A Guardian transforms defense into battlefield influence. Enemies who target an ally instead of the Guardian do so at their own risk. Enemies who target the Guardian directly find something that does not go down easily and gets more dangerous as it approaches the edge.

The Guardian is often the last one standing, not because they are lucky, but because they are built for exactly this.

**Stand Between** — Level 1 · Core Feature

When an ally within Short range is hit by an attack you can perceive, you may use your Reaction to intercept. The ally takes no damage from that attack. You take the full damage instead. No Reaction from any source other than your own features and Powers may be declared in response to this specific damage instance.

The method belongs to the character: a force field thrown up at the last second, a body placed directly in the path, a shield raised between the threat and the target, sheer physical refusal to let it through. The instinct belongs to the class.

**Iron Presence** — Level 1 · Core Feature

While you are conscious, allies within Short range have Advantage on saves against fear, the Shaken condition, and forced movement effects. This is passive and requires no action to maintain.

Once per Turn, you may spend your Bonus Action to rally an ally within Short range you can perceive. That ally may immediately spend one Hit Die as a free action outside of their own Turn.

**Breakthrough Resistance** — Level 3 · Secondary Feature

Choose one damage type when you take this feature. You have Resistance to that damage type. When you use Stand Between to intercept an attack of that damage type, you take the minimum possible damage from that attack rather than rolling.

**Guardian's Mark** — Level 5 · Major Feature

Once per encounter at the start of your Turn, as a free action, you may mark one creature you can perceive. The mark lasts until the start of your next Turn.

While a creature is marked, its Attack Value is reduced by 3 against any target other than you. If a marked creature attacks any target other than you, you may use your Reaction to immediately move up to your full speed toward that target and use Stand Between without expending a separate Reaction for that interception.

**Immovable** — Level 7 · Major Feature

You cannot be moved, knocked Prone, or Restrained against your will unless the effect that causes it deals damage exceeding half your current HP in a single instance. You are immune to the Shaken condition.

When you use Stand Between, you may reduce the intercepted damage by your CON before applying it to yourself.

**Last One Standing** — Level 10 · Capstone

The first time each encounter you are reduced to 25% of your maximum HP or below, you immediately gain temporary HP equal to your CON multiplied by your Prowess. Until the start of your next Turn, you may use Stand Between as a free action without spending your Reaction. Any creature that deals damage to you before the start of your next Turn is automatically marked by Guardian's Mark, regardless of whether your per-encounter mark has already been used and regardless of how many creatures are currently marked.

### Sentinel
