Alter local weather conditions within Short range (26–50 ft): create wind gusts, generate rain or fog, drop temperature, call small lightning strikes. Resistance to lightning and cold damage. Immune to harm from weather effects of any natural origin. Tier 1 access.

Weather Control 2  
*Tier 2 Passive*

Weather control extends to Medium range (51–120 ft) and can affect a full Zone. Immunity to lightning and cold damage (replaces Resistance). Sense atmospheric conditions and predict natural weather changes up to 24 hours in advance with perfect accuracy. Tier 2 access.

Weather Control 3  
*Tier 3 Passive*

Atmospheric mastery reaches world-class scale — affect weather across an entire city district from a central position. Weather attacks ignore Resistance to lightning and cold damage entirely. Once per encounter when you deal lightning or cold damage, arc the effect to one additional target within Close range (25 ft) of the original for half damage with no additional roll. Tier 3 access.

Weather Control 4  
*Tier 3 Apex Passive*

Once per day, enter **Eye of the Storm** for 1 minute: weather effects extend to Long range (121–300 ft) automatically; all weather conditions you create last until you dismiss them rather than having a duration; immunity to all damage from energy sources as the storm absorbs and redirects it; any creature starting their Turn within Short range (26–50 ft) Power Effect Value vs. STR — Failure: the target is knocked Prone by wind force.

#### Combat Powers

**Lightning Strike** — Tier 1 · At-Will · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 1*

Call a bolt down out of whatever sky is available. Straightforward damage with a Dazed rider waiting on a Strong Success — no setup, no cost, available every Turn of every fight. Weather Control does enormous things later; this is the one you actually throw most rounds.

* Range: Short (26–50 ft)  
* Attack: 1d20 \+ DEX \+ WIS \+ Prowess vs. Dodge  
* Hit: Default damage track (lightning). Strong Success: Power Effect Value vs. CON or Dazed until end of your next Turn.

**Wind Blast** — Tier 1 · Encounter · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 1*

Put a wall of moving air through up to three people standing near each other. The damage is slight; the point is that they end up fifty feet away, flat, and in a direction you chose rather than one they would have picked. Repositioning three enemies at once is worth more than most Tier 1 damage.

* Range: Short (26–50 ft) — up to three targets within Close range (25 ft) of each other  
* Attack: 1d20 \+ DEX \+ WIS \+ Prowess vs. Dodge of each target  
* Hit: 1 Power Die \+ WIS modifier bludgeoning damage. Power Effect Value vs. STR — Failure: pushed Short range in a direction you choose \+ knocked Prone; Success: pushed Close range only.

**Storm Surge** — Tier 2 · Encounter · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 2*

Call a concentrated weather event across a Zone — persists until end of your next Turn. Ice for terrain and Slowed, lightning for damage and Dazed, fog for taking the sight of everyone but yourself while you keep your own. One Encounter power carrying three genuinely different answers — work out what the fight needs before you commit, because you only get one.

Choose one storm type at activation:

* Ice Storm: Area (30-ft radius within 50–120 ft) becomes difficult terrain from ice. Power Effect Value vs. DEX — Failure: 2 Power Dice cold damage \+ Slowed; Success: 1 Power Die cold damage only.  
* Lightning Squall: Power Effect Value vs. DEX — Failure: 2 Power Dice lightning damage \+ Dazed; Success: 1 Power Die lightning damage only.  
* Fog Bank: Area becomes heavily obscured; all creatures in it are Blinded while inside it. You can see normally through your own fog.

**Gale Force** — Tier 2 · Encounter · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 2*

Until start of your next Turn, generate hurricane-force winds. All creatures without flight or magnetic/gravitational anchoring within Medium range (51–120 ft) must spend double movement to move against the wind direction (you choose direction at activation). Ranged attacks against the wind direction have Disadvantage. Against flying creatures without superpowered flight, Power Effect Value vs. STR at the start of each of their Turns — Failure: forced Short range in the wind direction, and knocked Prone if they contact a surface.

**Hurricane Spiral** — Tier 3 · Encounter · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 3*

Open a vortex thirty feet across and let it take everything inside. Enemies are dragged to the centre and held there by the wind, then thrown outward when it collapses — taking further damage from whatever they hit on the way. Gather, hold, and scatter in a single Action, which is three jobs most sets need three powers to do.

* Range: Medium area (30-ft radius within 50–120 ft)  
* Attack: 1d20 \+ DEX \+ WIS \+ Prowess vs. Dodge of each creature  
* Hit: 3 Power Dice bludgeoning damage. Power Effect Value vs. STR — Failure: pulled to the center of the vortex (Restrained until end of your next Turn as wind holds them) then blasted Short range outward at end of the effect, taking 1 Power Die additional damage on impact with any surface. Success: pulled to center only with no Restrained condition.

**Tempest** — Tier 3 · Daily · Action

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 3*

Unleash a full atmospheric catastrophe across the battlefield. A massive storm front descends. For the remainder of the encounter, the affected area has these persistent effects you do not need to maintain: area is heavily obscured by rain and cloud; wind force imposes Disadvantage on all ranged attacks; lightning strikes at the start of each of your Turns — make one Lightning Strike attack against any target in the area as a free action each Turn.

* Range: Long area (60-ft radius within 120–300 ft)  
* On activation: Power Effect Value vs. STR — Failure: 5 Power Dice lightning and cold damage combined \+ knocked Prone \+ Slowed until end of your next Turn; Success: half damage only.  
* Duration: Persistent storm for the remainder of the encounter.

#### Set-Specific Utility Powers

**Weather Sense** — Tier 1 · Utility

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 1*

Automatically know local weather patterns and predict natural weather changes up to 24 hours in advance with perfect accuracy. Sense approaching storms, temperature changes, and atmospheric pressure shifts before they are visible. Extensive applications in navigation, mission planning, and disaster response.

**Control Weather** — Tier 1 · Utility

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 1*

Over one minute of concentration, alter weather conditions in a 1-mile radius around you. Create or clear clouds, change temperature by up to 20 degrees, create or stop rain, generate or dispel fog, increase or decrease wind speed. Gradual changes — weather transitions over the minute of concentration. Extreme weather such as full storms requires Tier 2 or higher.

**Storm Travel** — Tier 2 · Utility

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 2*

Ride storm systems as transportation by merging with a storm front. Travel at atmospheric speed: cross a city in minutes, regional distances in under an hour. Arrive riding lightning or wind, appearing dramatically from the storm itself. Cannot bring passengers through storm travel unless they have weather immunity or equivalent protection.

**Suppress Weather** — Tier 3 · Utility

*Prerequisite: Weather Control 3*

Over one scene of sustained effort, suppress a major weather event: reduce a hurricane to tropical storm intensity, stop a tornado, clear a blizzard from a populated area, or prevent flooding by redirecting rainfall. Does not eliminate the weather system, only reduces it to a manageable level within range. The power that makes a weather controller an essential disaster response resource.

#### Enhancements

* **Chain Lightning:** When Lightning Strike achieves a Strong Success, the lightning arcs to a second target within Close range (25 ft) of the original for 1 Power Die lightning damage with no additional attack roll required.  
* **Persistent Storm Surge:** Storm Surge's effects persist until the start of your Turn after next rather than your next Turn — two full rounds of battlefield effect.  
* **Tailwind:** You and allies of your choice within Short range (26–50 ft) gain \+10 ft of movement speed as you generate favorable winds around them. Passive benefit active whenever you are conscious and not Stunned or Incapacitated.  
* **Eye of Calm:** Designate a Close range (25-ft radius) area around yourself as the eye of your storm. Within this area your allies are unaffected by weather effects you generate — no Disadvantage from wind, no difficult terrain from ice, no obscurement from fog. Enemies entering the eye are immediately subjected to full weather effects when they cross the boundary.

#### Limitations

* **Emotional Weather:** Powers respond to your emotional state in ways you cannot always control. When Frightened or Shaken, GM may introduce uncontrolled weather effects in your vicinity — sudden gusts, unexpected lightning, temperature drops. These are environmental hazards the GM manages, not attacks you control. \+1 Power Pick.  
* **Obvious Manifestation:** Power use is visible from miles away — storm clouds gather when you concentrate, lightning marks your position, wind patterns are unmistakable to any observer. Stealth while using Weather Control powers is essentially impossible. \+1 Power Pick.  
* **Slow Build:** Most powerful weather effects require atmospheric time to develop. Storm Surge and Hurricane Spiral cannot be used on the first Turn of combat. Tempest requires two rounds of preparation (two Turns of lesser weather effects already active) before it can be activated. \+1 Power Pick.

### **Creating New Power Sets**

HEROIC 5e cannot possibly include every conceivable superpower without becoming an encyclopedia. While the book provides dozens of fully realized Power Sets, your table will almost certainly want to create something new — whether it is a highly specific concept or a fresh take on a classic idea.

This section gives players and GMs a clear, consistent framework to design balanced, playable Power Sets that integrate seamlessly with the rest of the game.

#### **Design Principles**

* **Thematic Unity**: All powers should feel like expressions of one central idea.  
* **Governing Ability**: Every Power Set must have **one** primary governing Ability Score (STR, DEX, CON, FIG, INT, WIS, CHA, or PER). This determines the set’s Effect Value.  
* **Power Die**: Always use the campaign’s Power Die (d8 Street Level, d10 Mid-Level, d12 World Class).  
* **Balance Target**: New sets should feel roughly comparable in strength and versatility to published sets such as Gravity Control, Energy Generation, or Super Strength.  
* **Playability**: Powers must be fast and intuitive to resolve at the table.

#### **Step-by-Step Creation Process**

1. **Define the Core Concept** Write a single clear sentence that captures the essence of the Power Set.  
2. **Choose the Governing Ability** Select the Ability Score that best represents the set’s primary expression.  
3. **Build the Core Track** (usually 3–4 purchases) These represent increasing mastery and unlock better powers.  
4. **Design At-Will Powers** (2–4 options) Reliable abilities you can use every round.  
5. **Design Encounter Powers** (2–4 options) Stronger, limited-use abilities with significant impact.  
6. **Design Daily / Apex Powers** (1–2 options) Game-changing, high-cost abilities.  
7. **Design Utility Powers** (2–4 options) Non-combat, exploration, or situational tools.  
8. **Create Enhancements** (4–6 pairs) Improvements that can be added to existing powers (2 Enhancements \= 1 Power Pick).  
9. **Optional: Thematic Limitations** (2–4 options) Meaningful restrictions that grant \+1 Power Pick when taken.

#### **Power Strength Guidelines**

| Tier | Scope & Impact |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Tier 1** | Personal / street-level. Reliable but contained. |
| **Tier 2** | City / impressive scale. Strong area or sustained effects. |
| **Tier 3** | World / reality-bending scale. Dramatic, long-lasting, or massive effects. |

**Damage / Effect Baseline** (adjust for theme):

* At-Will: 1–2 Power Dice \+ modifier  
* Encounter: 2–3 Power Dice \+ modifier \+ strong condition  
* Daily: 4+ Power Dice or major narrative effect

**GM Approval**

All new Power Sets require GM approval. Start conservative — it is easier to strengthen a weak set than to nerf an overpowered one. Test new sets for 2–3 sessions before making them permanent.

---

### **Example Power Set: Absorption**

#### **Absorption** *(Governed by CON)*

You can absorb incoming energy, kinetic force, matter, or exotic effects and convert them into personal power, healing, or redirected force. You are the living sponge, the impact-absorbing tank, or the hero who grows stronger the harder you are hit.

##### Core Track

* **Absorption Core 1**: You can absorb physical impacts and energy attacks. Reduce incoming damage of one chosen type (bludgeoning, piercing, slashing, fire, cold, lightning, radiant, or necrotic) by 1 Power Die.  
* **Absorption Core 2**: Your absorption now applies to two damage types. Once per encounter when you absorb damage, gain temporary HP equal to half the amount reduced (rounded down).  
* **Absorption Core 3**: You can absorb a third damage type. You may store absorbed energy and release it later.  
* **Absorption Core 4 (Apex)**: You gain Resistance to all physical and energy damage types you have absorbed this encounter. Stored energy no longer dissipates at the end of the encounter.

##### At-Will Powers

* **Absorb & Redirect**: Reaction when you take damage of an absorbed type. Reduce the damage by 1 Power Die \+ CON, then make a ranged attack (CON) against a target within Short range dealing the same amount as bludgeoning damage.  
* **Fortified Shell**: Bonus Action. Gain temporary HP equal to 2 × CON modifier until the start of your next turn.

##### Encounter Powers

* **Energy Conversion**: Reaction when hit by an attack. Absorb the full damage, then immediately make an attack using the absorbed energy: 2 Power Dice \+ CON damage of a type you can absorb.  
* **Kinetic Burst**: When you absorb at least 10 damage in one hit, release it as a Short area burst: 3 Power Dice bludgeoning damage. Targets make DEX save vs your Effect Value or be pushed 15 ft and knocked Prone.

##### Daily Power

* **Total Absorption**: For 1 minute, you automatically absorb all incoming damage from absorbed types. Each time you absorb damage, gain temporary HP equal to half the absorbed amount. Once during this effect, you may unleash **Overload** as a Bonus Action: Short range burst dealing 5 Power Dice \+ CON damage (choose bludgeoning or one absorbed type).

##### Utility Powers

* **Matter Conversion**: You can safely absorb and dissipate non-harmful matter (walls, debris, etc.) over 1 minute, clearing paths or creating simple tools.  
* **Power Leech**: After 1 minute of physical contact with a willing or helpless target, absorb one of their temporary conditions or ongoing effects (GM discretion).  
* **Adaptive Resilience**: During a Breather, change which damage types you can absorb.

##### **Enhancements** (2 for 1 Power Pick)

* **Rapid Conversion**: When you use Absorb & Redirect, you may do so without spending your Reaction again this turn.  
* **Sustained Charge**: Stored energy lasts until the end of the encounter.  
* **Feedback Loop**: When you gain temporary HP from absorption, one ally within Close range gains half that amount.  
* **Kinetic Rebound**: When you absorb a melee attack, the attacker takes damage equal to your CON modifier.  
* **Energy Battery**: You may store up to 3 absorbed hits.  
* **Metabolic Absorption**: You can absorb and convert certain toxins, poisons, or diseases into healing.

##### **Limitations** (+1 Power Pick each)

* **Overload Risk**: The GM may call for a Burnout Check when you store large amounts of energy.  
* **Selective Only**: You can only absorb two damage types at a time.  
* **Painful Conversion**: Whenever you absorb damage, you also take 1 Power Die of untyped damage (cannot be reduced).

# Chapter Twelve  ·  General Utility Powers

General Utility Powers

Standalone powers for customizing your hero beyond your primary Power Sets. Minor superhuman capabilities, biological traits, sensory enhancements, and niche abilities — each costing 1 Power Pick.

General Utility Powers are standalone powers that let you customize your hero beyond your primary Power Sets. They represent minor superhuman capabilities, biological traits, sensory enhancements, and niche abilities that fit a hero's concept without requiring full Power Set investment. Each General Utility Power costs 1 Power Pick and is available according to your Campaign Rank and Tier limits.

How General Utilities Interact with Power Sets

General Utility Powers do not replace Power Sets. If a dedicated Power Set already covers a capability as a Core Track benefit, taking the General Utility version provides a lighter expression of that capability — not an equivalent one. Where a General Utility overlaps with a Power Set, the entry notes it explicitly.

A hero who takes a General Utility version of an ability and later invests in the corresponding Power Set should use the Power Set's superior version. The General Utility does not provide additional benefit on top of the Power Set.

The passive HP recovery stacking rule from Playing the Game applies throughout: passive per-Turn HP recovery from multiple sources uses the highest value only and does not stack.

Tier 1 General Utilities Available at Street Level and above 1 Power Pick each

Adhesive Grip

Climb any surface including overhangs and ceilings without making an Athletics check. Your hands and feet adhere to glass, metal, stone, and similar surfaces. Move at full speed while climbing and do not fall if you take damage during the climb.

Does not stack with Super Agility's wall-crawling utility — use whichever is superior.

Animal Empathy

Communicate simple ideas and emotions with animals as though you shared a language. Animals are naturally inclined toward friendliness unless you or your allies have harmed them recently. Advantage on Influence, Insight, and Survival checks to interact with, calm, or direct animals.

Does not stack with Animal Powers' Animal Communication. If you have that Power Set, use it instead.

Aquatic Adaptation

Gain a swimming speed equal to your walking speed and breathe underwater indefinitely. Ignore the effects of cold water and pressure at normal ocean depths. At Mid-Level Campaign Rank or higher, also survive extreme deep-sea pressure without harm.

Camouflage

As a Bonus Action, blend into your surroundings through pigment changes, adaptive coloration, or similar biological or technological adaptation. Advantage on Stealth checks and may attempt to Hide while obscured. While motionless in a natural environment, extremely difficult to detect without powers specifically designed to pierce concealment.

Echolocation

Perceive the world through sound, vibration, radar, or similar non-visual sensing. Gain blindsight out to Close range (25 ft). Detect invisible creatures through this sense unless they specifically move to avoid producing detectable signals.

Covers all non-visual sensing variants: echolocation, radar sense, tremorsense, and sonar. Choose the version that fits your concept. The mechanical effect is identical.

Emergency Shield

Once per encounter, as a Reaction when you or one ally within Close range (25 ft) would take damage, project a brief protective barrier. The protected creature reduces that damage by your Prowess.

Does not stack with Energy Shield or similar Power Set features.

Environmental Adaptation

Choose one hostile environment when you purchase this power: extreme heat, extreme cold, hard vacuum, deep underwater, or high radiation. Survive in that environment without harm and do not need to make saves against its natural effects. You still take damage from deliberate attacks using that environment as a weapon.

This power may be purchased more than once, choosing a different environment each time.

Gliding

When you fall, spread wings, a cape, or similar surfaces to glide. Fall at a rate of only 10 feet per round instead of the normal rate and move horizontally up to your full Speed while gliding. Take no falling damage when landing from a controlled glide. Cannot gain altitude through gliding alone.

**Rising Air.** Where a strong updraft exists — a thermal, the windward face of a building, the convection column above a fire — you may work the current to gain height. Roll Acrobatics (DEX) to ride the lift, or Athletics (STR) to hold form against it: DC 15 in a strong, stable updraft, higher in marginal or turbulent conditions. On a success, gain one Zone (25 ft) of altitude. The GM decides whether a usable current exists. In still air, none does.

This is not Flight. If you have the Flight Power Set, use that instead.

Healing Touch

As an Action, touch one creature and restore HP equal to your Prowess plus your WIS. You may use this once per Breather. Does not function on yourself.

Distinct from the Regeneration Power Set's passive recovery — does not trigger the passive HP recovery stacking rule since it is an active action rather than passive per-Turn healing.

Invisibility

As an Action, turn invisible until the end of your next Turn. While invisible, you gain the Hidden condition: attacks against you have Disadvantage and your attacks have Advantage. The Hidden condition ends if you attack, use a power that produces a visible effect, or take damage.

Sound and scent still betray your presence — a creature with enhanced hearing or smell can detect you and negate the Hidden condition normally.

This power may be taken as a Sustained Power, maintained with a Bonus Action each Turn. The source — biological transparency, technological camouflage, light-bending, psychic deflection — is chosen at character creation and is always consistent with the hero's concept.

Low-Light Vision

See in dim light as if it were bright light and in darkness as if it were dim light out to Close range (25 ft). Cannot see in total magical or supernatural darkness through this power alone.

A lighter version of Super Senses' Darkvision. If you have Super Senses Core Track 1, use that instead.

Psychic Resistance

Gain Resistance to psychic damage. This does not provide Advantage on psychic saves — that broader protection belongs to Telepathy's Mind Shield.

The passive HP recovery stacking rule does not apply here since this is damage Resistance rather than healing.

Quick Recovery

During a Breather, recover additional HP equal to your Prowess when spending Hit Dice. This bonus applies once per Breather regardless of how many Hit Dice you spend. Also gain Advantage on saves against lingering fatigue, exhaustion, and environmental stress during Downtime.

Does not trigger the passive HP recovery stacking rule since it applies only during Breathers, not passively per Turn.

Spirit Speech

Perceive and briefly communicate with spirits of the recently dead. A spirit is accessible if it died within the last week and its remains, a significant personal possession, or the location of its death is within Short range (26–50 ft). Willing spirits communicate freely for up to one minute. With one minute of contact with a corpse or death location, you also experience the subject's final moments — what they saw, heard, and felt in their last minutes. This is not a complete record: distress and the disruption of death affect what is retrievable.

You automatically sense the presence of spirits in your vicinity even when they do not speak. Advantage on Occult checks related to death and spiritual activity.

Stabilize

As a Bonus Action, touch a dying creature and stabilize them instantly without requiring a Medicine check. The creature stops making saves and is stable at 0 HP. They remain Unconscious.

A faster version of the standard Medicine stabilization — costs a Bonus Action rather than an Action.

Super Jump

Your jumping distance is multiplied by 5\. Ignore falling damage from heights equal to or less than your maximum jump distance. Leap horizontally, vertically, or between structures at comic-book scale, clearing gaps and reaching heights that would normally require climbing.

Swinging

Using webbing, grapple lines, cables, vines, or similar anchored lines, move by swinging between anchor points. You move up to twice your Speed as part of your normal movement, provided the route offers anchor points — buildings, trees, cliff faces, ceiling structures, bridge spans. Open ground, open water, and open sky offer none.

**The Arc.** Each swing drops 25 feet below your starting elevation at the low point, then rises to your ending elevation. If less than 25 feet of clearance exists below you, the low point is ground level. You may end a swing up to one Zone (25 ft) above where you began, but you cannot climb continuously — each swing must dip before it rises.

Attacks and effects that trigger on movement — Opportunity Attacks, Zone hazards, readied actions — resolve against the low point of the arc, not the endpoints. A hero who swings across a burning Zone passes through it.

Take no falling damage from a controlled swing. If the line is cut, the anchor fails, or you become Stunned, Slowed, or Prone mid-swing, you fall from the arc's current height.

This is not Flight. You cannot hover, and you cannot gain altitude without anchor points.

Telepathic Whisper

Send brief one-way mental messages of up to ten words to one willing creature you can see within Short range (26–50 ft). The target receives the message clearly regardless of ambient noise or language barriers. You cannot receive messages back through this power and cannot affect unwilling creatures.

This is not Telepathy and cannot be used for two-way communication or mental influence.

Thermal Vision

Perceive heat signatures through darkness, smoke, fog, and light cover out to Medium range (51–120 ft). Invisible creatures still emit detectable heat unless specifically shielded against thermal detection. Blocked by materials designed to mask heat signatures.

Toxin Resistance

Advantage on saves against poison, disease, venom, narcotics, intoxicants, radiation poisoning, and airborne chemical hazards. This does not grant immunity — full immunity belongs to Poison Immunity at Tier 2\.

Universal Translator

After hearing a spoken language for at least one minute, understand basic meaning and communicate simple ideas in that language. Complex technical language, coded speech, ancient dialects, or alien concepts with no equivalent in known languages may still require checks or be beyond translation. A practical communication tool, not fluency.

Tier 2 General Utilities Available at Mid-Level Campaign Rank and above 1 Power Pick each

Adrenaline Surge

Once per encounter as a Bonus Action, call on reserves of biological or superhuman endurance. Gain temporary HP equal to your Prowess plus your CON. These temporary HP last until the end of the encounter or until depleted.

Distinct from Super Durability Branch Powers — does not stack with them. If both grant temporary HP in the same encounter, use the higher pool only.

Aura of Fear

Once per encounter as a Bonus Action, project an unsettling presence. Choose one creature within Close range (25 ft) that can perceive you. Power Effect Value vs. WIS. On a failure the creature suffect Value. Failure: the creature is Shaken until the end of its next Turn. Success: no effect.

Minor single-target disruption. Area fear effects and the Frightened condition belong to dedicated Power Sets such as Super Presence and Shadow Control.

Bio-Electric Shock

As an Action, deliver a bio-electric charge through touch, claws, or conductive contact. Make a melee Power Attack against one creature within Close range (25 ft). On a hit, deal 2 Power Dice lightning damage. The target rolls 1d20 \+ CON against your Power Effect Value. Failure: Dazed until the end of its next Turn. Success: no additional effect beyond the damage.

Can also be used outside combat to overload, disrupt, or power small electrical systems through contact.

Burrowing

Gain a burrowing speed of Close range (25 ft) through earth, sand, clay, and soft stone. Leave a tunnel behind that other creatures may follow. Cannot burrow through reinforced concrete, solid metal, force barriers, or supernaturally reinforced structures unless another power specifically grants that capability.

Dimensional Pocket

Possess a small extradimensional storage space capable of holding up to 50 pounds or 5 cubic feet of material. Retrieving or storing an item costs a Bonus Action. The pocket is invisible and inaccessible to other creatures unless a power specifically interacts with extradimensional spaces. The pocket collapses if you die, depositing its contents in your space.

Object Reading

As an Action, touch an object and receive a brief psychic impression of the last creature to handle it meaningfully. Learn one of the following: their emotional state at the time, one sensory impression from the moment of contact, or one simple fact about what they did with the object.

Requires at least one round of concentration and produces vague impressions rather than detailed memories. Mundane objects with many handlers produce only the most recent or most emotionally charged impression.

Phase Shift

Once per encounter as a Bonus Action, become partially intangible until the start of your next Turn. While intangible, gain Resistance to non-energy weapon damage (bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing from physical sources) and may move through occupied spaces as difficult terrain. Cannot move through solid objects entirely in this state.

Moving through solid objects entirely belongs to Super Speed's Vibration Phase. Does not stack with Vibration Phase if both are held.

Photographic Reflexes

After observing a physical skill, combat technique, or trained maneuver for at least one round, gain Advantage on checks and attack rolls to replicate it during the current scene. Covers trained physical techniques only: athletics, acrobatics, martial techniques, and skilled physical performances.

Cannot copy Powers, supernatural abilities, or effects that require specific biological or technological capabilities you do not possess.

Poison Immunity

Immune to ordinary poisons, toxins, venoms, gases, chemical intoxicants, and natural diseases. Supernatural, cosmic, or specially engineered toxins designed to affect beings with your physiology may still affect you at GM discretion.

Super Speed Utility

Your Speed increases by 20 feet in all movement modes you currently possess. Passive enhancement applying to all forms of your movement.

This is not the Super Speed Power Set and does not grant Speed Actions, Disadvantage immunity on secondary attacks, or any other Super Speed feature. It is a simple speed increase.

Technopathy

As an Action, interface mentally with technological systems within Close range (25 ft). Read simple machine status, unlock basic electronic systems, bypass non-military security, issue simple commands to compatible devices, and detect nearby active technology. Complex systems, military-grade security, and alien technology may require a Technology check at the GM's set DC.

A lighter version of Machine Interface capabilities. If you have the Machine Interface Power Set, use that instead.

Venom Strike

When you hit a creature with an unarmed strike or while grappling it, deliver a venomous payload through claws, fangs, a stinger, or injected toxin as part of that hit. Power Effect Value vs. CON. Failure: the creature gains the Poisoned condition until the end of its next Turn. Success: no additional effect.

This does not add damage dice — the damage comes from the attack itself. The venom only delivers the condition.

Tier 3 General Utilities Available at World Class Campaign Rank only 1 Power Pick each

Astral Projection

Once per day as an Action, project your consciousness out of your body. Your projected form may travel up to Medium range (51–120 ft) from your body. Your body remains Unconscious and is vulnerable while you are projected. Your projected form can observe, speak, and use non-physical powers but cannot interact with physical objects or make physical attacks.

The projection lasts for up to one scene or until you choose to return. If your body is killed while you are projected, you return to your body immediately and must make a save.

A lighter version of the capability. The Sorcery Power Set's Astral Projection covers greater range and more detailed rules for extended astral travel.

Power Mimicry

Once per encounter as an Action, copy one Tier 1 Power you have directly observed being used within Close range (25 ft) during this encounter. You may use the copied power once before the end of the scene using your own Governing Ability and Prowess. You cannot copy Core Track steps, Apex powers, powers above Tier 1, or powers from Power Sets that require biological or technological components you do not possess.

The copied power uses your Power Effect Value and attack bonus.

Power Mimicry Upgrade

*Prerequisite: Power Mimicry*

Your mimicry now extends to Tier 2 powers. Once per encounter you may copy one Tier 2 power observed being used within Close range (25 ft) and use it once before the end of the encounter.

Additionally, you may retain one copied Tier 1 power for up to 24 hours after observing it. You may only retain one power this way at a time.

True Sight

Perceive the world as it truly is within Close range (25 ft). See invisible creatures, see through mundane and supernatural disguises, perceive illusions for what they are, identify transformed beings in their true form, and detect hidden dimensional distortions and extradimensional spaces.

You still require line of sight unless another power removes that restriction. True Sight does not automatically reveal the source or purpose of what you perceive, only its true nature.

# **Chapter Thirteen  ·  Equipment & Gear**

Equipment & Gear

Weapons, armor, gadgets, vehicles, invention, and crafting. Equipment rules should never slow the table down — they should create interesting decisions, dramatic moments, and occasionally spectacular failures.

Heroes punch through walls, fire energy blasts, fly at supersonic speeds, and reshape the battlefield with their minds. Equipment exists alongside all of that. It does not replace it.

Gear is the physical layer of a hero's life: the tools they carry, the vehicles they drive, the weapons they use when powers are not enough or not appropriate, and for some heroes, the devices they build that make them who they are. A billionaire in a powered suit is defined as much by their engineering genius as by what the suit can do. A street-level detective's lockpicks and scanner are as important to them as any power. A legacy hero's inherited equipment carries the weight of history.

This chapter covers everything a hero might own, use, build, or lose. For groups who want detailed resource tracking, the Resources and Wealth section at the end of this chapter provides an optional system for handling money, purchasing power, and the practical economics of heroic life. Groups who prefer narrative resource handling use the Cash Flow, Wealth, and Patron Merits from **Chapter 9** and do not need anything from that section.

## The Role of Gear

What Gear Is — and Is Not

**Gear is not a Power Set.** A hero who builds a sonic cannon from spare parts is using Technology, invention, and engineering genius. The sonic cannon is the result of those things expressed as equipment.

**Gear is not a Talent.** Talents represent trained edges and signature techniques. A hero with the Marksman Talent shoots better. The gun they are shooting is gear.

**Gear is not a Merit.** Cash Flow covers financial resources. The Vehicle Merit covers owning a significant vehicle. The Base of Operations Merit covers having a headquarters. Those Merits establish that things exist. This chapter covers how those things work mechanically.

Gear provides three things: **access** to situations the hero could not otherwise reach, **utility solutions** to problems that powers and skills alone cannot address, and **capability expressions** that fit the hero's concept without requiring a full Power Set purchase.

The line between gear and Powers matters when it comes to the **Gear Dependent Flaw**. A hero whose sonic cannon is a convenience carries it because it helps. A hero whose sonic cannon is the source of their primary offensive capability needs the Gear Dependent Flaw to reflect what happens when it is taken away. If losing a piece of equipment would significantly reduce the hero's effectiveness in their core role, it should carry the Gear Dependent Flaw at the appropriate Rating.

## Standard Equipment

Standard equipment is anything a hero might reasonably carry without special access, wealth, or a Merit to justify it. The GM should not require a roll or a resource check for a hero to have a flashlight, a first aid kit, a charged phone, or appropriate clothing for their concept.

The Rule of Thumb

If a reasonable person in the hero's position would have it, they have it. A street-level detective has a notebook, a camera, and a burner phone. A corporate hero has a tailored suit and an expense account. An alien hero has whatever their Origin package specifies.

When a hero wants something that is not obvious from their concept, the GM applies one of three rulings: they simply have it because it makes sense, they can get it with a Prepared Cache Merit use, or they need to seek it out through play, a Merit, or a Resource check if using the optional rules.

Standard equipment *never* produces Power-level effects. A hero cannot assert they have a portable EMP device that shuts down all electronics in a building just because they have a Technology Specialty. That is invention territory, not standard equipment.

## Weapons and Combat Equipment

Most heroes in HEROIC 5e do not rely on weapons as their primary combat expression. Powers, Class features, and martial training carry the offensive load. When a hero does use a weapon, it fits into one of four categories.

Unarmed

Punches, kicks, grapples, headbutts, and anything the hero does with their body.

Attack: 1d20 \+ FIG \+ Prowess

Damage: 1 Power Die \+ STR

The Martial Artist Talent improves unarmed damage and opens additional options.

Light Weapons

Knives, batons, collapsible weapons, small firearms, and anything that can be concealed or used quickly.

Attack: 1d20 \+ FIG \+ Prowess in melee, or 1d20 \+ DEX \+ Prowess at range

Damage: 1 Power Die \+ STR in melee, or \+ DEX at range

May carry the Concealable or Thrown property.

Heavy Weapons

Swords, axes, rifles, shotguns, heavy clubs, and anything that requires both hands or significant physical commitment.

Attack (melee): 1d20 \+ FIG \+ Prowess

Attack (ranged): 1d20 \+ DEX \+ Prowess

Damage: 1 Power Die \+ delivery damage modifier \+ 2

Not Concealable.

Ranged Weapons

Bows, crossbows, thrown weapons, firearms of all types, and any weapon that attacks at a distance.

Attack: 1d20 \+ DEX \+ Prowess — defends against **Dodge** rather than Parry/Block

Damage: 1 Power Die \+ DEX

Range: Short without penalty. See Range and Disadvantage in Chapter 15 for attacks beyond a weapon's stated band.

### Special Properties

| Property | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Reach | The weapon can attack targets in an adjacent Zone without moving into it. Useful for controlling space and making Opportunity Attacks across Zone boundaries. |
| Thrown | Can be used as a ranged attack, rolling DEX to hit and adding STR to damage. After being thrown it must be retrieved or replaced. Range: Close to Short without penalty. |
| Concealable | Can be hidden on the hero's person without a visible bulge. Notice or Investigation checks to detect it suffer Disadvantage. |
| Armor-Piercing | Ignores the flat bonus provided by armor. Does not ignore Resistance from Powers or Class features. |
| Nonlethal | Designed to incapacitate rather than kill. A target reduced to 0 HP by a Nonlethal weapon falls Unconscious and makes Grit Saves. |

### Improvised Weapons

Anything that is not a weapon but used as one — a fire extinguisher, a chair, a section of pipe, a car door. Improvised weapons deal 1 Power Die \+ STR damage and have no special properties unless the fiction supports one. The Improvised Fighter Talent significantly improves this option.

## Armor and Protection

Most heroes do not wear traditional armor. Their protection comes from Powers, Class features, and Active Defense rolls. For heroes who do wear armor, it reduces the damage that gets through rather than making them harder to hit — armor never modifies an Active Defense roll.

How Armor Works

Armor applies *after* an attack has already hit. Subtract the armor's flat damage reduction from the incoming damage before it is applied to HP; the Active Defense roll itself is unaffected, and a hero in heavy armor is no harder to hit than one in none. Flat damage reduction from armor stacks with flat damage reduction from any other source. On an NPC, armor is listed with its gear rather than built into the printed Defense Value.

Light Armor

Reinforced clothing, tactical vests, thin ballistic weave.

Flat damage reduction 2

Does not restrict movement or impose penalties. Concealable under loose clothing with a successful Stealth check.

Heavy Armor

Full tactical gear, ballistic plate carriers, medieval-style armor, dense environmental suits.

Flat damage reduction 4

Imposes Disadvantage on Acrobatics and Stealth checks. Not Concealable.

### Powered Armor (as Gear)

A commercially available exoskeleton or military powered suit has the following profile:

* Flat damage reduction 3  
* Built-in strength enhancement: \+2 to STR-based checks while wearing  
* Specific built-in features defined at acquisition with GM approval (integrated communications, environmental sealing, enhanced sensors, etc.)

Powered Armor vs. the Armor Systems Power Set

A hero whose powered armor is their primary Power Set expression is using the Armor Systems Power Set from Chapter 11\. That armor is a Power Set, not equipment, and does not use the rules in this section.

The distinction: if the armor could theoretically be removed and given to another character who would benefit from it equally, it is gear. If the armor is an expression of the hero's unique genius, cannot be easily replicated, and losing it would remove their primary powers, it is a Power Set with the Gear Dependent Flaw.

## Gadgets and Specialist Equipment

Gadgets are single-use or limited-use items that produce specific effects — smoke grenades, sensor drones, medical injectors, grappling lines, signal jammers, and specialized restraints that populate a hero's utility belt.

Gadgets *never* directly replicate Power Set effects. A smoke grenade does not replicate the Concealment power. It creates smoke, which is an environmental effect the GM adjudicates based on the fiction. A specialized restraint does not replicate Telekinetic Bind. It physically restrains a target, which requires the target to be cooperative or already subdued.

### Using Gadgets

* **Simple gadgets** activate with a Free Object Interaction or Bonus Action.  
* **Complex gadgets** require an Action and sometimes a Technology or relevant Skill check. The GM sets the DC using the standard difficulty scale based on the complexity of the task and the pressure of the situation.  
* Gadgets used in combat that require targeting use the same attack and defense resolution as Powers: roll an attack, the defender rolls Active Defense, compare results, apply Degrees of Success.

### Acquiring Gadgets

* **Standard gadgets:** available through Cash Flow, standard equipment assertion, or the Prepared Cache Merit.  
* **Restricted or military-grade gadgets:** require Legal Authority, Connected, Patron, or Gear Access at an appropriate Rating.  
* **Custom or unique gadgets:** require the Invention rules below.

The Prepared Cache Merit and Gadgets

A hero with Prepared Cache 1 can declare they previously stored one gadget in a plausible nearby location once per session. This covers the classic superhero moment of "I stashed an EMP device here last week just in case." The GM may reject items that are implausible given the hero's concept or the location.

## Vehicles

Vehicles are significant equipment. A hero who owns a notable vehicle should have the Vehicle Merit at the appropriate Rating. A hero who drives a car they borrowed or commandeered does not need the Merit for that one scene.

### Vehicle Ratings

All vehicles have three ratings that govern their mechanical expression in play.

#### Speed Rating

How fast the vehicle moves. Expressed in Zones per Turn for combat and chase scenes.

| Speed Rating | Category | Combat Speed |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Rating 1 | Standard road vehicle | 1–2 Zones per Turn |
| Rating 2 | High-performance vehicle or light aircraft | 2–3 Zones per Turn |
| Rating 3 | Jet aircraft, speedboat at full throttle | 3–4 Zones per Turn |
| Rating 4 | Supersonic aircraft or spacecraft | Effectively unlimited within atmosphere |

#### Armor Rating

How much punishment the vehicle can absorb before becoming non-functional. Expressed as hits, using the same framework as Minion tiers from the Combat chapter.

| Armor Rating | Category | Hits |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Rating 1 | Standard civilian vehicle | 3 hits |
| Rating 2 | Reinforced or military vehicle | 5 hits |
| Rating 3 | Heavily armored or advanced vehicle | 8 hits |
| Rating 4 | Iconic super-vehicle | 12 hits or more (defined at creation) |

#### Special Features

Specific capabilities defined when the vehicle is acquired. A motorcycle has none. An advanced pursuit vehicle might have:

* **Stealth Systems:** Disadvantage on checks to detect or track it.  
* **Pursuit Systems:** Advantage on Vehicles checks during chases.  
* **Ejection Systems:** The hero can exit safely at any speed.

Special features are negotiated with the GM at acquisition and should reflect the vehicle's concept and the hero's resources.

### Vehicles and Zone Movement

A vehicle moves according to its Speed Rating during combat and chase scenes. A hero piloting a vehicle uses their Vehicles Skill for maneuvers. Standard movement and Dash apply: a vehicle can move its Speed Rating in Zones as a standard move, or double that on a Dash.

### Vehicle Combat

When heroes fight from, on, or against vehicles:

* Attacking a vehicle targets its Armor Rating using normal attack and defense resolution.  
* The vehicle's Armor Rating does not roll Active Defense — attacks against vehicles compare the attacker's roll against a static Defense Value of **10 \+ Armor Rating \+ pilot's Prowess**.  
* Vehicles do not take conditions. They take hits. When a vehicle reaches 0 hits it is disabled or destroyed, determined by the fiction and the GM.  
* A hero attacking from inside or on top of a moving vehicle rolls attacks with **Disadvantage** unless they have a Vehicles Specialty or a relevant Class feature or Talent that removes the penalty.  
* A hero attacking a moving vehicle from outside rolls attacks with **Disadvantage** unless the vehicle is stationary or they have a relevant Talent.

### Pursuit Rules

A chase is a structured encounter using the Zone system. The GM defines the starting Zone positions of pursuer and quarry. Each Turn, both sides take actions using the Vehicles Skill or relevant movement Powers.

The goal for the **pursuer** is to reduce the distance to Close range and maintain it. The goal for the **quarry** is to increase the distance to Long range or beyond and maintain it, or reach a specific escape point.

| Chase Action | Mechanic |
| :---- | :---- |
| Push | Attempt to increase or decrease distance by 1 Zone. Vehicles check DC 15\. |
| Maneuver | Attempt to force the other party into difficult terrain or a hazard. Opposed Vehicles check. |
| Hazard | Introduce an environmental complication. Vehicles check DC 15 for the other party to navigate. |
| Attack | Make a standard attack while maintaining speed, at Disadvantage unless a relevant Talent removes it. |

Degrees of Success in Chases

A **Strong Success** on a Push gives the acting party 2 Zones of movement instead of 1\.

A **HEROIC Success** produces a Momentum Effect: the pursuer gets Advantage on their next check, or the quarry loses a Turn of movement from a collision or near-miss.

The chase ends when the pursuer achieves Close range and can make a direct intervention, when the quarry reaches their escape point, when a vehicle is disabled, or when the fiction makes continuing the chase impossible.

## Invention and Crafting

Some heroes do not just use gear. They build it. HEROIC 5e uses two modes of invention: **Downtime Invention** for planned creation with proper resources and time, and **Kitbashing** for improvised field assembly when there is no time and no guarantee of safety.

Both modes use the Technology Skill and the standard difficulty scale. Both use Degrees of Success to determine the quality of the result. Neither produces permanent Power Set effects without the appropriate Power Set and Origin to support it.

### Who Can Invent

* Any hero with Technology trained can attempt Downtime Invention.  
* Kitbashing requires Technology trained and is significantly harder without a relevant Specialty such as Electronics, Power Armor, or Security Systems.  
* A hero's Origin and Power Sets determine what they can build. A Super-Science hero can invent devices that replicate effects from their existing Power Sets up to their current Tier. A Gearbound hero can upgrade and modify their existing gear. A hero without a relevant Origin or Power Set can build mundane technological devices but cannot build devices that replicate Power effects.

### Downtime Invention

During Downtime, a hero with Technology trained may attempt to build a device. The process has four steps.

#### Step 1: Define the Device

The player describes what the device does, what effect it replicates (if any), and what Power Set and Tier it draws from. The GM approves the concept or suggests modifications.

#### Step 2: Determine Resources

The GM determines what materials are needed based on the device's complexity. Resources are either:

* **Available:** the hero has the appropriate Cash Flow, Wealth, or Patron to cover them without a check.  
* **Limited:** the hero must make a Resource check or narrative effort to acquire them.  
* **Unavailable:** the materials cannot be found without a significant story arc.

#### Step 3: Make the Technology Check

Downtime Invention DCs

15Simple utility device with a known effect

20Complex device replicating an Encounter-tier Power effect

25Cutting-edge device pushing the limits of known science or replicating a powerful effect

Add relevant Specialties and Expertise as normal.

#### Step 4: Apply Degrees of Success

| Result | Outcome |
| :---- | :---- |
| Normal Success | The device works as intended. It has a number of uses equal to the hero's Prowess before requiring repair or recharging during a Breather or Downtime. It functions reliably within its defined parameters. |
| Strong Success | The device works as intended and the player may define one additional benefit within reason — extra uses, a secondary minor effect, reduced size making it Concealable, or faster activation time. The GM approves the benefit. |
| HEROIC Success | The device exceeds expectations. It has unlimited uses until destroyed, has an unexpected additional capability the player and GM define together, or is so well-built that it provides a bonus to the first use in a session. |
| Failure | The device does not work. The materials are spent. The hero may try again during their next Downtime if they can acquire new materials. |

Invented Gear and the Gear Dependent Flaw

If a hero builds a device that becomes central to their heroic identity and primary combat effectiveness, the Gear Dependent Flaw applies at the Rating appropriate to how devastating its loss would be. A hero who builds a utility scanner they use occasionally does not need the Flaw. A hero whose entire offensive capability comes from a self-built energy projector should take Gear Dependent at Rating 2 or 3\.

### Kitbashing

Kitbashing is invention under pressure. No proper workspace, no guaranteed materials, no time to do it right. It is the hero pulling a device apart and rebuilding it into something new in the middle of a collapsing building because there is no other option.

Kitbashing requires available materials. The GM determines whether the scene contains materials appropriate to what the hero is attempting. A hero cannot Kitbash a sonic emitter in an empty room. A hero absolutely can Kitbash a signal jammer from a broken drone, a phone, and a fire suppression system panel.

#### Action Cost

* **Simple devices** (one effect, no moving parts, immediate use): Bonus Action.  
* **Complex devices** (multiple effects, requires assembly, needs calibration): Action.  
* **Extremely complex devices:** Full Round Action (Movement, Action, Bonus Action, and Reaction all consumed — result available at the start of the hero's next Turn).

#### DCs and Constraints

Kitbashing DCs

15Reasonable device from adequate materials under moderate pressure

20Complex device from poor materials under significant pressure

25Complex device from poor materials under extreme pressure

Kitbashed devices replicate **At-Will or Encounter tier effects only**. Kitbashing never produces a Daily Power equivalent.

| Result | Outcome |
| :---- | :---- |
| Normal Success | The device works as intended for one use or until the end of the current scene, whichever comes first. After that it breaks down, runs out of power, or simply stops. The hero gets their moment. |
| Strong Success | The device works and has one additional use, or the player may define a minor additional benefit — a slightly broader effect area, a bonus to the first roll made with it, or the ability to pass it to an ally who can use it effectively. |
| HEROIC Success | The device works exceptionally well. It functions for the entire scene, grants a Momentum Effect equivalent on its first use, or produces a better outcome than anyone expected. |
| Failure | The device does not work. The materials are spent. There is no separate catastrophic failure mechanic. Failure is failure. The scene moves on and the hero finds another way. |

### Worked Examples

Example — Downtime Invention

**Ghostwork** (Super-Science Origin, Technology trained with Expertise, Electronics Specialty) wants to build a miniaturized sensor drone during Downtime. She and the GM agree the drone replicates an At-Will surveillance effect from her existing Power Set at her current Tier. Materials are available through her Patron Merit.

She rolls Technology with Expertise: 1d20 \+ INT \+4 \+ double Prowess (+6) \= 1d20 \+ 10\. She rolls 14\. Total: 24\. The DC was 15 for a straightforward At-Will device. **Strong Success** by a margin of 9\.

The drone works as intended with Prowess uses, and Ghostwork chooses the additional benefit: the drone is small enough to be Concealable in a coat pocket.

Example — Kitbashing

**Crashpoint** (Guardian, Technology untrained) is trapped in a power substation with a villain controlling the electrical systems. She cannot build anything sophisticated — the GM rules Kitbashing is not available to her here, as she lacks Technology training entirely.

Later, **Ghostwork** arrives. She assesses the materials (moderate quality), the complexity (simple: she wants to short-circuit the villain's control interface, an At-Will equivalent effect), and the time pressure (high: the villain is active). The GM sets DC 20\.

Ghostwork rolls Technology with Expertise: 1d20 \+ 10\. She rolls 11\. Total: 21\. **Normal Success**. The improvised short-circuit works once. The villain's control interface goes dark for one round. The heroes use the opening.

## Gear and Origins

Different Origins interact with gear in different ways.

### Gearbound

A Gearbound hero derives their primary powers from equipment. Their gear is their Power Set. The Gear Dependent Flaw applies at Rating 2 or 3 for primary gear. A Gearbound hero who loses their primary equipment loses their Power Set access until the gear is recovered or rebuilt.

A Gearbound hero has natural access to Downtime Invention for their own gear and may Kitbash modifications to their existing equipment at lower DCs: **reduce the Kitbashing DC by 3** when modifying their own established gear.

### Super-Science

A Super-Science hero invents things. Their Power Sets represent the categories of technology they have mastered. Downtime Invention is a core part of their concept and they should be encouraged to use it regularly.

A Super-Science hero may build devices for other heroes during Downtime with GM approval: the receiving hero must have the Gear Access Merit or pay a Resource Cost appropriate to the device's tier to represent the materials.

### Legacy

A Legacy hero may have inherited significant equipment from a predecessor. This equipment is defined at character creation with GM approval and functions as established gear with the appropriate Vehicle or Gear Access Merit already built into the Origin package. Legacy equipment that is central to the heroic identity carries the Gear Dependent Flaw.

Legacy equipment can be upgraded through Downtime Invention if the hero has Technology trained and the relevant expertise.

### Alien

An alien hero may carry technology that is beyond current Earth manufacturing capability. Alien gear functions as described in this chapter but **cannot be repaired using the Technology Skill alone** : repairing alien technology requires either the alien hero themselves, a specific alien resource, or a Technology check at DC 25\. An alien hero with Technology trained can repair their own equipment normally.

## Losing, Repairing, and Upgrading Gear

### Losing Gear

Gear can be destroyed in combat, stolen, confiscated by authorities, or simply lost in the chaos of a desperate fight. The GM introduces gear loss as a narrative consequence of combat damage, villain action, or dramatic failure.

* When a hero loses gear that carries the Gear Dependent Flaw, the Flaw activates at its full Rating until the gear is recovered or replaced.  
* When a hero loses gear that does not carry the Flaw, they lose access to that item's benefits until it is recovered or replaced. No Flaw activates but the practical loss still matters.

### Repairing Gear

| Damage Level | When | Check |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Minor repairs | Cosmetic damage, depleted power cells, minor component replacement | Technology DC 10 during a Breather. Success restores full function. |
| Significant repairs | Structural damage, destroyed components, major system failure | Technology check during Downtime. DC set by severity. Failure means the repair takes another Downtime period, or the gear requires specific materials the hero must acquire through play. |

Alien or exotic technology increases repair DCs as described in the Gear and Origins section above.

### Upgrading Gear

Existing gear can be upgraded during Downtime using the Invention rules. Upgrading existing gear is easier than building from scratch: **reduce the DC by 3** when modifying a piece of gear the hero already owns and understands. The upgrade must represent a plausible improvement to the existing item, not a wholesale replacement.

A hero who upgrades gear through play may also improve the Vehicle Merit or Gear Access Merit associated with that gear during an advancement choice, with GM approval and story justification. The fiction must support it: a hero who has spent three story arcs improving their vehicle has earned the right to call it Rating 3 without simply paying an advancement cost.

## Resources and Wealth *(Optional Rules)*

Using This Section

The default resource system in HEROIC 5e is narrative. The Cash Flow, Wealth, and Patron Merits from **Chapter 9** establish what a hero can reasonably access. The GM interprets these Merits to determine what the hero can acquire without tracking individual purchases.

Groups who want more granular resource tracking may use the following optional system. If your group is not using this system, the Merits are sufficient and this section can be ignored entirely.

### Resource Rating

Every hero using this system has a Resource Rating from 0 to 5\. This rating is derived from their Merits and story circumstances. It is not fixed: it can rise or fall with story events.

| Rating | Level | Real-World Equivalent |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0 | Destitute | No reliable income. The Destitute Flaw applies. Survival is the daily concern. |
| 1 | Street Level | Basic needs covered. Irregular income, cheap equipment, public transport. |
| 2 | Comfortable | Reliable income. A car, an apartment, professional equipment, modest savings. |
| 3 | Wealthy | Significant resources. High-end equipment, property, professional access. |
| 4 | Rich | Major personal wealth. Custom vehicles, private facilities, significant social access. |
| 5 | Vast | Billionaire, institutional, or royal scale. Effectively unlimited for personal purchases. |

### Deriving Resource Rating from Merits

| Merit / Condition | Resource Rating |
| :---- | :---- |
| No relevant Merits | 1 (Street Level) |
| Cash Flow 1 | 2 (Comfortable) |
| Cash Flow 2 | 3 (Wealthy) |
| Cash Flow 3 or Wealth 1 | 4 (Rich) |
| Wealth 2 or Wealth 3 | 5 (Vast) |
| Patron 2 or Team Membership 2 | \+1 to Resource Rating for mission-specific purchases only |
| Destitute Flaw | 0 (Destitute) — overrides all other Merits |

### Resource Cost

Every significant purchase has a Resource Cost from 0 to 5\.

* If the hero's Resource Rating **meets or exceeds** the Resource Cost, the purchase happens without a roll. They simply have it.  
* If the Resource Cost **exceeds the hero's Rating by 1** , they may attempt a Cash Flow or Influence check against DC 15 to stretch their resources. Success means they acquire it with some effort. Failure means they cannot manage it this session but may try again later.  
* If the Resource Cost **exceeds the hero's Rating by 2 or more** , the purchase is beyond their means without GM approval and a significant story justification — a major heist, a windfall, or a generous ally.

### Reference Price Table

The following prices are modern ballpark figures provided as reference. The GM assigns Resource Cost based on the fiction, using these examples as anchors. Prices in real markets vary enormously based on condition, location, and availability.

### Resource Rating Fluctuation

Resource Ratings are not permanent. Story events change them. A hero who is defrauded, whose assets are frozen, or whose Patron withdraws support may drop a Rating level temporarily or permanently. A hero who discovers a cache of alien technology, inherits a fortune, or wins a major lawsuit may gain a Rating level as a campaign reward.

Resource Rating changes require GM approval and story justification. They are not advancement choices. They are story consequences.

### A Note on Group Resources

When the party operates as a team with shared infrastructure — a Base of Operations or Team Membership Merit — the group's combined resources may be treated as a shared Resource Rating for mission-specific purposes. The GM determines how the group's resources combine based on their Merits.

A team with one billionaire member (Resource Rating 5\) and three street-level heroes (Resource Rating 1\) has access to Rating 5 resources for team operations, but individual heroes still have their personal Rating for personal purchases.

# **Chapter Fourteen  ·  Playing the Game**

Playing the Game

The authoritative reference for how the rules work moment to moment. When another chapter references a core mechanic, this is where it lives.

HEROIC 5e is built around one goal: creating exciting, dramatic, fast-moving superhero action at the table. This chapter explains how the game actually runs from moment to moment. When another chapter references a core mechanic, this is where it lives.

## The Core Loop

A session of HEROIC 5e moves through a series of scenes. The GM frames each scene: where the heroes are, what is happening, and what is at stake. The players declare what their heroes do. The table resolves the outcome through the rules, decisions, and narrative.

Most of what heroes do does not require a roll. Walking down a street, having a conversation, searching a room at leisure, or doing anything where failure carries no meaningful consequence does not need dice. The GM calls for a roll when the outcome is uncertain and the consequences of failure matter.

Scenes end when the situation is resolved: the fight is over, the investigation reaches a conclusion, the social encounter finds its outcome. The GM then frames the next scene.

Core Design Principle — Dice Always Belong to the Players

This is foundational. Player Characters always roll. NPCs and enemies never roll in any exchange that involves a PC. The GM holds static values. The PC rolls against them.

This applies universally:

* **PC attacks** → rolls 1d20 \+ delivery modifier \+ Governing Ability modifier (Powers only) \+ Prowess against the enemy's Static Defense Value.  
* **PC defends** → rolls Active Defense against the enemy's Static Attack Value.  
* **PC resists an effect** → rolls 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against the enemy's Static Effect Value.  
* **PC applies an effect** → rolls 1d20 \+ relevant modifier \+ Prowess against the enemy's Static Save Value.

The enemy never picks up a die. The GM reads a static number from the NPC stat block. The PC rolls. NPC vs. NPC interactions may use rolls at GM discretion. Everything that involves a PC is resolved by that PC's roll against a static number.

## The Core Reference

Every formula in HEROIC 5e is printed here, once. Other chapters point back to this page rather than restating it. If a number anywhere else in the book disagrees with this page, this page is correct.

| What | Formula |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Attack roll** | 1d20 \+ delivery modifier \+ Governing Ability modifier (Powers only) \+ Prowess |
| **Basic attack roll** | 1d20 \+ delivery modifier \+ Prowess |
| **Damage** | Power Dice \+ Governing Ability modifier (Powers only) \+ delivery damage modifier |
| **Active Defense** | 1d20 \+ two Ability modifiers \+ Prowess |
| **Save** | 1d20 \+ relevant Ability modifier \+ Prowess if trained in that save |
| **Skill check** | 1d20 \+ Ability modifier \+ Prowess if trained (double Prowess with Expertise) |
| **Effect Value (PC)** | 10 \+ governing Ability modifier \+ Prowess |
| **Vigilance** | 10 \+ PER \+ Prowess if trained in Notice |
| **Initiative** | 1d20 \+ DEX \+ PER |
| **Starting HP** | (full Constitution score \+ Hit Die maximum) × Campaign Rank multiplier \+ Prowess |
| **Campaign Rank multiplier** | ×1 Street Level · ×2 Mid-Level · ×3 World Class |
| **HP per level after 1st** | Hit Die median \+ CON \+ current Prowess |
| **Hit Die spent** | higher of the roll or the die's median, \+ CON \+ Recovery Modifier |
| **Defense Value (NPC)** | 10 \+ two Ability modifiers \+ Tier Bonus |
| **Attack Value (NPC)** | 10 \+ primary combat modifier \+ Tier Bonus |
| **Save Value / Effect Value (NPC)** | 10 \+ governing Ability modifier \+ Tier Bonus |
| **NPC HP** | (Constitution score \+ Power Die maximum) × Tier multiplier |

**Delivery modifiers.** Melee uses FIG to hit and STR for damage. Ranged uses DEX for both. Mental uses INT for both. Social uses CHA for both. Melee is the only delivery method that splits the two — Fighting lands the blow, Strength is the force behind it. These apply universally regardless of Class, Origin, or Power Set.

**Medians.** Half the die size, rounded down: d6 = 3, d8 = 4, d10 = 5, d12 = 6.

**Ties.** Ties always favour the character rolling the dice — in practice, the player. A hero's attack roll that ties a Defense Value hits. A hero's Active Defense roll that ties an Attack Value means the attack misses. A hero's roll that ties a Save Value applies the effect.

Converting Advantage and Disadvantage on NPC Rolls

Because NPCs never roll, any rule that would grant or impose Advantage or Disadvantage on an NPC's roll converts to a static adjustment instead. Apply whichever line fits:

* A rule that would give an **NPC Disadvantage on an attack** → the defending hero gains **Advantage on their Active Defense** against that attack.
* A rule that would give an **NPC Advantage on an attack** → the defending hero has **Disadvantage on their Active Defense** against that attack.
* A rule that would give an **NPC Disadvantage on a save** → the acting hero treats that NPC's **Save Value as 5 lower** for that effect.
* A rule that would give an **NPC Advantage on a save** → the acting hero treats that NPC's **Save Value as 5 higher** for that effect.
* A **condition that imposes Disadvantage on attack rolls** (Blinded, Poisoned, Restrained, Shaken) reduces an affected NPC's **Attack Value by 3** instead.

This conversion is automatic and requires no ruling. It exists so that conditions and effects written for heroes work identically when they land on an NPC.

## Dice, Rolls, and the Resolution System

HEROIC 5e uses the d20 as its primary resolution tool. Every meaningful roll is 1d20 plus relevant modifiers compared to a target number. There are three types of rolls.

### Skill Checks

Made when a hero attempts something where training and ability matter. Roll 1d20 \+ Ability Score modifier \+ Prowess if trained in the relevant Skill. The GM sets the Difficulty Class (DC) based on how challenging the task is.

### Saves

Made when a hero resists something happening to them. Roll 1d20 \+ relevant Ability Score modifier \+ Prowess if the hero has save training in that Ability Score. Saves use fixed Effect Values set by the source of the effect.

### Attack Rolls

Made when a hero attempts to hit a target with an attack or Power. Roll 1d20 \+ delivery modifier \+ Prowess, adding the Power Set's Governing Ability modifier as well if the attack comes from a Power. The result is compared to the target's static Defense Value.

| DC | Difficulty |
| :---- | :---- |
| 10 | Easy |
| 15 | Standard |
| 20 | Hard |
| 25 | Extreme |
| 30 | Near-Impossible |
| These are GM-set Skill check targets, not Effect Values. The label distinction avoids confusion with Effect Values generated by characters. |  |

### Advantage and Disadvantage

When a hero has Advantage, they roll 2d20 and take the higher result. When they have Disadvantage, they roll 2d20 and take the lower result. Multiple sources of Advantage do not stack — a roll never uses more than two dice regardless of how many sources apply. The same is true for Disadvantage. If a roll has both Advantage and Disadvantage from any source, they cancel completely and the roll is made normally with a single d20.

### **Natural 20 and Natural 1**

A natural 20 on an **attack roll made during combat** is a critical hit. The attacker deals **maximum damage on all damage dice** — no rolling required, just take the highest possible result on every damage die. Flat modifiers are added normally. Calculate the Degree of Success as per normal.

If the attack already deals **maximum damage on all dice** through a Power, Class feature, or other effect, a critical hit changes nothing further — the damage is already at its maximum.

A natural 1 on an **attack roll made during combat** is a fumble (it automatically misses, regardless of modifiers). This is not a botch or a chance to humiliate the character, just a miss. If this is done on a defense roll, the attacker is considered to have scored a Critical Hit against the defender.

**Natural 1s and Natural 20s on other rolls** (including Saves, Skill Checks, and any rolls made outside of combat) have **no special effect** unless a specific rule states otherwise. They are resolved normally based on the final total. The Grit Save, the Lethal Save, and the HEROIC Challenge fumble rule are the only exceptions in this book.

## Degrees of Success

HEROIC 5e does not use Degrees of Failure. Failure is failure — the scene moves on. What the game does use is Degrees of Success: when a roll succeeds, how well it succeeds changes what happens next.

| Result | Requirement | Effect |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Success | Meets or exceeds the target | The action succeeds normally |
| Strong Success | Beats the target by 5 or more | The action succeeds and generates 1 Momentum Effect |
| HEROIC Success | Beats the target by 10 or more | The action succeeds and generates 2 Momentum Effects or 1 HEROIC Effect |

HEROIC Success Is Determined by Margin, Not the Die

A natural 20 attack roll against a defender who rolled 15 on their Active Defense is a Strong Success (margin of 5), not a HEROIC Success, unless the attacker's total reaches 10 above the defender's total.

### Momentum Effects

When a hero achieves a Strong Success on an attack or relevant check, they may choose one Momentum Effect. On a HEROIC Success, they may choose two Momentum Effects or one HEROIC Effect.

Momentum Effects that affect a target allow that target to resist with a save. The player who applied the Momentum Effect rolls 1d20 \+ relevant Ability Score modifier \+ Prowess against the target's static Save Value (10 \+ relevant Ability Score modifier \+ Tier Bonus). Momentum Effects do not stack with themselves — reapplying the same Momentum Effect refreshes its duration rather than doubling the effect.

| Momentum Effect | Result | Common Save |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Push | Target is moved one Zone (grid: 10 ft) | STR or CON |
| Knockdown | Target falls Prone | STR or DEX |
| Off-Balance | Target loses Reactions until end of its next Turn | DEX |
| Pressure | Target has Disadvantage on its next roll before end of its next Turn | WIS or CHA |
| Opening | Next attack against the target gains Advantage | PER |
| Delay | Target cannot Dash, and its movement is halved until end of its next Turn | CON |
| Disarm | Target drops one held object | STR or DEX |
| Suppress | Target cannot gain Advantage until end of its next Turn | WIS |
| Expose | Target loses the Hidden condition and any Cover it is using | PER |
| Rattle | Target becomes Shaken until end of its next Turn | WIS or CHA |
| Shift | Acting character repositions within their Zone (grid: 10 ft) without provoking Reactions | No save |
| Rally | One ally gains temporary HP equal to Prowess | No save |
| Contain | Reduce collateral damage from the action | No save |
| Settle | End Shaken or Slowed on one ally | No save |

### HEROIC Effects

HEROIC Effects are larger, scene-defining consequences. They come from HEROIC Successes, Class Features, Powers, Team Combos, or major dramatic moments. They are not simply bigger Momentum Effects — they change the shape of the scene.

Power Dice granted by a HEROIC Effect are rolled once. They are never maximized or doubled by a critical hit.

| HEROIC Effect | Failed Save | Successful Save |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Send Flying | Push one Zone and knock Prone | Push within the Zone |
| Daze | Target becomes Dazed until end of its next Turn | Target loses Reactions |
| Overwhelming Force | \+1 Power Die damage and target is Slowed until end of its next Turn | \+1 Power Die damage and target loses Reactions until end of its next Turn |
| Smash Through | Destroy cover, barrier, or terrain feature | Damage or weaken it |
| Pin | Target becomes Restrained until end of its next Turn | Target is Slowed |
| Break Focus | End one Sustained Power | Target has Disadvantage to maintain it |
| Multi-Impact | Affect one nearby secondary target for half effect | Secondary target suffers minor effect |
| Crater Impact | Create difficult terrain or a hazard in the impact area | Create minor difficult terrain |
| Rescue Swing | Move one ally or civilian up to full Speed safely | Move them up to half Speed safely |
| Tactical Insight | Allies gain Advantage on attacks against target until start of your next Turn | One ally gains Advantage |
| Full Containment | Completely prevent collateral damage | Greatly reduce collateral damage |

## Action Economy

On your Turn you normally have:

* **Movement**  
* **1 Action**  
* **1 Bonus Action**  
* **1 Reaction** (used on triggers, usually on other characters' Turns)  
* **1 Free Object Interaction**  
* **Speech and communication**  
* **Minor cinematic actions** approved by the GM

You may take these in any order unless a specific rule says otherwise. You do not have to use all of them.

### Actions

The full list of available Actions: **Attack, Use a Power, Dash, Disengage, Evade, Help, Hide, Ready, Recovery, Search, Steady On,** and **Use an Object.** Some Class features and Powers create additional Action options.

### Bonus Actions

You only have a Bonus Action when a rule, Power, Talent, or Class feature gives you something to do with it. You cannot spend a Bonus Action on nothing.

### Reactions

A Reaction is a response to a specific trigger. You normally have 1 Reaction per round. A Reaction resets at the start of your Turn. A Reaction interrupts the triggering event unless the specific rule says otherwise.

### Secondary Attacks

Unless a rule explicitly states otherwise, all secondary attacks and granted actions are made at Disadvantage. This includes bonus attacks, Reaction attacks, granted attacks, follow-up attacks, chain attacks, assist attacks, and extra attacks created by Team Combos.

### The Ready Action

When you take the Ready action, choose an action and describe a trigger in one sentence. The trigger must be a specific observable event, such as "when an enemy moves within Close range of me" or "when an ally is hit by an attack." Broad triggers like "when anything happens" are not valid.

When the trigger occurs before the start of your next Turn, you may fire your readied action as a Reaction. If the trigger does not occur, the readied action is lost. A readied Encounter Power expends the resource whether or not the trigger fires. Daily Powers cannot be readied. At-Will Powers may be readied freely.

### Speed Actions

Speed Actions are a specialized action type granted exclusively by the Super Speed Power Set, in addition to the normal Action, Bonus Action, and Reactions. They may only be spent on movement, basic movement-related actions, and Powers specifically tagged as Speed Action powers. Speed Actions are subject to the secondary attacks Disadvantage rule when used to make attacks. See the Super Speed entry in Chapter 11 for complete rules.

### **Movement**

A character's **Speed** is **30 feet** — six squares on a grid, or one Zone in Zone play. Speed is the same for every character unless a Power, Talent, or Class feature changes it. The full movement rules, including Zones, difficult terrain, forced movement, jumping, climbing, and falling, are in Chapter 15: Combat.

## Attack and Defense

### Governing Abilities for Attack Rolls

Universal Governing Ability Rule
