Trained enforcer, armed operative, mid-tier soldier

Lieutenant 3 hits to defeat

Skilled operative, field commander, dangerous specialist

### Minion Rules

* **Conditions** apply to Minions normally — a Dazed Thug still cannot take Reactions.  
* **Area effects** deal 1 hit to each Minion within the area, regardless of damage amount. Five Thugs hit by one burst: all five defeated immediately.  
* **Minions act as groups** on a shared initiative count per Minion type — reduces initiative tracking significantly in large encounters.  
* **Lieutenants are not Bosses.** They have 3 hits and no special protections. A GM who wants a field commander to feel more threatening should designate them as a Boss instead.

Example — Minion Combat

**Ghost Fox** faces a Syndicate squad: four Thugs, two Goons, one Lieutenant. She uses a burst Power hitting all seven. Each takes 1 hit: the four Thugs are immediately defeated. The two Goons now have 1 hit remaining each. The Lieutenant has 2 hits remaining. Next Turn, Ghost Fox attacks one Goon: defeated. The remaining Goon charges. Ironclad intercepts with Stand Between. Ghost Fox attacks the Lieutenant: 1 hit, 1 remaining. The encounter moves fast — three checkboxes per Minion.

## The Complete Combat Round

The following example shows one complete combat round from Initiative through all Turns. Every number in it is traceable to a printed rule or to the stat block below. Use it as a reference for running your first session.

The Scene

**Meridian Bridge.** Director Vayne has three Syndicate Goons blocking the bridge. Three heroes are present: Ghost Fox (Striker, Level 5), Ironclad (Sentinel, Level 5), Brightheart (Beacon, Level 5). The campaign is Mid-Level, so every hero's Power Die is a d10 and every hero's Prowess is \+3. A group of civilians needs to cross.

**Director Vayne** · Medium Power · Boss

| STR | DEX | CON | FIG | INT | WIS | CHA | PER |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| \+1 | \+2 | \+2 | \+2 | \+2 | \+1 | \+1 | \+2 |

**Tier Bonus:** \+3 | **Power Die:** d10 | **HP:** 85 *(Constitution 14 \+ d10 max 10) × 2 \= 48, \+ 37 Bonus HP as an arc-anchoring Boss* | **Initiative:** 14 *(10 \+ DEX \+ PER)*

**Active Defense:** Parry/Block 17 · Dodge 17 · Willpower 16 · Social 16
**Attack Value:** 15 *(energy blast, ranged)* | **Damage:** 2d10\+2 \[12\] radiant
**Save Values:** STR 14 · DEX 15 · CON 15 · INT 15 · WIS 14

**Syndicate Goons (×3)** · 2 hits each · **Initiative:** 10 · **Attack Value:** 13 · **Damage:** 1d8\+2 \[6\] bludgeoning

**The heroes' relevant numbers**

| | Ironclad | Ghost Fox | Brightheart |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| STR / DEX / CON | \+1 / \+1 / \+2 | \+2 / \+3 / \+2 | \+0 / \+2 / \+1 |
| FIG / INT / WIS / CHA / PER | \+2 / \+1 / \+1 / \+0 / \+3 | \+4 / \+1 / \+1 / \+0 / \+2 | \+0 / \+2 / \+2 / \+4 / \+1 |
| Parry/Block | \+8 | \+9 | \+4 |
| Dodge | \+7 | \+8 | \+6 |
| Initiative | \+4 | \+5 | \+3 |

#### Step 1: Initiative

The GM calls for Initiative. Only the heroes roll — Vayne and the Goons use the static values on their stat blocks. Prowess is not added to Initiative unless a specific feature grants it.

* **Ironclad** (\+4): Reactive Awareness grants Advantage — rolls 15 and 8, takes 15\. **Total: 19\.**  
* **Ghost Fox** (\+5): Rolls 10\. **Total: 15\.**  
* **Director Vayne:** static **14\.**  
* **Brightheart** (\+3): Rolls 8\. **Total: 11\.**  
* **Syndicate Goons:** static **10\.**

**Initiative Order:** Ironclad (19) → Ghost Fox (15) → Director Vayne (14) → Brightheart (11) → Goons (10).

#### Ironclad's Turn — Initiative 19

Threat Assessment fires automatically at the start of the encounter, telling her which enemy has the highest current HP and the highest Attack Value. She uses her Bonus Action to designate Vayne as her Threat Lock target, gaining Advantage on all attacks against him. She moves one Zone, closing to Close range.

**Attack:** basic melee, 1d20 \+ FIG \+2 \+ Prowess \+3 \= 1d20 \+5. Advantage from Threat Lock — rolls 8 and 17, takes 17\. **Total: 22\.**

The GM reads Vayne's Parry/Block Defense Value: **17\.** Twenty-two beats it. Hit, margin 5 — a **Strong Success**.

**Momentum Effect — Rattle.** Ironclad rolls 1d20 \+ WIS \+1 \+ Prowess \+3 \= 1d20 \+4 against Vayne's WIS Save Value of **14\.** She rolls 12, total 16\. The effect lands. Vayne is **Shaken** until the end of her next Turn.

**Damage:** 1 Power Die \+ STR. She rolls a d10 for 7, \+1 \= **8**. Vayne drops to **77 HP**.

#### Ghost Fox's Turn — Initiative 15

She chooses **Offense** for Focused Fighter this Turn, adding FIG to her damage. She moves into Close range and attacks.

**Attack:** basic melee, 1d20 \+ FIG \+4 \+ Prowess \+3 \= 1d20 \+7. Rolls 16\. **Total: 23\.**

Vayne's Parry/Block is **17\.** Hit, margin 6 — a **Strong Success**.

**Bonus Action — Exploit Opening.** Vayne is Shaken, so he is suffering a Condition and the trigger is met. She rolls one additional Power Die of damage, then rolls 1d20 \+ FIG \+4 \+ Prowess \+3 against his WIS Save Value of **14** — he was mentally pressured. She rolls 9, total 16\. Vayne is **Dazed** until the end of her next Turn. He now carries two conditions, which is the Boss Condition Cap.

**Momentum Effect — Pressure.** She rolls 1d20 \+7 against Vayne's WIS Save Value of 14\. Rolls 11, total 18\. It lands. Pressure would normally give Vayne Disadvantage on his next roll — but Vayne is an NPC and never rolls, so the standing conversion applies: **his Attack Value drops by 3** for that attack.

**Damage:** 1 Power Die \+ STR \+2 \+ FIG \+4 (Focused Fighter, Offense) \= d10 rolls 6, so 6 \+ 2 \+ 4 \= 12\. Exploit Opening adds a second d10 for 5\. **Total: 17\.** Vayne drops to **60 HP**.

#### Director Vayne's Turn — Initiative 14

Vayne is **Shaken** (−3 to his Attack Value on his next attack) and **Dazed** (Action or Bonus Action, not both; no Reactions). Pressure is also active (−3). His Attack Value for this attack is 15 − 3 − 3 \= **9**.

He targets Ghost Fox with his energy blast. The GM announces Attack Value **9**.

**Ghost Fox's Dodge:** 1d20 \+ DEX \+3 \+ PER \+2 \+ Prowess \+3 \= 1d20 \+8. She rolls 11\. **Total: 19\.**

Nineteen beats 9\. The blast scorches the bridge railing. Shaken is spent on that attack and ends; Pressure is spent as well. Vayne still has Dazed. Because he is Dazed he cannot also move and act, so he holds position and snarls at the civilians.

#### Brightheart's Turn — Initiative 11

She uses her Bonus Action on **Taunt**: 1d20 \+ CHA \+4 \+ Prowess \+3 \= 1d20 \+7 against Vayne's **Social Defense Value of 16**. She rolls 12, total 19\. Success, margin 3 — a normal Success. Until the start of her next Turn, **Vayne's Attack Value is reduced by 3 against any target other than Brightheart**.

Her Action goes to an Influence check to move the civilians clear. The GM sets DC 10 — they want to go. She rolls 1d20 \+ CHA \+4 \+ Prowess \+3, gets an 8, total 15\. Success. The civilians start moving.

#### Syndicate Goons' Turn — Initiative 10

Three Goons, 2 hits each, all undamaged. Two target Ghost Fox and one targets Ironclad. **Taunt does not affect them** — Brightheart taunted Vayne specifically, and Taunt only ever affects the creature it was used against.

**Goon 1 vs. Ghost Fox:** Attack Value 13\. Ghost Fox rolls Parry/Block, 1d20 \+9, gets a 9\. **Total 18\.** Miss.

**Goon 2 vs. Ghost Fox:** Attack Value 13\. She rolls a 4\. **Total 13\.** An exact tie — and ties favour the player. Miss.

**Goon 3 vs. Ironclad:** Attack Value 13\. Ironclad rolls Parry/Block, 1d20 \+8, gets a 3\. **Total 11\.** Eleven falls short of 13, so the attack lands. Ironclad takes **6** damage.

End of Round Summary

**Director Vayne:** 60 HP. Conditions: Dazed. Taunt restriction active until the start of Brightheart's next Turn. Resolve unused.

**Three Syndicate Goons:** Undamaged, 2 hits each remaining.

**Heroes:** Ironclad at −6 HP. Ironclad has used Threat Lock; Ghost Fox has used Exploit Opening; Brightheart has used Taunt.

**Civilians** are moving toward safety. Round 2 begins with Ironclad's Turn.

Count the Dice

Across the entire round the GM rolled **nothing**. Every die on the table was rolled by a player — three attack rolls, three Momentum and Exploit rolls, one skill check, and four Active Defense rolls. The GM read eleven static numbers off two stat blocks. That is the whole engine.

## Falling and Impact

In HEROIC 5e, gravity is the one force that does not negotiate. A hero can trade punches with something that bench-presses trains and walk away. A hero who comes off a rooftop the wrong way may not. Falling is the game's honest danger, and the rules treat it that way.

### Falling Damage

Falling damage uses a flat **d8 regardless of Campaign Rank** — gravity applies equally to street-level vigilantes and world-class titans. What differs is how much punishment the body on the receiving end can absorb, and that is already handled by Campaign Rank's effect on Hit Points.

| Fall Distance | Damage |
| :---- | :---- |
| Close (up to 25 ft) | 2d8 bludgeoning |
| Short (26–50 ft) | 4d8 bludgeoning |
| Medium (51–120 ft) | 8d8 bludgeoning |
| Long (121–300 ft) | 12d8 bludgeoning |
| Extreme (300+ ft) | 16d8 bludgeoning, \+1d8 per additional Zone (25 ft) beyond 300 feet |

Falling damage is not capped. A fall from orbit is not a bigger version of a fall from a fire escape — it is a different event entirely.

### Surviving a Fall

When a fall reduces a creature to 0 HP, compare the **excess damage** — the amount dealt beyond what was needed to reach 0 — against that creature's **Constitution score** (the full score, not the modifier).

| Excess Damage | Result |
| :---- | :---- |
| Less than Constitution score | Unconscious and dying. Make Grit Saves normally. |
| Equal to or greater than Constitution score | Unconscious and dying. Make **Lethal Saves** in place of Grit Saves, whether or not the table uses the optional Lethal rules. |
| Twice Constitution score or greater | The creature dies. |

A creature that lands hard enough to reach any of these thresholds needs more than a Breather. Recovery from a serious fall is a medical problem and a story beat — the GM should treat it as one.

**Injured.** Any creature reduced to 0 HP by a fall also gains the **Injured** condition. The GM and player agree on the specific impairment based on how the landing went — a wrenched shoulder, a bad ankle, cracked ribs — and the resulting Disadvantage applies to the matching Skill check type or Physical save type. A fall hard enough to put a hero down leaves a mark that outlasts the fight.

Gravity Is the Exception

Everywhere else in HEROIC 5e, killing a hero takes intent. A Killing Blow must be declared. Falls are the exception, and they are the exception on purpose: a hero thrown from a skyscraper is in genuine danger, and the table should feel it. This is what makes a rescue matter.

**Softening Falls (Optional).** Groups who want death entirely off the table may cap falls at the Lethal Save threshold — a creature that takes twice its Constitution score or more beyond 0 HP makes Lethal Saves rather than dying outright. Gravity stays frightening; it stops being final. Discuss this before play, alongside the campaign's approach to Killing Blows and Mortal Wounds.

### Civilians and Minions

**Civilians.** A creature without Powers, Talents, or heroic training does not survive serious falls. A civilian reduced to 0 HP by a fall of Medium range (50+ ft) or greater dies. No threshold comparison is made and no saves are rolled. The bystander going off the bridge is not a math problem — they are a clock, and the only answer is a hero who gets there in time.

**Minions.** Minions are tracked in Hits rather than Hit Points and do not use the threshold rules. A fall of Close or Short range costs a Minion 1 Hit. A fall of Medium range (50+ ft) or greater removes a Minion outright.

### Reducing Falling Damage

A creature that is aware they are falling and has a moment to react may make an **Acrobatics check (DC 15)** to halve the damage from a fall of **Short range (up to 50 ft) or less**. Beyond fifty feet there is simply too much speed to shed — halving a longer fall requires something to catch, using Slowing a Fall below.

The following powers and features remove falling damage entirely or modify it significantly: Controlled Fall (Martial Mastery Utility), Perfect Landing (Super Agility Utility), Super Jump (General Utility), Gliding, Swinging, Flight (any tier), and Size Control at Huge or larger.

### Slowing a Fall

Awnings tear. Flagpoles bend. Clotheslines snap. All of them take speed out of a fall before the ground finishes the job, and a hero who catches one on the way down walks away from something that should have killed them.

A creature that encounters a yielding obstacle during a fall — an awning, flagpole, clothesline, tree branch, vine, fire escape, or similar — may attempt to use it. Roll either:

* **Acrobatics (DEX)** — swing, redirect, and roll clear of the impact.  
* **Athletics (STR)** — catch hold and take the strain through the arms.

The DC is **15, plus 1 for each Zone (25 ft) fallen before reaching the obstacle.** A hero who catches a flagpole after dropping fifty feet rolls against DC 17. A hero who catches one after dropping two hundred feet rolls against DC 23.

**On a success,** the fall deals half damage. **On a failure,** the obstacle gives way and the fall resolves normally.

Obstacle reduction and the Acrobatics halving above do not stack — use whichever applies, never both.

A Rigid Surface Is Not an Obstacle

A car roof, a dumpster lid, a concrete ledge, or a parked truck does not slow a fall. It is simply where the fall ends. The obstacle must give — that is the entire mechanism. If it does not bend, tear, or swing, the GM should rule that it offers no benefit.

### Forced Movement and Impact

When a creature is pushed, thrown, or launched into a solid surface by a Power or Momentum Effect, they take impact damage in addition to any falling damage: **1d8 per Zone of distance traveled into the surface, maximum 4d8**. A creature launched upward and then falling takes both the impact from any surface hit on the way up and the falling damage from the height reached.

### Falling onto Creatures

When a large creature falls onto a smaller creature: the smaller creature takes falling damage as though they had fallen the same distance; the larger creature takes half the normal falling damage. The GM determines when size difference makes this apply — generally Huge or larger falling onto Medium or smaller.

### Collateral Damage from Falling

A creature that falls in a populated area, onto a vehicle, or into a structure creates environmental damage. The GM determines scope based on size and height. A hero who falls from a rooftop leaves a body-shaped crater. A Colossal hero falling from extreme height causes city-block-scale damage. These consequences play out through the Response system and Merits and Flaws — not through additional mechanical damage to the hero.

## Creature Size

Size determines a creature's token footprint on the battlefield, melee reach, interactions with forced movement, and tactical implications. The Size Control Power Set references this table for all size modifier details.

| Size | Token Footprint | Melee Reach | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Fine | Sub-square; invisible to naked eye | Same space only | Immune to targeted attacks; area effects still apply |
| Diminutive | Shares a square with up to 4 | Same or adjacent square | Advantage on all physical Active Defense rolls; effectively invisible at this size |
| Tiny | Shares a square with up to 4 | Same square or adjacent square | Advantage on Stealth and saves against area effects |
| Small | 1×1 square (5×5 ft) | Adjacent squares | Advantage on Stealth; access to spaces too small for Medium creatures |
| Medium | 1×1 square (5×5 ft) | Adjacent squares | Default hero size |
| Large | 2×2 squares (10×10 ft) | Adjacent squares (from token edge) | \+2 to Parry/Block; \+1 Size Bonus Die on unarmed attacks; Disadvantage on Stealth |
| Huge | 3×3 squares (15×15 ft) | Adjacent squares (from token edge) | \+3 to Parry/Block and Dodge; \+2 Size Bonus Dice; Disadvantage on Stealth |
| Gargantuan | 4×4 squares (20×20 ft) | Short range (26–50 ft) | \+4 to Parry/Block and Dodge; \+3 Size Bonus Dice; Stealth auto-fails |
| Colossal | 4×4 squares or larger | Medium range (51–120 ft) | \+5 to all Active Defense rolls; \+4 Size Bonus Dice; count as terrain feature; Stealth auto-fails |
| Titanic | Special — GM determines | Long range (121–300 ft) | \+6 to all Active Defense rolls; \+5 Size Bonus Dice; scene-scale combat rules may apply |
| Size Bonus Dice are flat d8 regardless of Campaign Rank — they represent physical scale, not heroic power level. The Size Control Power Set entry in Chapter 11 contains the full progression and mechanics for heroes who change size. |  |  |  |

## Grid and VTT Combat

The Zone system is the recommended default. This section is for groups using physical battle maps, miniatures, or virtual tabletops who want tactical precision. All rules in this chapter apply exactly as written — this section provides grid-specific additions and conversions only.

### Grid Basics

* **Square size:** 1 square \= 5 feet.  
* **Diagonals:** Cost 5 feet per square — same as horizontal or vertical. No alternating cost.  
* **Zone boundaries:** The GM defines and marks Zones before the encounter. Zone lines are literal: a drawn boundary, a wall, a colour overlay. Zone-triggered rules apply at the boundary.

### Movement on the Grid

A hero's Speed is expressed in feet. On the grid, a hero moves up to their Speed in feet per Turn — a hero with Speed 30 moves up to 6 squares. Splitting movement is unchanged: move, take Action, move again as long as total does not exceed Speed. Difficult terrain costs 10 feet per square to enter.

### Forced Movement on the Grid

| Distance | Squares |
| :---- | :---- |
| 5 feet | 1 square |
| 10 feet | 2 squares |
| Close range (25 ft) | 5 squares |
| Short range (26–50 ft) | 5–10 squares (use stated feet value) |
| Forced movement travels in a straight line from the source. Never triggers Opportunity Attacks. |  |

### Flanking

When two heroes are positioned on directly opposite sides of the same enemy, both gain Advantage on melee attack rolls against that enemy. Opposite sides means directly opposite — north/south or east/west. Diagonal positions do not qualify. Flanking applies to melee attacks only.

For Large and Huge enemies, opposite sides means opposite edges of the token footprint.

### Cover on the Grid

Cover is anything that physically obstructs a direct line between attacker and target. Because only players roll, Cover always lands on player dice:

* Players attacking a target with Cover: roll attack at Disadvantage.  
* Players defending from Cover: roll Dodge Active Defense at Advantage.  
* **Total Cover:** cannot be targeted by attacks or single-target Powers requiring line of sight. Area effects can still reach Total Cover targets at GM discretion.  
* **Destroyable Cover:** the GM assigns HP. When it reaches 0, it no longer provides its benefit.

**Line of sight:** Draw an imaginary line from any corner of the attacker's square to any corner of the target's square. If any such line reaches the target without passing through a solid obstacle, the target does not have Cover.

### Elevation

Track elevation in 5-foot increments on maps that include vertical space. Elevation uses the standard Vertical Range rule — measure horizontal and vertical distance separately and use **whichever is greater**. Never add the two together. A flying hero 60 feet directly above a ground enemy is at Medium range, because the vertical distance governs.

**Melee and elevation:** Close range includes a vertical tolerance of 10 feet. A hero cannot punch an enemy flying at 30 feet. A hero flying at 10 feet or lower can make a melee attack against a ground target. A flying hero above 10 feet does not occupy the ground Zone for melee purposes — ground enemies cannot make Opportunity Attacks against them.

### Area Effects and Templates

| Power Area | Grid Template |
| :---- | :---- |
| Close area (15-ft radius) | Circle, 3-square radius from center |
| Short area (20-ft radius) | Circle, 4-square radius from center |
| Short area (25-ft radius) | Circle, 5-square radius from center |
| Medium area (30-ft radius) | Circle, 6-square radius from center |
| Medium area (40-ft radius) | Circle, 8-square radius from center |
| Zone fill | 5×5 square area |
| Cone (25-ft) | 5-square cone from attacker |
| Line (stated length) | Straight line, stated length in squares |
| Overlap rule: if any part of a template overlaps a creature's square, that creature is affected. Area effects are not blocked by Cover — only Total Cover in a fully sealed enclosure can block an area effect. |  |

### Token Sizes on the Grid

| Size | Token Footprint | Melee Reach |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tiny | Shares a square (up to 4 per square) | Same or adjacent square |
| Small / Medium | 1×1 square | Adjacent squares |
| Large | 2×2 squares | Adjacent squares (from token edge) |
| Huge | 3×3 squares | Adjacent squares (from token edge) |
| Colossal | 4×4 squares or larger | As stated in the Creature Size table |

### VTT Setup Checklist

* Set grid scale to 5 feet per square.  
* Set diagonal movement to uniform cost — every square equals 5 feet. Disable alternating diagonal cost if your VTT uses it by default.  
* Use built-in template tools: circle templates for Burst/Blast, cone templates for Cones, line templates for Lines.  
* Mark Zone boundaries with coloured area overlays, wall tools, or text labels before the encounter begins.  
* Add Minion groups to the initiative tracker as a single entry per group type. Place individual tokens on the map.  
* Use the ruler or measurement tool to confirm range bands before declaring attacks across multiple Zones.

| Range Band | Zone Distance | Feet | Squares |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Close | Same Zone | 0–25 ft | 0–5 |
| Short | Adjacent Zone | 25–50 ft | 5–10 |
| Medium | 2–3 Zones | 50–120 ft | 10–24 |
| Long | 4–6 Zones | 120–300 ft | 24–60 |
| Extreme | Beyond normal battlefield | 300+ ft | 60+ |

# **Chapter Sixteen  ·  GM’s Section**

Running the Game

Everything on the other side of the table: how to run the game moment to moment, build enemies and encounters, run social scenes and investigations, use downtime, and sustain a campaign over time.

Running HEROIC 5e is a different job from running most roleplaying games. The heroes are extraordinary. The stakes are city-scale or larger. The action is cinematic and fast. The emotional temperature of every scene is higher than most games aim for. A GM who tries to run HEROIC 5e like a careful fantasy dungeon crawl will find it fights back. A GM who leans into what it is will find it one of the most rewarding games they have ever run.

This section covers everything on the other side of the table. It assumes you have read the player-facing chapters. It does not repeat them — it builds on them from the perspective of the person who makes the world move.

## Running HEROIC 5e

### The Philosophy

HEROIC 5e is built around three words that appear throughout this book. They are not aspirational. They are the design standard against which every ruling, every scene call, and every mechanical decision should be measured.

Fast The table is always moving. No pause lasts longer than it needs to. When in doubt, make a call and move on. A slightly wrong ruling that keeps the energy high beats a perfectly correct ruling that kills momentum.

Fun Everyone at the table is engaged, invested, and enjoying themselves — including you. If something is not working, change it. If a rule is producing bad outcomes, ignore it for this session and fix it later. The rules serve the game.

Dynamic The situation is always changing. The villain adapts. Consequences of last session arrive in this one. Heroes who won decisively face a world that has noticed. Heroes who caused collateral damage face a world that remembers.

### When to Roll and When to Say Yes

This is the most important skill in running HEROIC 5e and the one that separates sessions that feel exciting from sessions that feel like paperwork.

**Roll** when the outcome is genuinely uncertain and the consequences of failure are meaningfully different from success. If both paths lead to the same place, do not roll. If failure produces nothing interesting, do not roll. If the hero has a relevant Power, Talent, or Skill that makes the task trivially achievable given who they are, say yes and move on.

**Roll** when tension serves the story. A Striker leaping between two rooftops does not need a roll unless something significant happens if they fail. A Striker leaping between rooftops while being shot at with civilians below and a villain getting away: now the roll means something.

The Guide

Ask yourself what happens if they fail before you call for the roll. If the answer is nothing interesting, say yes.

Never call for a roll as a tax on player agency. A hero who spends an hour investigating a crime scene should find the clue. The roll determines how much they find and how clean the information is — not whether they find anything at all. Dead ends from dice rather than decisions are frustrating, not dramatic.

### The GM as Reactive Architect

HEROIC 5e does not reward GMs who build elaborate plans and execute them regardless of what players do. It rewards GMs who build *situations* and then react to how players move through them.

Build a villain with a goal and a method. Build an environment with features that matter. Build stakes that are clear and personal. Then put the heroes in contact with all three and see what happens. Your job in the session is not to execute your plan — it is to react to theirs.

Preparation should be in the form of tools, not plots. Know your villain's personality and goals. Know the environment's features and hazards. Know the stakes. Have a sense of what happens if the heroes do nothing. Beyond that, react.

### Making Failure Move the Story

Failure in HEROIC 5e should never stop the story. It should change the direction. A failed Stealth check does not mean the heroes cannot infiltrate the building — it means they are detected while doing it, which changes what kind of scene the infiltration becomes. A failed Influence check does not mean the NPC is permanently hostile — it means the approach that just failed is not working, which tells the heroes something true about the situation.

The question after a failure is never "what do the heroes do now that they cannot proceed?" It is "how does the story move differently because this failed?" Failure is information. Use it to reveal character, complicate relationships, and raise stakes. Do not use it to stop play.

### The Turn Checklist

Standard Turn Order — Print and Keep at the Table

* Announce intent: describe what your character is trying to do before touching dice.  
* Declare movement if any.  
* Use your Action (attack, Power, skill use, or other).  
* Use your Bonus Action if available.  
* Declare Speed Actions if you have the Super Speed Power Set.  
* Announce Edge spends as they arise throughout your Turn.  
* Reactions fire when their triggers occur, on any Turn, not just yours.

The most common table problem is players holding their Bonus Action waiting for the perfect moment and then forgetting it. Encourage players to declare their Bonus Action at the same time as their Action.

### Collateral Damage as Story

Every session of HEROIC 5e produces collateral damage. In a superhero game this is not a failure state — it is the texture of the genre. What matters is consequence. A hero who causes enormous collateral damage and faces no consequence is playing in a morally weightless world. A hero whose collateral damage produces Response shifts, Flaw triggers, Merit erosion, and story complications is playing in a world that feels real.

Track collateral damage narratively, not mechanically. Ask yourself: who noticed this and how do they feel about it? A neighborhood that watched a hero destroy three parked cars during a fight will remember that hero. A journalist who filmed the damage will file a story. A villain who saw the hero's restraint in a residential area will exploit that restraint in the next encounter. Collateral damage is the GM's most powerful tool for making heroism feel meaningful. Use it.

## Building Villains and Enemies

### Bosses Are Characters

The most memorable villain you will ever run is not the one with the highest attack bonus. It is the one your players still talk about three years after the campaign ended. What makes that villain memorable has nothing to do with their stat block.

A memorable villain has **a reason** — a specific, personal reason why they are doing what they are doing that makes sense to them even if it is wrong. A villain who believes they are right is more interesting than a villain who knows they are evil. A memorable villain has **a relationship with the heroes** — they know who the heroes are, have opinions about them, and react to what the heroes do between encounters, not just during them. A memorable villain has **a flaw the heroes can find and exploit** — a character flaw that generates story rather than a combat weakness to be discovered through investigation.

### Building a Boss Villain: The Five Questions

Before you write a single stat, answer these five questions. Everything else follows.

1. **What do they want?**

Not vaguely. Specifically. Not power in the abstract but this city's infrastructure controlled by their organization. The more specific the goal, the more consistently the villain will behave across sessions.

2. **Why do they want it?**

What happened to make this goal feel necessary or justified to them? The answer does not have to be sympathetic. It has to be coherent. A villain with a coherent internal logic is one you can play consistently without notes.

3. **What will they not do?**

Every compelling villain has a line they will not cross, and that line reveals character. The line creates the moment when the heroes can predict the villain's behavior and use it against them.

4. **What is their relationship to the heroes?**

Do they know them? Respect them? Feel contempt? Want something from them specifically? A villain who has no opinion about the heroes has not noticed the most interesting thing in their world.

5. **What happens when they lose?**

Not defeat in the final sense — setback. When the heroes disrupt a plan, how does the villain respond? Do they adapt? Escalate? Retreat and regroup? This question is your session-to-session campaign engine.

### Using the Full Build

Once you have answered those questions, build the villain as a full character using the same rules players use. Choose an Origin that fits their background. Choose a Class that reflects how they act under pressure: a villain who controls through information and manipulation is a Mastermind. One who overwhelms through sheer force is a Bruiser. One who makes everyone around them feel something is a Beacon. Choose Power Sets based on their concept, not based on what would be mechanically challenging to fight.

Apply Boss Rules from Chapter 15: Resolve (once per encounter, ignore a condition) and Condition Cap (maximum two simultaneous conditions). Give them a Flaw — not a mechanical limitation from the Power Sets chapter, but a Merits and Flaws chapter Flaw that creates story. The heroes who discover and exploit that Flaw have earned their victory.

### Running Minions

When running large groups of Minions, give each group a personality rather than an individual voice. The Syndicate enforcers are professional and quiet. The street gang members are loud and overconfident. The corporate security team is coordinated and tactical. These personalities require no mechanical expression — they change how you describe what the Minions do and make them feel like a presence rather than an obstacle.

Minion groups that have been depleted behave differently from fresh ones. Two Goons left from a squad of eight are not acting the same way they were at the start. They are scared. They may hesitate. They may break. This is purely narrative, but it is the difference between combat that feels alive and combat that feels like resource management.

### The One-Page Villain Sheet

When running a Boss villain in play, you do not need their full character sheet at the table. You need the following on one page:

* Name and concept in one line  
* Active Defense values for all four defenses  
* Current HP and Bloodied threshold  
* Power Sets and which specific powers they will use this encounter  
* Class features that will come up  
* Effect Values  
* Conditions they currently have  
* Resolve: has it been used this encounter  
* Any Flaw-relevant information

Everything else can be found in your prep notes if it comes up. A villain who acts decisively every Turn creates better combat than a villain whose GM is flipping through notes between each action.

## Building Encounters

### What an Encounter Is

An encounter is not a fight. It is a situation with stakes, opposition, and possible outcomes. A confrontation with a powerful NPC whose cooperation the heroes need is an encounter. A chase through a collapsing building is an encounter. A public speech where the heroes are trying to shift crowd sentiment before a villain's plan succeeds is an encounter.

Before you design any encounter, identify: what are the heroes trying to achieve? What opposes them? What does success look like? What does failure look like? If you cannot answer all four, the encounter is not ready to run.

### The Encounter Budget

For combat encounters, use the following guidelines to calibrate the number and type of enemies for a party of four heroes. Adjust for party size by adding or removing one Standard enemy per hero above or below four.

| Campaign Rank | Standard Encounter | Hard Encounter | Boss Encounter |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 4 Thugs or 2 Goons | 1 Lieutenant \+ 2 Goons | 1 Boss \+ 2 Goons |
| Mid-Level | 3 Goons or 2 Lieutenants | 1 Lieutenant \+ 3 Goons | 1 Boss \+ 1 Lieutenant \+ 2 Goons |
| World Class | 2 Lieutenants or 4 Goons | 2 Lieutenants \+ 2 Goons | 1 Boss \+ 2 Lieutenants \+ 2 Goons |
| Calibrated for 3–5 rounds. When an encounter is running longer than expected and the drama has peaked, end it. The villain escapes. Remaining Minions surrender. The environment forces resolution. Do not run combat past the point where it is interesting simply because enemies have hit points remaining. |  |  |  |

### Terrain as Participation

An empty room is the worst superhero battlefield. Every combat encounter should have terrain features that give multiple character types something to do beyond trading attacks.

Design each combat encounter with at least three terrain features the heroes can interact with or exploit: height differentials that reward flying heroes and punish grounded ones; crowds of civilians that create choices; environmental hazards that change every few rounds; cover that can be destroyed; moving elements that shift Zone positions automatically. Let players discover them through play rather than announcing them.

### Objectives Beyond Defeat

Adding a secondary objective changes how heroes make decisions and makes combat feel more like a superhero story. Options include:

* **Protect the civilian:** one or more bystanders who will be harmed if the heroes do not actively position between them and the threat.  
* **Retrieve the object:** something specific must be recovered, destroyed, or protected during the fight.  
* **Hold the line:** the heroes must keep the enemy from reaching a specific Zone for a specific number of rounds.  
* **Capture not kill:** a specific enemy must be subdued rather than defeated, restricting which powers the heroes can use at full effectiveness.  
* **Time pressure:** something happens at the end of Round 5 regardless of the fight's outcome.

### Civilian Danger as Story

Civilians are not obstacles or backdrop — they are the reason the heroes are fighting. Encounters that include endangered civilians and give heroes meaningful choices about protecting them create the moments superhero games exist to produce.

Civilian danger should create genuine choices, not simply demand correct behavior. A hero who abandons civilians to chase the villain is making a choice with consequences. A hero who splits attention between the fight and evacuation accepts reduced effectiveness to do the right thing. Both should feel meaningful. Do not use civilians as gotcha mechanics — a villain whose plan puts civilians at risk as a side effect of their goal is more interesting than one who murders a civilian purely to demonstrate their evil.

## Social Scenes and Investigation

### Social Scenes with Response

Response is the mechanical spine of social encounters. Start every social scene by setting starting Response based on the fiction: what does this person know about the heroes? What do they want from this interaction? What is at stake for them? A government official who has seen the heroes' collateral damage starts Resistant. An ally who the heroes rescued last session starts Favorable.

Do not call for a Response Check every time a hero says something. Roll when the outcome is uncertain and the stakes are meaningful. A hero with Influence trained and a Favorable Response NPC does not need to roll to get basic cooperation — the Merit and the fiction have already established that. Roll when the situation is tense, the request is significant, or the hero is pushing beyond what the current Response would normally allow.

### Running Investigation

Investigation scenes work best when the GM thinks in terms of information layers rather than clue checklists.

* **Surface information:** available without a roll to anyone who looks.  
* **Careful information:** available to a hero who makes a deliberate effort.  
* **Deep information:** available only with a Strong Success or specific expertise.  
* **Hidden information:** available only through exceptional play, specific powers, or contacts with the right access.

When a hero fails an Investigation check they still get something — surface information, or an inaccurate version of careful information that points them somewhere useful even if it is not the direct path. Failure slows the investigation and complicates it. It does not stop it. The goal of an investigation scene is a revelation that changes what the heroes understand about the situation — not a confirmation of what they already suspected.

### Social Versus Combat Pacing

Social scenes become tedious when they run like combat. Do not call for Initiative in a negotiation. Do not require every participant to take a Turn before the scene can progress. Social scenes work through conversation, player decisions, and Response tracking. One or two rolls per scene is usually sufficient. More than three is almost always too many.

The exception is when a social scene tips into confrontation — a negotiation that breaks down, an interrogation where the subject is actively resistant and the heroes are running out of time. In these cases a more structured approach is appropriate. This is also when a HEROIC Challenge may be warranted.

## Downtime

### What Downtime Actually Is

Downtime is not a mechanical system. It is a type of scene — scenes that happen between the action, when the heroes are not in immediate danger and have some control over how they spend their time. Use downtime scenes to deepen relationships, develop contacts into meaningful NPCs, advance personal story threads, establish what the heroes do when the world is not ending, and plant the seeds of what comes next.

### Running Downtime at the Table

Downtime does not need to be played out in real time. A montage is legitimate. A brief description of what each hero does with their time, followed by one or two short scenes that capture the most dramatically interesting moment, is better than a full session of shopping and recovery.

Ask each player: what does your hero do during this downtime? What matters to them right now? Then follow up on the answer that creates the most interesting scene. A hero who says they are working on their suit gets a scene where something goes wrong with the suit in an interesting way. A hero who says they are visiting family gets a scene where a family relationship becomes complicated by their heroic life.

### Merits and Flaws in Downtime

Merits develop or erode during downtime based on what the heroes do. Public Trust damaged by a public incident requires active effort to rebuild: visible community work, interviews, demonstrating judgment in public. If the heroes spend downtime in isolation, their Public Trust stays damaged.

Flaws create downtime complications. A hero with the Debt Flaw receives contact from the people they owe. A hero with the Dependent Flaw gets a scene involving the dependent. A hero with the Obligation Flaw has an obligation that comes due. These are not punishments — they are story hooks the player agreed to when they chose those Flaws. The heroes who engage with their Flaws during downtime are the ones whose stories feel complete.

### Planting Seeds

Every downtime session should end with at least one seed planted for a future session. A contact mentions something they heard that seemed unimportant but was not. A news item connects to something the heroes have been tracking. A villain who was defeated three arcs ago reappears in a small way. Plant more seeds than you intend to use. Players will latch onto the ones that resonate and ignore the ones that do not. The seeds they pursue become the campaign.

## HEROIC Challenges

Optional Rule HEROIC Challenges work best for scenes where time pressure is real, the stakes are clear, and more than one hero has something to contribute. Not every tense scene needs one.

Some situations don't fit neatly into a single roll, and they shouldn't. A building collapsing floor by floor. A hostage negotiation unraveling in real time. A team racing to evacuate a neighborhood before a chemical plant explodes. These are not moments resolved by one hero making one check — they are structured crises that demand sustained effort, creative problem-solving, and the full range of what the team can do.

A HEROIC Challenge is a structured sequence that gives these moments the mechanical weight they deserve. It tracks cumulative progress and failure across multiple contributions, keeps every hero relevant regardless of build, and uses HEROIC 5e's existing Degrees of Success to make every roll feel meaningful.

### When to Call a HEROIC Challenge

Use a HEROIC Challenge when the situation has all three of the following:

* **A clear goal with real stakes.** Something specific that failure changes. Not just "you don't get what you wanted" — something actually gets worse, someone gets hurt, or an opportunity closes.  
* **Sustained pressure.** The situation unfolds over time and demands repeated effort. One roll would trivialize it.  
* **Room for the whole team.** Multiple heroes can contribute in meaningfully different ways. A Challenge where only the team's most skilled hero matters isn't a Challenge — it's a showcase.

Situations That Call for a HEROIC Challenge

* A massive structural collapse: floors buckling, gas lines rupturing, trapped civilians on multiple levels  
* A hostage negotiation where the gunman is escalating and the police commander is losing patience  
* Infiltrating a heavily secured facility: biometric locks, camera feeds, guards, asset extraction  
* Evacuating a neighborhood ahead of an approaching catastrophe  
* A political crisis in real time: testifying before a Senate subcommittee while the opposition attacks  
* Cracking a serial villain's coded message before the next strike  
* A runaway train with failing brakes and a crowded station at the end of the line

### How HEROIC Challenges Work

#### Step 1 — The GM Sets the Challenge

Before the scene begins, the GM privately establishes the Complexity and Failure Threshold. Players are never told these numbers — they know the situation and the stakes, not the math.

Simple 4 Fast-moving crisis, small team, one clear obstacle. Failure Threshold: 3\.

Standard 6 Multi-layered situation, full team, meaningful stakes. Failure Threshold: 3\.

Complex 8 Major set piece, high consequences, multiple simultaneous problems. Failure Threshold: 4\.

Before the Challenge begins, the GM should privately decide what **partial failure** looks like. Reaching the failure threshold before Complexity does not have to be a complete loss — the heroes rescue most of the civilians but not all, or they get into the facility but the alarm is raised on the way out. Complete failure is always an option when it fits the story, but the goal is consequences with forward momentum, not dead stops.

#### Step 2 — Heroes Contribute

Each hero contributes once per round of the Challenge. Contributions take one of the following forms:

* **Skill Check.** The hero describes what they are doing and rolls the appropriate Skill. The GM sets the DC based on the difficulty of that specific obstacle using the standard difficulty scale. Each obstacle in a Challenge has its own DC — bypassing a biometric lock is harder than clearing rubble.  
* **Power Use.** If a hero has a Power that directly applies to the obstacle, they use it. Powers clearly relevant to the fiction resolve automatically as a success — no roll required. If the application is creative or uncertain, the GM may call for a Skill check with the Power providing Advantage.  
* **Assist.** A hero with no directly applicable Skill or Power uses the Help action, granting Advantage to the next hero who rolls this Challenge round. Assist does not advance the success counter on its own — it improves a teammate's odds. A brawler who can't pick a lock can absolutely hold a ceiling up while the tech hero works.  
* **Narrative Action.** Once per Challenge round, one hero may make a purely narrative contribution — invoking a relevant Merit, spending Edge for Narrative Advantage, or leaning into their Calling in a way that creates a meaningful dramatic beat. The GM decides whether this counts as an automatic success or grants Advantage to the next roll. Reserved for moments of genuine dramatic weight, not routine play.

#### Step 3 — Apply Degrees of Success

| Result | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| HEROIC Success (beats DC by 10+) | \+3 successes, or collapse an entire obstacle entirely |
| Strong Success (beats DC by 5+) | \+2 successes; the GM describes a meaningful gain in the fiction |
| Success (meets DC) | \+1 success |
| Failure (misses DC) | \+1 failure |
| Fumble (natural 1\) | \+2 failures, *or* \+1 failure and Disadvantage on the next roll in this Challenge (GM's choice based on fiction) |

#### Step 4 — Advantage and Disadvantage

The same rules that govern Skill checks throughout HEROIC 5e apply inside a Challenge. A hero rolls with Advantage if they have a Power, Talent, or Merit that directly and specifically applies — a hero with Super Strength has Advantage on clearing structural debris but not on talking a panicked civilian down from a ledge. A hero rolls with Disadvantage if the GM invokes a relevant Flaw (Reckless, Enemy, Famous Identity, etc.). If Advantage and Disadvantage both apply, they cancel as normal. Flaws invoked during a Challenge should earn the affected player 1 Edge, as with any meaningful Flaw complication.

#### Step 5 — Resolution

The team **succeeds** when they reach the Complexity target. The fiction should reflect the quality of the victory — a team that hit 8 successes with only 1 failure got everyone out clean. A team that scraped through with the last success as the failure threshold loomed got everyone out, but it was close and there are questions to answer.

The team **fails** when they hit the Failure Threshold. The GM describes the consequences established before the Challenge began. Partial failures are valid.

### Challenges and Scene Types

* **In an Action Scene:** A Challenge runs alongside combat using the existing round structure. Heroes can fight and contribute to the Challenge in the same round, but splitting attention has a cost — a hero fighting for their life may not have clean access to the objectives the Challenge demands.  
* **In an Investigation or Social Scene:** The Challenge provides structure to moments where single rolls feel insufficient — a negotiation genuinely at risk of collapse, an interrogation with a hard deadline, a press conference going sideways.  
* **In Downtime:** Challenges are rarely appropriate. Downtime is space to breathe, not to escalate. If a downtime moment requires a Challenge, it has probably become something else.

Example of Play — The Ashford Arms Fire

The Ashford Arms is a six-story tenement in the Margin District, and it is burning. Three-quarters evacuated. One person has not: a child named Dani, seven years old, trapped in a sixth-floor apartment behind a fire door that warped shut in the heat. The stairwell below is compromised. The window is forty feet up.

GM sets a **Standard Challenge: 6 successes before 3 failures.** Partial failure: the team gets Dani out, but the building collapses with a hero still inside — a major public incident and a physical consequence.

**Round 1\.**

**HARDBODY** looks up at the building. The fire escape ends at the fourth floor — the upper section collapsed. She has Super Strength. She doesn't need it. "I'm going up the outside. Bare hands." Athletics check, Super Strength applies — Advantage. She rolls a **Strong Success. \+2 successes (total: 2/6).** HARDBODY is on the sixth-floor ledge in seconds, finding the apartment window — warped in its frame, but not yet fused shut.

**GHOST FOX** is on comms, coordinating with fire crews below. She invokes Streetwise and her Connected Merit — she knows which city inspectors looked the other way on this building's permits, which tells her exactly how it was built. Narrative Action — automatic success. **\+1 success (total: 3/6).**

**NIGHTSHADE** notices a woman near the barrier hyperventilating, staring up at the sixth floor. Dani's mother, and she knows something. Insight check. Normal success. **\+1 success (total: 4/6).** The mother says there's a service corridor that connects to the roof access — warped, but it might open from the outside.

**Round 2\.** 4 successes in, 2 to go. 0 failures. The building groans.

HARDBODY takes the intel and moves along the exterior to the roof access door. The door is buckled. "I'm not asking it to open." Athletics again, Advantage. She rolls a **HEROIC Success — beats the DC by 12\. \+3 successes. Challenge resolved.**

The door comes off its hinges. HARDBODY finds Dani under a table, hands over ears, terrified and completely unharmed. She wraps the child in her jacket and drops six floors to the ladder platform GHOST FOX coordinated into position.

*The crowd goes silent as HARDBODY falls, the child pressed against her chest. She lands on the platform with a sound like a car hitting pavement. The ladder shudders. Dani is crying. HARDBODY is on one knee, grinning through soot. Clean extraction. Zero failures. The Margin District is going to remember this one.*

**GM Note:** If HARDBODY had rolled a Fumble on that final check, the GM would have chosen: 2 failures (total 2, one away from partial failure — sudden stakes spike) or 1 failure and Disadvantage on the next roll (the door holds, the corridor fills with smoke, whoever tries next is working half-blind). Either way the scene continues — it just gets harder and the margin disappears.

## Running a Campaign

### Milestone Advancement in Practice

The cleanest approach is to tie advancement to story beats rather than session counts. A completed arc earns a level. A major victory that cost something earns a level. A significant failure with lasting consequences earns a level. Heroes advance when they have done something that changed who they are, not simply because they have accumulated enough sessions.

Communicate this standard to your players at the start of the campaign — they will make decisions differently when they understand that advancement comes from meaningful story engagement rather than time served. Avoid advancement at the end of every session. Save it for moments that matter.

### Between Session Tracking

The GM's job between sessions is not extensive preparation. It is maintaining awareness of the state of the world so that it can react consistently to what the heroes do. Keep a simple running record of:

* **Response states** for recurring NPCs and factions: how does each significant NPC currently feel about the heroes and why?  
* **Active story threads:** what is the villain currently doing? What plans are in motion? What are the consequences of the last session rippling forward?  
* **Flaw status:** which Flaws have been triggered recently and which are due to complicate things? Players forget their Flaws. The GM's job is to remember them.  
* **Merit erosion:** which Merits are under pressure from story events?

This does not need to be a formal document. Notes on a single page per session, updated as you run, are sufficient.

### Using Callings as Campaign Fuel

Callings are the most underused tool in a campaign GM's toolkit. Every hero has three Edge triggers in their Calling that describe specific moments the player agreed to pursue. Those triggers are not just Edge rewards — they are a map of what this player finds dramatically interesting.

A hero with the Protector Calling has agreed that scenes where they must choose between the mission and the person are interesting to them. Build those scenes. A hero with the Avenger Calling has a vendetta they want to explore. Bring the target into the campaign. The Callings tell you what each player at your table is hoping to experience. Use them.

### Arc Structure

The Complication 2–4 sessions

The situation becomes clear. The heroes understand what the villain wants, what is at stake, and what they need to do.

The Escalation 3–6 sessions

The situation becomes worse. The villain succeeds at something. A plan that was working fails. A hero's Flaw creates a crisis. Stakes rise.

The Resolution 1–2 sessions

The situation comes to a head. The final confrontation. The choice that cannot be avoided. The consequence of everything that came before.

Between arcs, use a downtime period to let the heroes breathe, develop relationships, and plant the seeds of the next arc. The next villain need not be announced immediately. Let the world settle for a session before the next threat emerges. The contrast makes both feel more real.

### When Things Go Wrong

Sometimes a session fails. The encounter was too easy or too hard. A social scene went flat. A player made a choice that derailed the prepared material completely. A rule was misapplied and nobody noticed until three scenes later. These are not failures — they are information.

When an encounter ends in one round without drama, note what the heroes did and make the next encounter account for it. When a social scene goes flat, ask what was missing: were the stakes clear? Did the NPC have a genuine perspective? When a player derails your material, follow them. The thing they chose to do is more interesting to them than what you had planned, which means the table will be more engaged if you go there.

The Rule for Running HEROIC 5e Over Time

It is the same as the rule for running it in a single session: **react.**

The world reacts to the heroes. You react to the players. The campaign that emerges from genuine reaction is always better than the campaign that was planned in advance.

# **Chapter Seventeen · NPC and Opponents**

## NPCs in HEROIC 5e

Player characters have levels. They have Prowess derived from experience. They have Callings that earn Edge, Classes that define how they fight, and Advancement Tables that track every step of their growth. All of that exists because player characters are the protagonists of the story — the people at the center of everything, growing and changing over time.

NPCs are not that.

A crime boss does not have levels. A genetically engineered enforcer does not have a Class. A cosmic entity older than the sun does not have a Prowess score derived from how many sessions it has survived. These beings exist at a power tier. They are what they are. The GM's job is not to build them like heroes — it is to deploy them like the world they inhabit.

This means NPCs follow different rules from player characters, and that is not a flaw in the design. It is the design. When a villain feels more dangerous than the math should allow, that is not the rules breaking down. That is the GM making a deliberate choice about the kind of threat this encounter represents. Players should never look at an NPC stat block and ask whether the GM followed the rules correctly. They should look at it and ask how they are going to survive.

NPCs do not roll dice. They provide static numbers. The players roll against those numbers. This is consistent throughout the system regardless of how powerful the NPC is — a Cosmic-tier entity operates on exactly the same mechanical principle as a street thug. The GM reads a number. The player rolls against it. The dice always belong to the players.

### **NPC Power Tiers**

Every NPC in HEROIC 5e belongs to one of five Power Tiers. The tier determines the NPC's **Tier Bonus** — the flat number added to all of their static values — and their **Power Die**, used to calculate damage expressions and pre-built into every stat block's printed numbers.

| Tier | Tier Bonus | Power Die | Best Fit |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Day Player | \+1 | d6 | Human-scale supporting cast |
| Low Power | \+2 | d8 | Street-level superhuman threats |
| Medium Power | \+3 | d10 | City-scale threats, Mid-Level campaign staples |
| High Power | \+4 | d12 | World-scale threats, World Class campaign staples |
| Cosmic Power | \+6 | d12+d6 † | Reality-adjacent threats, campaign-defining villains |

*† Cosmic Power uses d12+d6 for optional rolled damage. Pre-calculated stat blocks use the median by default. See Cosmic Power — A Special Case below.*

These tiers are tools for the GM, not constraints. A Medium Power threat dropped into a Street Level campaign is a serious escalation — a villain the heroes may not be ready to face alone. A Low Power NPC in a World Class campaign is a nuisance, a distraction, or a named character with plot importance whose combat capability is deliberately modest. The tiers describe what the NPC is. How that maps to the current campaign is the GM's call.

#### **Tier Bonus**

The Tier Bonus replaces what Prowess does for player characters. It is not Prowess. NPCs do not have Prowess. They have a Tier Bonus assigned by their power tier, and that bonus feeds into every static number on their stat block.

The formulas are the same formulas used throughout the game — they just use Tier Bonus instead of Prowess:

- **Defense Values:** 10 \+ relevant modifier(s) \+ Tier Bonus — Parry/Block, Dodge, and Willpower each add PER alongside their primary modifier, since noticing a threat is always part of surviving it  
- **Attack Value:** 10 \+ primary combat modifier \+ Tier Bonus  
- **Effect Values / Save Values:** 10 \+ governing modifier \+ Tier Bonus  
- **Trained Skills:** add Tier Bonus to relevant checks

Showing the math on a stat block looks like this for a Medium Power villain with FIG \+3 and PER \+2:

Parry/Block: 10 \+ FIG \+3 \+ PER \+2 \+ Tier Bonus \+3 \= **18**

Everything is pre-calculated. The GM reads 18\. The player rolls against it. The Tier Bonus is shown so GMs who want to adjust an NPC on the fly — increasing their tier, changing an attribute — can see exactly where every number comes from.

### **Power Die**

The Power Die determines damage output. Like Tier Bonus it is pre-calculated into every printed damage expression, so GMs never need to look it up mid-encounter. It is listed here so GMs building custom NPCs or adjusting existing ones understand the damage scale each tier represents.

A Low Power NPC built around a d8 hits meaningfully at Street Level and is still a nuisance at Mid-Level. A High Power NPC built around a d12 is a genuine threat to a full team of experienced heroes regardless of campaign scale.

### **Cosmic Power — A Special Case**

Cosmic Power NPCs are categorically beyond the normal threat spectrum. They are not simply High Power threats with larger numbers. They are the kind of being whose existence shapes the campaign around them — the arrival of a Cosmic Power NPC should feel like an event, not just a difficult encounter.

All Cosmic Power stat blocks use pre-calculated numbers like every other tier. The GM reads static values. The players roll against them. There is no additional mechanical complexity at this tier — the numbers are simply large.

### **How NPC Stat Blocks Are Built**

Every NPC stat block — whether a named recurring villain or a generic archetype — uses the same structure. Understanding the structure lets GMs adjust entries on the fly, build custom NPCs from scratch, and scale existing entries to fit their campaign's needs.

#### **The Eight Modifiers**

NPC stat blocks list all eight Ability Score **modifiers**, not scores. STR, DEX, CON, FIG, INT, WIS, CHA, PER. These are the numbers that feed into formulas. The underlying scores are not listed because GMs never need them — every calculation uses the modifier.

#### **Defense Values**

Four static numbers representing how difficult this NPC is to hit, manipulate, or affect.

| Defense | Formula |
| :---- | :---- |
| Parry/Block | 10 \+ FIG \+ PER \+ Tier Bonus |
| Dodge | 10 \+ DEX \+ PER \+ Tier Bonus |
| Willpower | 10 \+ WIS \+ PER \+ Tier Bonus |
| Social | 10 \+ CHA \+ INT \+ Tier Bonus |

When a hero attacks this NPC, the hero rolls 1d20 \+ their attack modifier \+ their Prowess and must beat the relevant Defense Value. The NPC never rolls. The GM reads the number and waits.

#### **Attack Value**

The single number representing this NPC's offensive capability.

Attack Value \= 10 \+ primary combat modifier \+ Tier Bonus

When this NPC attacks a hero, the GM announces the Attack Value and the hero rolls their Active Defense. If the hero's roll meets or beats the Attack Value, the attack fails. If it falls short, the attack lands and damage is applied.

#### **Effect Values**

The number a hero must overcome when this NPC applies a condition, force, or power effect.

Effect Value \= 10 \+ governing modifier \+ Tier Bonus

The governing modifier is determined by the nature of the effect — the same logic as for player characters. A physical force uses STR. A psychic attack uses WIS or INT. A toxic effect uses CON. Each NPC entry specifies the Effect Value for each power or ability that requires a save, with the governing modifier visible in the formula.

#### **Damage**

Damage expressions are listed as dice \+ modifier with the median value in brackets.

2d10 \+ FIG modifier \[median\]

The median is there for GMs who want speed. The dice are there for GMs who want drama. Both are always available.

#### **Hit Points**

Named NPCs use HP calculated from the NPC's Constitution score and their Power Tier's Hit Die. Always use the maximum value of the Hit Die — NPCs start at full potential, not average. The Constitution score is added inside the parentheses before the multiplier is applied — the multiplier scales the whole sum, not just the die.

HP \= (Constitution \+ dX) × Y

| Power Tier | HP Formula | Example (Constitution 18, max die) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Day Player | (Constitution \+ 1d6) × 1 | (18 \+ 6\) × 1 \= **24** |
| Low Power | (Constitution \+ 1d8) × 1 | (18 \+ 8\) × 1 \= **26** |
| Medium Power | (Constitution \+ 1d10) × 2 | (18 \+ 10\) × 2 \= **56** |
| High Power | (Constitution \+ 1d12) × 3 | (18 \+ 12\) × 3 \= **90** |
| Cosmic Power | (Constitution \+ 1d12+1d6) × 4 | (18 \+ 18\) × 4 \= **144** |

**Bonus HP** — The formula gives a baseline. Story gives the rest. A recurring villain designed to survive multiple sessions, a Boss built to anchor a climactic encounter, a Named NPC with narrative reasons to endure — add Bonus HP on top of the formula result as needed. There is no cap. A final-boss villain who should survive two full rounds of focused fire from a five-hero team needs more HP than the formula alone provides. State the Bonus HP explicitly in the stat block so it is visible when adjusting the NPC later.

Minions do not use this formula. Minions use hits. → Minions, below.

#### **Skills**

A trained Skill adds the NPC's Tier Bonus to relevant checks. Where an NPC has Advantage on a particular Skill, that is noted. Only Skills likely to come up in play are listed — GMs do not need to track every possible competency an NPC might theoretically possess.

#### **Class Abilities**

NPCs do not have Classes, but they can have Class Abilities — specific features borrowed from the Class chapters that make mechanical sense for the concept. A villain who fights like a Bruiser might have Heavy Hitter. A manipulative crime boss might have the Beacon's Taunt. A trained assassin might carry the Striker's Exploit Opening.

This is a scalpel, not a shovel. One or two Class Abilities per NPC is enough. Three is the absolute ceiling for a complex Named villain. Beyond that, the GM is tracking too many triggers at once, combat slows down, and the NPC stops feeling dangerous and starts feeling bureaucratic.

Choose abilities with obvious triggers — features that fire on their own without requiring the GM to remember they exist. Passive abilities and once-per-encounter reactions are ideal. Complex chains of conditions and follow-up effects are not.

#### **Powers and Features**

Named and archetype NPCs list their key powers under each Power Set heading. List only what will come up in play. Three to five entries is enough for most NPCs. A Named villain anchoring a major arc might have more. A one-session antagonist needs less. If a power is not listed on the stat block, it does not exist for this NPC at this table. The stat block is the source of truth.

### NPC Roles in Encounters

Not every NPC in an encounter functions the same way. HEROIC 5e recognizes three distinct encounter roles, each with different mechanical weight at the table.

#### Minions

Minions are the rank and file. They exist in numbers. Their purpose is to create pressure, fill space, and make the heroes feel the weight of opposition before the real threat makes its move. Individually they are not dangerous. In groups they absolutely are.

Minions are tracked by **hits**, not HP. A hit is any attack or Power that deals damage — one point or fifty points both count as one hit.

| Minion Type | Hits to Defeat | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Thug | 1 | Foot soldier, untrained criminal, basic drone |
| Goon | 2 | Trained enforcer, armed operative, mid-tier soldier |
| Lieutenant | 3 | Skilled operative, field commander, dangerous specialist |

**Minion Rules:**

- Conditions apply to Minions normally — a Dazed Thug still cannot take Reactions.  
- Area effects deal 1 hit to each Minion within the area, regardless of damage amount.  
- Minions act as groups on a shared initiative count per Minion type.  
- Lieutenants are not Bosses. They have 3 hits and no special protections. A GM who wants a field commander to feel threatening should designate them as a Boss instead.

Minions do not have Power Tiers in the traditional sense — their danger comes from numbers and positioning, not raw mechanical power. However, the GM should assign Attack Values and damage expressions appropriate to the campaign's scale. Thugs in a Street Level campaign hit differently than Thugs in a World Class campaign. A one-line note on the encounter prep sheet is enough: *"Syndicate Thugs: Attack Value 12, 1d6+1 \[4\] bludgeoning."*

#### Named NPCs

Named NPCs are specific individuals with identities, histories, and roles in the story that extend beyond a single encounter. They have full stat blocks, defined Power Sets, and Merits and Flaws that make them feel like people rather than obstacles. They have HP. They can return. They carry Flaws the heroes can discover and exploit.

Named NPCs can be any Power Tier. A Low Power Named NPC might be a recurring street-level contact who occasionally needs rescuing — or who occasionally pulls the heroes out of trouble. A Cosmic Power Named NPC is a campaign-defining figure whose presence reshapes the story.

#### Boss

Any Named NPC can be designated as the Boss of a specific encounter. This is a per-encounter designation, not a permanent trait. The same villain is a Boss in the climactic confrontation at the end of Act Two and a standard Named NPC in the brief appearance where they escape mid-session.

Designating a Boss adds two mechanical layers on top of their normal statistics:

**Resolve** — Once per encounter, when a hero's roll would successfully apply a condition or resisted effect to the Boss, the Boss may ignore that condition or effect entirely. Resolve does not prevent damage. Resolve cannot be used against the same type of effect consecutively.

**Condition Cap** — A Boss can only be affected by two conditions simultaneously. If a third condition would apply, the GM chooses which existing condition ends to make room.

Only one NPC per encounter can be the Boss.

These rules exist because a party with optimal play can lock down an unprotected villain in two rounds. Boss Rules prevent that without making the villain invincible. The heroes still win by being clever and relentless — they just cannot do it by stacking conditions on Round 1 and waiting.

### Cross-Tier Deployment

The Power Tier system is most useful when GMs treat it as a design tool rather than a constraint. A tier describes what an NPC is, not where it belongs.

**Punching up** — placing a Medium or High Power threat against heroes operating at Street Level — creates escalation, urgency, and the feeling that the world contains things beyond the party's current reach. Use this for threats that are meant to be fled from, bargained with, or defeated through cleverness rather than direct combat.

**Punching down** — placing Low Power threats against High Power heroes — is not a mistake. Named Low Power NPCs with story importance belong in any campaign. A beloved civilian ally, a morally complex informant, a former villain trying to go straight: these people matter narratively regardless of their combat tier. Do not over-power every NPC just because the heroes are powerful.

**Tier mismatches as storytelling** — A High Power villain who has been presented as untouchable since session one, finally faced in a climactic encounter after the heroes have grown to match them, hits differently than the same stat block dropped in session three. The Power Tier is fixed. The narrative context is everything.

### Building a Custom NPC

When no existing archetype fits the concept, build from scratch. The process is fast.

**Step 1 — Establish the concept.** One sentence. What is this NPC, what do they want, and what makes them a threat or an asset?

**Step 2 — Assign the Power Tier.** Choose Day Player, Low, Medium, High, or Cosmic based on the role this NPC plays and the campaign's current scale. Note the Tier Bonus and Power Die.

**Step 3 — Assign modifiers.** Distribute modifiers based on concept. A bruiser has high STR and FIG. A manipulator has high CHA and INT. A martial artist has high FIG and DEX. No modifier should exceed \+6 for anything below Cosmic Power. Cosmic Power NPCs may go higher for specific standout attributes.

**Step 4 — Calculate static values.** Apply the formulas. Defense Values: 10 \+ relevant modifier(s) \+ Tier Bonus (PER joins FIG, DEX, or WIS for Parry/Block, Dodge, and Willpower) Attack Value: 10 \+ primary combat modifier \+ Tier Bonus Effect Values: 10 \+ governing modifier \+ Tier Bonus

**Step 5 — Set HP.** Use the HP formula for the NPC's Power Tier, always taking the maximum Hit Die value. Add Bonus HP if the NPC's role demands it.

**Step 6 — Assign Class Abilities (Optional).** One or two at most. Choose passive abilities and once-per-encounter reactions over complex triggered chains.

**Step 7 — Define powers and features.** Three to five entries covers most NPCs. List only what will come up in play.

**Step 8 — Write the Notes.** How does this NPC fight? What do they do when losing? What do they want beyond this encounter? One short paragraph. This is the most important part of the stat block.

### The Notes Field

Every Named NPC entry ends with a Notes section. This is not flavor text. It is operational information.

A stat block without Notes is a number generator. An NPC with Notes is a person.

Notes answer four questions:

- **Tactical priority** — What does this NPC try to do on their turn? Who do they target first and why?  
- **Losing behavior** — What changes when they drop below half HP? Do they fight harder, attempt to flee, offer a deal, call for backup?  
- **Personality** — One or two sentences. Enough that the GM can improvise dialogue without breaking character.  
- **Story hook** — What exists beyond this encounter? A Flaw to exploit, an allegiance that could shift, a secret that changes what the heroes think they know.

The best villain the players will ever face is not the one with the highest Attack Value. It is the one whose Notes made the GM feel like they understood someone, and played them accordingly.

## **Opponents**

Every hero needs a world to operate in. That world is populated by people who want things, organizations that pursue agendas, villains who believe they are right, soldiers who follow orders, civilians who need protecting, and creatures that follow nothing but instinct. This chapter gives GMs everything they need to fill that world without building every inhabitant from scratch.

The entries here fall into three broad categories.

**Archetypes** are fully realized superhuman NPCs at Street Level, Mid-Level, and World Class. A Blaster, a Brick, a Speedster, a Mage. Heroic archetypes can serve as allies, rivals, guest heroes, or rescued colleagues. Villainous archetypes are ready-made antagonists. Every archetype entry gives you a complete stat block at all three Campaign Ranks so the same concept scales with your campaign. Use them straight from the page, rename them, change their Side, or swap a Power Set to make them feel like your own.

**Day Players** are the supporting cast of a superhero city. Law enforcement officers, federal agents, doctors, reporters, lawyers, scientists, criminals, soldiers, and mercenaries. These are the people the heroes interact with in every session who are not themselves superhuman. They have stats because sometimes a fight breaks out, but their real value is as the human texture of the world: the detective who becomes a Contact, the reporter whose coverage shifts public Response, the scientist whose knowledge unlocks a plot.

**Animals and Creatures** cover the non-human threats and complications heroes encounter, from ordinary predators to creatures of monstrous scale. Because sometimes a mad scientist does release a dinosaur, and the GM should not have to invent the stat block on the spot.

## **How to Read These Entries**

Every NPC entry in this chapter is built with the formulas in **How NPC Stat Blocks Are Built**, above. Nothing here overrides them — this section covers only the presentation.

The eight Ability Score modifiers are listed in the book's standard order: **STR, DEX, CON, FIG, INT, WIS, CHA, PER**. These are modifiers, not scores.

* **Active Defense values** are static targets. When a hero attacks this NPC, the hero rolls and must meet or beat the listed value. The NPC never rolls.  
    
* **Attack Value** is the NPC's static attack number. When this NPC attacks a hero, the GM announces the number and the hero rolls their Active Defense against it.  
    
* **Initiative** is the static value 10 \+ DEX \+ PER. NPCs do not roll for Initiative either.  
    
* **Damage** is listed as dice \+ modifier with the median value in brackets. A GM who wants speed uses the median. A GM who wants drama rolls the dice.  
    
* **HP** is the total from the tier formula, plus any Bonus HP, which is stated separately where it applies.  
    
* **Tier Bonus** is shown on every block so a GM re-tiering an NPC on the fly can see where every number came from. NPCs do not have Prowess.  
    
* **Power Sets** list the NPC's superhuman capabilities. Only the powers likely to come up in play are listed. If a power is not on the block, it does not exist for this NPC at this table.  
    
* **Skills** note training. A trained Skill adds the Tier Bonus to relevant checks, and the NPC gains Advantage where noted.  
    
* **Merits and Flaws** are listed where they directly affect how the NPC functions at the table. A GM running a Crimelord with a Dependent Flaw has a built-in dramatic lever. Use it.  
    
* **Notes** tell you how to run this NPC: tactical priorities, behaviour when losing, personality, and what makes them feel like a person rather than a stat block.

Minion Attack Values and Damage

Minions do not get full stat blocks. Use this table, adjusted to taste.

| Campaign Rank | Attack Value | Damage |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Street Level | 12 | 1d6\+1 \[4\] |
| Mid-Level | 14 | 1d8\+2 \[6\] |
| World Class | 16 | 1d10\+3 \[8\] |

Lieutenants add \+1 to Attack Value and one step to the damage die. A one-line note on the encounter sheet is all the prep a Minion group needs.

## Adjusting Archetypes

Every archetype entry is a starting point. Change the name. Change the Side. Swap Fire Control for Cold Control and the Elemental Master becomes a different villain with the same mechanical skeleton. Increase the HP by 20 percent and the encounter runs longer. Add a Flaw and suddenly the NPC has a vulnerability the heroes can find and exploit.

The archetypes are not sacred. They are tools.
