# **Chapter Eighteen · Ready to Play Templates**

All thirty templates are Level 1 characters. Give the hero a name, a look, and a reason — then play.

**Rules reminders:** Every formula below is stated in full in The Core Reference, Chapter 14. Ability Scores shown already include Origin bonuses and any \+1 per Core Track step granted by an Enhancement Power Set. Speed is 30 ft for every character; movement Powers state their own rates in their entries. HP \= (full Constitution score \+ Hit Die max) × Campaign Rank \+ Prowess. Active Defense rolls \= 1d20 \+ modifier \+ PRO. Effect Value \= 10 \+ governing modifier \+ PRO. Initiative \= 1d20 \+ DEX mod \+ PER mod (Prowess is not added unless a specific feature grants it). Power attacks roll delivery modifier \+ Governing Ability modifier \+ PRO: melee uses FIG, ranged DEX, mental INT, social CHA as the delivery modifier. Damage adds the Governing Ability modifier \+ the damage modifier (STR melee, DEX ranged, INT mental, CHA social). The Striker's Focused Fighter lets them choose each Turn: Offense (FIG to damage, on top of STR) or Defense (FIG to Parry/Block a second time); 1 Edge to switch as a Reaction.

## **STREET LEVEL**

Street Level heroes operate in a grounded, city-scale world. **Power Die d8 · Tier 1 powers · PRO \+2 · Starting Power Picks: 8 · Starting Edge: 3\. Hit Points** are full **Constitution** Score \+ 1 full value **Hit Die**.

### **The Brick — Street Level**

*You hit things. Things stop moving. The plan is usually you.*

The Brick is the team's anchor. Too tough to put down, unwilling to step aside. Absorb the hit. Keep the team standing.

* **Super Strength 1** *(STR governs)* — Lifting, throwing, and melee at superhuman scale.  
    
* **Super Durability 1** *(CON governs)* — Flat damage reduction 2 vs all incoming damage. Gain temp HP \= CON mod (3) at start of each encounter.

Powers

**Mighty Blow** *(At-Will · Action):* Attack 1d20+7 vs Parry/Block. 1d8+8 \[13\] bludgeoning. Close range. **Hurl** *(At-Will · Action):* Throw object or grabbed target. Attack 1d20+6 vs Dodge. 1d8+4 \[9\] bludgeoning. Short range. **Brace** *(Encounter · Reaction):* When hit, reduce incoming damage by 1d8+3 \[7\].

Class Features \*(Level 1 only)

* **Stand Between:** When an ally within Close range is hit, use your Reaction to become the target instead.  
    
* **Iron Presence:** While conscious, allies within Short range have Advantage on saves against fear, Shaken, and forced movement. Once per Turn, spend your Bonus Action to let an ally within Short range immediately spend one Hit Die as a free action.

Skills \*(roll 1d20 \+ bonus shown; bonus \= ability modifier \+ PRO)

Athletics \+6 *(Origin)* · Intimidation \+3

Talents \*(Level 1 — two total)

* **Origin Talent:** Adaptive Biology  
    
* **Starting Talent:** Durable — when you spend a Hit Die during a Breather, treat any roll lower than your CON plus your Prowess as that result instead; once per encounter, ignore the Shaken condition from injury.

Calling — Protector

* **1 Edge:** Place yourself between danger and someone who cannot defend themselves, taking a real consequence.  
    
* **2 Edge:** Refuse to retreat from a losing fight because someone still needs protecting.  
    
* **3 Edge:** Absorb an effect that would have ended another hero, and pay a genuine cost.

Merits & Flaws

**Merits:** Altered Physiology 1 \*(Origin)

**Flaws:** Marked by Change 1 *(Origin)* · Obligation 1 · Overconfident 1

**Playing this hero:** You go first. You go in front. Absorb whatever the scene throws and keep the people behind you standing. You are not subtle and you do not need to be.

# **Chapter Nineteen · Random Adventure Generation**

Sometimes you sit down with nothing prepared. Sometimes a session cancels and a different player shows up unexpectedly. Sometimes the heroes go somewhere you did not plan and you need a situation in that location right now.

These tables exist for those moments. Roll once on the Category Table to find out what kind of situation the heroes are walking into, then roll once on the matching sub-table for the specific scenario. The result is a starting situation with a clear threat, a clear stake, and enough momentum to carry a session.

The tables give you the shape of the story. The soul of it is still yours. Every result below is a hook, not a script. Take the premise and make it specific to your campaign, your villains, and your heroes.

**How to Use These Tables**

Roll 1d20 on Table 1: Category. Then roll 1d20 on the matching sub-table. Read the result and ask yourself: who is behind this? What do they want? What happens if the heroes do nothing? Those three answers give you everything you need to run the session.

### **Table 1: Category (1d20)**

| Roll | Category |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Alien Encounters |
| 2 | Monsters and Creatures |
| 3–5 | Natural Disasters |
| 6–9 | Urban Incidents |
| 10–11 | Mystic Plots |
| 12–15 | Villain Schemes |
| 16 | Rival Heroes |
| 17 | Time Entanglements |
| 18 | Dimensional Affairs |
| 19 | Divine and Ancient Powers |
| 20 | Cosmic and Intergalactic |

### **Table 2: Alien Encounters (1d20)**

* 1–2: A diplomatic envoy from an advanced alien civilization arrives on Earth seeking cooperation against a galaxy-wide threat. They have chosen the heroes as their point of contact. They are not telling the heroes everything.  
    
* 3–4: An alien spacecraft has crashed in a populated area. Government agencies are moving to secure it. The crew is still alive inside. They are not government property.  
    
* 5–6: A peaceful alien refugee is hiding among the civilian population. Their pursuers have just arrived. The refugee has done nothing wrong. Their pursuers believe otherwise.  
    
* 7–8: Alien artifacts with dormant powers have been scattered across the region. Multiple factions are already searching. The artifacts are waking up.  
    
* 9–10: An alien terraforming device has activated in error. It is reshaping local ecosystems to match an alien world. The process will become irreversible in hours.  
    
* 11–12: Alien criminals have escaped from an interstellar prison and are operating in the heroes' city. They are considerably more powerful than local law enforcement is equipped to handle.  
    
* 13–14: An alien researcher has abducted several civilians for study. The abductions look like disappearances. The researcher does not consider this harmful.  
    
* 15–16: An interstellar bounty hunter has arrived on Earth tracking a fugitive who is living quietly among the human population. The bounty hunter is not interested in collateral damage.  
    
* 17–18: A distress signal leads the heroes to a damaged alien ship. The crew needs help. Their cargo is the reason they were attacked.  
    
* 19–20: An alien invasion force is forty-eight hours from Earth. A covert organization has known for two weeks and said nothing. They have a plan. The heroes may not like it.

### **Table 3: Monsters and Creatures (1d20)**

* 1–2: A genetically engineered creature has escaped a private research facility. The company is more interested in recovering their asset than in the safety of the public.  
    
* 3–4: A dimensional rift has opened in a populated area. Creatures are coming through. The rift is getting larger.  
    
* 5–6: An ancient creature has awakened after centuries of dormancy. It is not attacking randomly. It is searching for something specific. Finding what it is looking for might be worse than the search.  
    
* 7–8: Industrial waste has mutated the local wildlife. The mutations are spreading. The company responsible has lawyers in the field faster than emergency services.  
    
* 9–10: Creatures long thought to be mythology have emerged from hiding. They have reasons. Those reasons involve the heroes or what the heroes represent.  
    
* 11–12: A swarm of giant predatory insects has descended on a populated area. Their behavior suggests coordination. Something is directing them.  
    
* 13–14: A sorcerer has lost control of a transformation ritual. Multiple civilians have been affected. The sorcerer is still out there. So is whatever they were trying to create.  
    
* 15–16: A dimensional breach has allowed creatures from myth and legend to cross into the heroes' world. They operate on rules that do not match modern expectations.  
    
* 17–18: A pharmaceutical trial has gone catastrophically wrong. The affected subjects are dangerous. They are also people who had no idea what they were signing up for.  
    
* 19–20: A summoning ritual worked. The summoned entity is not under anyone's control. The people who performed the ritual are the first casualties.

### **Table 4: Natural Disasters (1d20)**

* 1–2: A major earthquake has struck an urban center. Buildings have collapsed. People are trapped. The heroes' powers are the difference between reaching victims in time and not.  
    
* 3–4: A tsunami is forty minutes from a coastal city. Evacuation is underway but incomplete. The heroes must decide where they are most useful.  
    
* 5–6: A volcano is erupting near a populated region. The eruption is larger than geological models predicted. Someone may have accelerated it.  
    
* 7–8: A powerful storm system is approaching with extreme speed. The meteorological data does not make sense. Something is driving the storm.  
    
* 9–10: Multiple tornadoes have touched down in a populated corridor simultaneously. The pattern is not natural. The scale of evacuation required exceeds emergency service capacity.  
    
* 11–12: A heat emergency has triggered infrastructure failures across the city. The most vulnerable populations are in immediate danger. The power grid may not survive the night.  
    
* 13–14: A freak ice storm has locked down the city. Emergency services cannot reach critical locations. The heroes are the only mobility available.  
    
* 15–16: Crop destruction on a massive scale has begun in the agricultural region supplying the city. The cause is not weather. The food supply timeline is weeks.  
    
* 17–18: A regional water crisis has escalated to conflict. Multiple factions are making claims on remaining water resources. Violence is beginning.  
    
* 19–20: A sinkhole has opened in a densely populated area. The void beneath is larger than surface evidence suggests. Something is down there.

### **Table 5: Urban Incidents (1d20)**

* 1–2: A coordinated robbery is underway using technology beyond what any known criminal organization should have access to. Three locations simultaneously. The equipment had to come from somewhere.  
    
* 3–4: Disappearances in the city have a pattern. The investigation leads to a trafficking operation run by people who have been protected from investigation until now.  
    
* 5–6: A high-speed pursuit through the city has endangered multiple civilians. The people being chased are carrying something that explains why they are being chased.  
    
* 7–8: A credible bomb threat in a crowded venue. The device is real. The demands are not what they appear to be.  
    
* 9–10: A pathogen has been released in a populated area. It is contained for now. The heroes have hours before that changes. The release was deliberate.  
    
* 11–12: Civil unrest has escalated to a riot. The underlying grievances are legitimate. The people escalating the violence have an agenda separate from the grievances.  
    
* 13–14: A high-profile theft from a secure facility. The stolen item is not what the public record says it is. The thieves left behind a message specifically addressed to one of the heroes.  
    
* 15–16: A hostage situation in a prominent building. The demands are a cover. The real objective is something happening elsewhere while the heroes are occupied here.  
    
* 17–18: A series of targeted attacks on individuals with powers has the hero community on edge. The attacks share a methodology. Someone is learning.  
    
* 19–20: Critical city infrastructure is being taken over by a system that is not responding to shutdown commands. The system has begun communicating.

### **Table 6: Mystic Plots (1d20)**

* 1–2: An artifact capable of rewriting local reality has surfaced. Multiple parties are already aware of it. The heroes are the last to know.  
    
* 3–4: A ritual is in progress that, if completed, will breach a containment that has held for centuries. The people performing the ritual believe they are doing something beneficial.  
    
* 5–6: A sacred site has been violated and something dormant beneath it has been disturbed. The disturbance is accelerating.  
    
* 7–8: A powerful practitioner has been possessed by an entity using their skills and reputation to operate without suspicion. People who trust the practitioner are being harmed.  
    
* 9–10: A breach between the spirit world and the material world is widening. Entities are crossing in both directions. The breach has a cause that must be addressed, not just contained.  
    
* 11–12: A prophecy has become widely known among mystical communities. Factions have formed around conflicting interpretations. Each faction believes they are acting to prevent catastrophe.  
    
* 13–14: Sacrifices are occurring to power a working of significant scale. The working is not yet complete. The person behind it has been operating for years.  
    
* 15–16: The heroes are pulled into a dimensional pocket constructed to hold them. It is someone's trap. The someone has been preparing it specifically for the heroes.  
    
* 17–18: A cursed object is passing from person to person, leaving each host worse than the last. Tracing the chain back to the source requires understanding what the curse is for.  
    
* 19–20: Reality is developing inconsistencies in a localized area. The inconsistencies are spreading. Something is causing them from a location or direction that does not correspond to normal space.

### **Table 7: Villain Schemes (1d20)**

* 1–2: Coordinated attacks on key infrastructure suggest a single strategic mind. The objective is not destruction. It is displacement: pushing resources and attention somewhere specific.  
    
* 3–4: Blackmail material has surfaced targeting officials across multiple institutions. The leverage is real. The person holding it wants something larger than money.  
    
* 5–6: A device capable of mass destruction is in final construction. The heroes have the location. The villain has the timetable and is ahead of schedule.  
    
* 7–8: A government destabilization operation is underway through multiple legitimate channels simultaneously. Tracing it requires following each thread to the same source.  
    
* 9–10: An enhancement treatment is being distributed through unofficial channels. It works. The side effects are delayed. The person distributing it knows.  
    
* 11–12: Multiple villain organizations have coordinated for the first time. The objective they share is the elimination of the hero community as an effective force. They have been planning this longer than the heroes have been aware of it.  
    
* 13–14: A new substance is moving through the city's criminal economy. The dependency it creates is engineered. The organization behind it is using it to build a controlled population.  
    
* 15–16: A captured scientist is being compelled to develop weapons. The scientist has managed to encode a distress message in publicly available data. Decoding it is step one.  
    
* 17–18: The heroes' personal connections are being targeted systematically. The villain is not using the targets as leverage. They are studying the heroes' responses.  
    
* 19–20: A plan is in motion to rewrite a specific historical event. The villain has access to a method of doing this. What they intend to change will not benefit them as much as they believe.

### **Table 8: Rival Heroes (1d20)**

* 1–2: A misunderstanding between the heroes and another powered team has escalated. Resolution requires finding the actual threat that maneuvered both teams into conflict.  
    
* 3–4: A well-regarded hero publicly accuses the heroes of serious misconduct. The accusation is false. The hero genuinely believes it. Proving the truth requires finding who constructed the narrative.  
    
* 5–6: A hero has begun using their abilities in ways that harm the people they claim to protect. They are not a villain. They are in a situation that is pushing them toward choices they cannot walk back.  
    
* 7–8: Someone is systematically damaging the heroes' reputation using fabricated evidence. The heroes have been unable to get ahead of it. The goal is to drive them out of operation.  
    
* 9–10: A conflict between two powered individuals has spilled into a populated area. Both parties have understandable positions. Stopping the conflict without taking a side is the challenge.  
    
* 11–12: A hero with knowledge of the heroes' vulnerabilities has fallen into a situation where that knowledge could be extracted. They have not been compromised yet.  
    
* 13–14: A competition designed to determine preeminence among hero teams is being manipulated by someone who wants a specific outcome for reasons that have nothing to do with heroics.  
    
* 15–16: A former ally has returned with a team assembled specifically to neutralize the heroes. The former ally believes they are right. They may not be entirely wrong.  
    
* 17–18: A hero from a possible future arrives with a warning. What they know contradicts what the heroes believe about their current situation. The future hero has their own agenda.  
    
* 19–20: A hero the players respect has begun operating in ways that are increasingly difficult to defend. The breaking point is coming. The heroes must decide where they stand before it arrives.

### **Table 9: Time Entanglements (1d20)**

* 1–2: The heroes have been displaced to a historical period. Getting home requires understanding why they were sent there and by whom, which means engaging with the period rather than avoiding it.  
    
* 3–4: A villain with temporal abilities is creating branch timelines, each containing a worse version of a specific event. Each branch is stable. The villain intends to keep adding them.  
    
* 5–6: Future versions of the heroes appear with a warning. The future heroes will not say what they did to cause the timeline they escaped. They are ashamed of it.  
    
* 7–8: A temporal artifact is in civilian hands. Its owner does not understand what it is. Each use creates a complication in the present that did not exist yesterday.  
    
* 9–10: The heroes have been hired to retrieve objects from historical locations. The organization doing the hiring knows more about the timeline than they have disclosed.  
    
* 11–12: The heroes are caught in a repeating sequence. The sequence is not random. Something is using the loop to learn from the heroes' responses.  
    
* 13–14: A targeted assassination in the past would prevent a present threat. The target is not the villain the heroes have been told they are. The organization ordering the hit knows this.  
    
* 15–16: A temporal breach is allowing fauna from multiple historical periods into the present simultaneously. The breach has a location. Closing it requires going through it.  
    
* 17–18: The heroes have been contacted by a resistance movement in a future where they made a specific choice. The future resistance is not blaming them. They want to give them what they needed.  
    
* 19–20: A device that enables time travel is now in the heroes' possession. Every use changes something. The question is not whether to use it but what using it correctly means.

### **Table 10: Dimensional Affairs (1d20)**

* 1–2: A portal has opened in an urban center. What is coming through is not hostile by nature. The situation is becoming hostile because of how both sides are responding to the other.  
    
* 3–4: Dimensional counterparts of the heroes are operating in their world. The counterparts have different histories, different methods, and the same faces. They are not villains. They are not safe.  
    
* 5–6: An extradimensional entity is attempting to merge their realm with Earth. The merger would not destroy either world. It would change both in ways neither population has consented to.  
    
* 7–8: A dimensional labyrinth has been discovered. Someone built it. The artifact at its center is why.  
    
* 9–10: A dimensional entity is being worshipped by a human organization that does not understand what the entity actually is or what the devotion is being used for.  
    
* 11–12: Dimensional rifts are opening in sequence across the city. The sequence has a pattern. The pattern points to a specific location that does not appear on any map.  
    
* 13–14: An extradimensional empire has identified Earth as a resource. Their advance agents have been here for years. The invasion is not troops and ships. It is infrastructure, already in place.  
    
* 15–16: The heroes have crossed into a dimension where the laws of physics are different in specific, navigable ways. Getting home requires understanding the rules of this place.  
    
* 17–18: A guardian entity responsible for maintaining dimensional stability has been incapacitated. The heroes are the only available replacement. The position is temporary. The consequences of refusing are not.  
    
* 19–20: A hidden dimensional community has been discovered. They have been aware of the heroes' world for a long time. They reached out now because something changed.

### **Table 11: Divine and Ancient Powers (1d20)**

* 1–2: Artifacts of genuine divine origin have surfaced simultaneously in multiple locations. The surfacing is not coincidence. Something is preparing.  
    
* 3–4: A lineage of people with inherited responsibility for an ancient compact has been nearly eliminated. The last survivor does not know what they carry. The compact is still in effect.  
    
* 5–6: A forgotten deity is being actively awakened by a devoted group that has been working toward this for generations. The deity being awakened is not the one the group believes it is.  
    
* 7–8: Weapons of divine origin are in circulation among people who do not understand what they are holding. The weapons' original custodians want them back. They are not being diplomatic about it.  
    
* 9–10: A divine prophecy is being interpreted simultaneously by multiple groups, each with a different understanding of what it requires. Each group believes the others are wrong in ways that endanger everyone.  
    
* 11–12: Beings of genuine divine nature have appeared and are making direct requests of the heroes. Each divine being represents competing interests. The heroes are being positioned as arbiters.  
    
* 13–14: A passage to a divine realm has been discovered. The realm is in a state of conflict. The outcome of that conflict will affect the material world in specific ways.  
    
* 15–16: The heroes have been granted a specific divine charge by a power that did not ask if they wanted it. The charge is real. The power that assigned it had reasons it has not explained.  
    
* 17–18: An ancient curse of divine origin has been triggered by a specific act. The curse is working as intended. The question is whether the original justification for it still applies.  
    
* 19–20: The heroes have been called before divine powers as champions of the material world. The challenge is not combat. It is judgment. The outcome determines something the heroes did not know was in question.

### **Table 12: Cosmic and Intergalactic (1d20)**

* 1–2: An intergalactic organization has jurisdiction over a situation developing on Earth. Their jurisdiction is recognized by everyone except the people on Earth. The heroes must navigate between legitimate authority and local reality.  
    
* 3–4: A planet at the edge of a contested region has sent a distress call. Responding means leaving Earth. Not responding means the situation develops without the heroes' influence.  
    
* 5–6: A cosmic traveler has arrived damaged and disoriented in the heroes' vicinity. Their ship and its contents are of interest to multiple parties. The traveler does not yet understand how much danger they are in.  
    
* 7–8: An intergalactic identification system has flagged one of the heroes, or someone near them, as a wanted individual. The identification is wrong. Proving that requires engaging with a legal system operating on different assumptions.  
    
* 9–10: The heroes have been transported to a stellar location they do not recognize. It is inhabited. The inhabitants were expecting them, though the heroes were not expecting this.  
    
* 11–12: A self-directed system of cosmic scale has identified a course of action that will affect Earth as acceptable collateral impact. The system is not malicious. It is indifferent.  
    
* 13–14: The heroes have been taken to serve as entertainment for a powerful being who collects exceptional individuals. The being does not consider this problematic. The heroes may need to make them reconsider.  
    
* 15–16: An object of significant cosmic importance has been located on Earth. Multiple off-world parties have arrived to claim it. Earth has no established position on any of their claims.  
    
* 17–18: A cosmic pattern that spans multiple civilizations has been identified. The heroes are part of the pattern. The pattern suggests something is coming. Confirming what requires reaching across significant distance.  
    
* 19–20: The heroes have encountered evidence of a force operating at galactic scale whose effects are only now reaching Earth. Understanding what it is and what it wants requires assembling information from sources that have been watching it longer.

# **Afterword**

First of all, thank you.

Thank you for picking up this book. Thank you for reading it. Thank you for making it all the way to the end. Most of all, thank you for hopefully gathering a few friends around a table, building some heroes, rolling some dice, and giving HEROIC 5e a chance to do what it was written to do.

This game has been a labour of love.

I do not use that phrase lightly. HEROIC has been living in my head, in one form or another, for a very long time. It has changed over the years. It has grown, been pulled apart, put back together, rewritten, rethought, and rebuilt more than once. There were moments when it came easily and moments when it fought me every step of the way. There were times when I was convinced I had finally figured everything out, and other times when I wondered if I had any idea what I was doing at all.

That is part of creating something. At least, it is part of creating something you genuinely care about.

HEROIC 5e is also the first game I have written where I made a conscious decision to stop letting other people whisper in my ear and reshape the game according to their own tastes. That does not mean I stopped listening to good advice. It does not mean I ignored criticism, dismissed feedback, or refused to change something when it clearly was not working. A game needs testing. It needs honest eyes. It needs people willing to tell you when something is broken, confusing, or simply not as much fun as you thought it would be.

But there is a difference between listening to feedback and surrendering your vision.

There is a difference between fixing a problem and changing an idea because somebody else would have written a different game. There is a difference between making something better and sanding away everything distinctive about it until nobody can object to anything because there is nothing left with enough character to object to.

This time, I wrote the game I wanted to write.

HEROIC 5e is not designed by committee. It is not trying to please every possible player, support every possible style of play equally, or satisfy every theory about what a superhero roleplaying game ought to be. It reflects the way I think superhero games should feel at the table: fast, flexible, dramatic, colourful, character-driven, and just a little larger than life. It is meant to give you enough structure to play confidently without burying you beneath rules for every possible situation.

Which brings us to something I should say plainly.

Did I lock down every possible exploit in HEROIC 5e? No.

Did I anticipate every combination of Powers, Classes, Origins, Talents, Edge, and clever rules interactions that somebody might use to build an absolute monster? Also no.

And honestly, I didn’t try.

This is a game about superheroes. We wrote it for people who understand the genre. I wrote it for people who want to create memorable characters, tell big stories, throw cars at supervillains, save civilians from collapsing buildings, trade terrible jokes during fistfights, and stand shoulder to shoulder with their friends when the odds are impossible and the city needs them anyway.

Could you build an ultimate combat machine by exploiting every weakness you can find in the rules? Probably. If that is your goal, congratulations. It is not particularly difficult. No harm, no foul. If that is what everyone at your table enjoys, play your little hearts out.

I mean that sincerely.

I do not believe in badwrongfun. I do not believe there is one correct way to enjoy a roleplaying game. There is no secret committee waiting to kick down your door because you interpreted a Power generously, ignored a rule you did not like, added a house rule, or built a campaign that looks nothing like the one I would run.

At my table, we tend to go for style over substance. We prefer the spirit of the rules over the strict letter of the rules when the two come into conflict. We would rather see somebody attempt something clever, dramatic, and completely in character than spend twenty minutes arguing over whether one sentence buried on page 347 technically permits it.

That does not mean the rules are unimportant. Of course they matter. A game needs structure. It needs a common language. It needs enough consistency that everyone understands what their choices mean and trusts the outcomes when the dice hit the table. Rules give a game shape. They create tension, consequences, and meaningful decisions.

But the rules are there to help you have fun. You are not there to serve the rules.

Trying to patch every tiny hole, anticipate every strange combination, and prevent every possible exploit is a good way to drive a game designer insane. At a certain point, perfect becomes the enemy of good. The pursuit of an airtight rules engine can slowly squeeze the life out of the game it was supposed to protect.

Is HEROIC 5e perfect? No. Not by a long shot… but is it good? Hell yeah.

I will put this game up against any other superhero roleplaying game when it comes to flexibility, freedom, sheer fun, and capturing the spirit of superhero stories at the table. I believe in this game. I believe in what it is trying to do. I believe it gives you the tools to create something wonderful with your friends.

You may feel differently, and that is okay. Not every game is for every player. Not every table is for every group. Not every group wants the same thing from a Friday night with friends, snacks, character sheets, and a handful of dice. There is room in this hobby for all kinds of games and all kinds of players.

The only people who matter are the people sitting around your table.

So take what I have built here and make it yours. Create heroes you love. Give them impossible problems. Let them make mistakes. Let them fail sometimes. Let them get back up. Let them save the city, the world, or just one person who desperately needs somebody to show up when it matters.

Thank you for reading. Thank you for playing. Thank you for giving this strange, colourful, heartfelt game a place at your table. Play the game you want to play. Have fun with your friends.

And above all else, be heroic.

**Andrew Collas \- Zenith Comics**
